claims.title: External conditions alone cannot explain complex coadaptations
claims.chapter: Introduction
claims.statement: Complex adaptations and coadaptations between organisms, such as the woodpecker's feeding structures or the misseltoe's dependence on particular trees, birds and insects, cannot be accounted for by the direct effects of external conditions such as climate and food.

claims.title: Overproduction plus slight profitable variation leads to natural selection
claims.chapter: Introduction
claims.statement: Because more individuals of each species are born than can survive, there is a recurring struggle for existence, so any individual that varies even slightly in a way profitable to itself has a better chance of surviving and thus of being naturally selected.

claims.title: Natural selection causes extinction of less improved forms and divergence
claims.chapter: Introduction
claims.statement: Natural selection almost inevitably causes much extinction of less improved forms of life and produces divergence of character.

claims.title: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species
claims.chapter: Introduction
claims.statement: Species are not independently created and immutable; species of the same genus are lineal descendants of some other, generally extinct, species, just as varieties of one species descend from that species.

claims.title: Natural selection is the main but not exclusive means of modification
claims.chapter: Introduction
claims.statement: Natural selection has been the main, but not the only, cause of the modification of species.

claims.title: Domesticated forms vary more among individuals than wild species do
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Individuals of the same variety of long-cultivated plants and domesticated animals generally differ much more from each other than individuals of any one species or variety in nature.

claims.title: Greater domestic variability is caused by changed, less uniform conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: The greater variability of domestic productions is due to their being raised under conditions of life less uniform than, and somewhat different from, those of their parent species in nature.

claims.title: Variability arises mainly from effects on reproductive elements before conception
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: The most frequent cause of variability is that the male and female reproductive elements have been affected by the conditions of life before conception, the reproductive system being more sensitive to changed conditions than any other part of the organisation.

claims.title: Inherited effects of use and disuse modify domestic animals
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Habitual use and disuse of parts produce inherited changes in domestic animals; for example, domestic ducks have lighter wing bones and heavier leg bones relative to the skeleton than wild ducks because they fly less and walk more.

claims.title: Selecting one trait unconsciously modifies other correlated parts
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Because of laws of correlation of growth, when man selects for and augments any peculiarity, he almost certainly also modifies other parts of the structure without intending to.

claims.title: Inherited peculiarities appear in offspring at the age they appeared in parent
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: A peculiarity tends to appear in the offspring at the same period of life at which it first appeared in the parent, though sometimes earlier.

claims.title: Domestic races differ like congeneric species, but usually less
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Apart from their lesser uniformity, their often monstrous development of one part, and their fertility when crossed, domestic races of a species differ from each other in the same manner as closely allied species of a genus in nature, though in most cases to a lesser degree.

claims.title: Any wild species domesticated as long would vary as much as existing domestics
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Domesticated species were not chosen for an unusual inherent tendency to vary; any comparable set of wild animals and plants, bred under domestication for as many generations, would on average vary as much as the parent species of existing domesticated productions have.

claims.title: Domestic dogs descend from several wild species
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Domestic dogs have probably descended from several distinct wild species rather than from a single one.

claims.title: All domestic pigeon breeds descend from the rock-pigeon
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: All domestic pigeon breeds, however different, have descended from the rock-pigeon (Columba livia) and its geographical sub-species, not from several aboriginal wild stocks.

claims.title: Domestic breeds arise mainly by man's accumulation of successive variations
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Domestic breeds were not produced suddenly in their present useful form; their key cause is man's accumulative selection, nature supplying successive variations and man adding them up in directions useful to him.

claims.title: Races differ most in the parts man selects
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Continued selection of slight variations in one part valued by man, such as leaves, flowers or fruit, produces races that differ from each other chiefly in that part, while other parts differ only slightly.

claims.title: Unconscious selection over centuries modifies any breed
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Unconscious selection, in which people simply breed from their best animals without aiming to change the breed, would over centuries improve and modify any breed, as methodical breeders have done within their lifetimes.

claims.title: Slow accumulated change hides the wild parents of old cultivated plants
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Because a large amount of change has been slowly and unconsciously accumulated in long-cultivated plants, in many cases their wild parent-stocks can no longer be recognised.

claims.title: Domestic races differ greatly externally but little internally
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Because man can select mainly on externally visible deviations, domestic races differ greatly in external characters and relatively slightly in internal parts or organs.

claims.title: Keeping large numbers of individuals favours successful selection
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Because useful variations appear only occasionally, keeping a large number of individuals greatly increases the chance of useful variations appearing and is of the highest importance to success in selection.

claims.title: Accumulative selection is the predominant cause of change in domestic races
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication
claims.statement: Among the causes of change in domestic races, including conditions of life, use and disuse, correlation and crossing, the accumulative action of selection, whether methodical or unconscious, is by far the predominant power.

claims.title: Individual differences supply the material for natural selection
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: The slight individual differences among members of a species provide the materials that natural selection accumulates, in the same way that man accumulates individual differences in domestic productions.

claims.title: Polymorphic genera vary in traits of no use, unfixed by selection
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: In polymorphic genera such as Rubus, Rosa and Hieracium, the inordinate variation concerns structures that are of no service or disservice to the species and so have not been seized on and made definite by natural selection.

claims.title: Doubtful forms of mobile animals are rare within a country but common between areas
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: Among highly locomotive animals that unite for each birth, doubtful forms ranked as species by some and varieties by others are rarely found within the same country but are common in separated areas.

claims.title: No clear line separates species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: No clear line of demarcation exists between species and sub-species, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences; they blend into one another in an insensible series.

claims.title: Natural selection turns slight varieties into more distinct ones and species
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: Individual differences lead to slight varieties, these to more distinct and permanent varieties, then to sub-species and species, the passage being mainly due to natural selection accumulating structural differences in definite directions, so that a well-marked variety is an incipient species.

claims.title: The term species is arbitrary and not essentially different from variety
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: The term species is given arbitrarily, for convenience, to a set of closely resembling individuals and does not differ essentially from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.

claims.title: Dominant species, widespread and abundant, produce the most varieties
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: The dominant species, those that range widely over the world, are most diffused in their own country and are most numerous in individuals, most often produce well-marked varieties.

claims.title: Species of larger genera more often present varieties
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: Within a country, a larger proportion of the species in larger genera present varieties than of the species in smaller genera, and those that vary have on average more varieties.

claims.title: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: Over geological time small genera have often increased greatly in number of species, and large genera have often reached a maximum, declined and disappeared.

claims.title: Where many species of a genus have formed, many are still forming
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: On the view that species are strongly marked varieties, where many species of a genus have been formed, on average many new species should still be forming.

claims.title: Species in large genera differ from one another by small amounts
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: In large genera the amount of difference between species is often exceedingly small, so that their species resemble varieties more than do species of small genera.

claims.title: Species of large genera cluster unequally around certain species
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: Species of large genera are not equally distinct from one another but are clustered in little groups around certain other species, as varieties are clustered around their parent species.

claims.title: Species very closely allied to others have restricted ranges, like varieties
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: Species that are very closely allied to other species, and so resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges, similar to the restricted ranges of acknowledged varieties.

claims.title: Analogies between species of large genera and varieties support descent
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: The analogies between species of large genera and varieties (more varieties, small and unequal differences, restricted ranges) are understandable if species once existed as varieties, and inexplicable if each species was independently created.

claims.title: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature
claims.statement: Because the dominant species of larger genera vary most and varieties become new species, larger genera tend to become larger, and dominant forms tend to become more dominant by leaving many modified, dominant descendants.

claims.title: Overproduction makes a struggle for existence inevitable
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: Because all organisms tend to increase at a high (geometrical) rate, more individuals are produced than can survive, so every species must undergo a struggle for existence with members of its own species, with other species, or with physical conditions.

claims.title: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: The extraordinarily rapid increase and wide spread of introduced (naturalised) animals and plants in new countries is explained by geometrical increase under favourable conditions with reduced mortality, not by any rise in their fertility.

claims.title: Average abundance depends only indirectly on fecundity
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: The average number of individuals of an animal or plant species depends only indirectly on how many eggs or seeds it produces; high fecundity mainly compensates for heavy destruction, usually early in life.

claims.title: Predation, more often than food supply, sets average numbers
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: Although food sets the upper limit to a species' increase, very often it is destruction by predators rather than food supply that determines the species' average numbers.

claims.title: Periodic extreme cold or drought is the most effective check
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodic seasons of extreme cold or drought are the most effective of all checks on increase.

claims.title: Competitors decline poleward, so climate acts more directly there
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: The number of species, and therefore of competitors, decreases going northward, so that going north or up a mountain one more often finds stunted forms caused by the direct harmful action of climate than going south or downhill.

claims.title: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring competitors
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring their competitors and enemies; for example, many garden plants that tolerate the local climate never become naturalised because they cannot compete with native plants or resist native animals.

claims.title: Many species need a large local stock to persist
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: In many cases a large number of individuals of a species, relative to the number of its enemies, is necessary for the species to survive, which explains why rare plants can be very abundant in the few spots where they occur.

claims.title: Balanced struggles keep communities uniform over long periods
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: Although competition between organisms constantly recurs with shifting outcomes, the opposing forces are so finely balanced that community composition stays roughly the same for long periods, even though a trifling change could tip the balance toward one organism.

claims.title: Chains of interaction link distant species' abundances
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: Very different organisms are linked by chains of interaction, so that the abundance of one species can determine the frequency of another through intermediate species; for example, cats may control the frequency of red clover and heartsease by way of field-mice and humble-bees.

claims.title: Struggle is most severe between members of the same species
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: The struggle for existence is almost always most severe between individuals of the same species, because they live in the same places, need the same food and face the same dangers; between varieties of a species it is nearly as severe.

claims.title: Congeners compete more severely than species of different genera
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: Because species of the same genus are usually similar in habits and constitution and always in structure, competition between them is generally more severe than between species of different genera.

claims.title: Each organism's structure is shaped by its relations to other organisms
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: The structure of every organism is related, in essential but often hidden ways, to the structure of the other organisms with which it competes, from which it must escape, or on which it preys.

claims.title: Few species reach range edges where climate alone kills them
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence
claims.statement: Only a few plants or animals extend their ranges so far that they are destroyed by the severity of climate alone; competition continues everywhere except at the extreme limits of life.

claims.title: Natural selection preserves favourable and destroys injurious variations
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Because more individuals are born than can survive, individuals with any advantage, however slight, have the best chance of surviving and reproducing, while injurious variations are eliminated; this preservation of favourable and rejection of injurious variations is natural selection.

claims.title: Neutral variations escape selection and remain fluctuating
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Variations that are neither useful nor harmful are not acted on by natural selection and stay variable, which may explain the variability of so-called polymorphic species.

claims.title: No native biota is so well adapted that it cannot be improved
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: No country's native inhabitants are so perfectly adapted that none could be improved, as shown by introduced species having established firmly in every country.

claims.title: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Seemingly trivial characters such as colour can be shaped by natural selection; colours that match the background, as in green leaf-eating insects and heather-coloured grouse, protect their bearers from predators that hunt by sight.

claims.title: Natural selection can modify organisms at any age
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Because variations arising at a particular life stage tend to be inherited at the same stage, natural selection can modify organisms at any age, for instance adapting larvae independently of adults.

claims.title: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Fighting between males for females is perhaps most severe in polygamous animals, and the males of such species are the most often equipped with special weapons.

claims.title: Female choice over many generations can produce male ornaments
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Female birds, by choosing the most melodious or beautiful males over thousands of generations, can produce a marked change in male song or plumage.

claims.title: Sex differences in species with shared habits are mainly sexually selected
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: When males and females of a species share the same general habits of life but differ in structure, colour or ornament, those differences were mainly caused by sexual selection, although not all such differences are.

claims.title: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: A flower and a bee can slowly become modified and adapted to each other, at the same time or one after the other, by the continued preservation of individuals with mutually favourable slight differences in structure.

claims.title: Natural selection works only by accumulating very small modifications
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Natural selection acts only by preserving and accumulating very small inherited modifications, each profitable to its bearer, and so excludes continued creation of new organisms or large sudden changes of structure.

claims.title: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: In animals and plants, crosses between different varieties or between different strains of the same variety give vigour and fertility to the offspring, while close interbreeding reduces vigour and fertility.

claims.title: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: It is a general law of nature that no organism fertilises itself for an unlimited number of generations; an occasional cross with another individual, perhaps at long intervals, is indispensable, even in hermaphrodites.

claims.title: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Trees, across all plant orders, have separate male and female flowers more often than other plants do, which helps pollen move between trees (though Hooker reported the rule fails in Australia).

claims.title: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: A large number of individuals favours natural selection because it gives a better chance for profitable variations to arise within a given period, compensating for lower variability in each individual.

claims.title: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Although small isolated areas can favour new species, modification is generally faster on large areas, and forms produced there, having beaten many competitors, spread most widely and give rise to the most new varieties and species.

claims.title: Freshwater biotas evolve and go extinct more slowly, keeping relict forms
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Because all freshwater basins together form a small area, competition among freshwater organisms has been less severe, so new forms have arisen more slowly and old forms have been exterminated more slowly there, which is why fresh water holds ancient and anomalous forms.

claims.title: Natural selection acts slowly, intermittently and on few species at a time
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Natural selection always acts very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of a region at the same time.

claims.title: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Because every area is already fully stocked, as a favoured form increases in number the less favoured forms decrease and become rare, and rarity precedes extinction.

claims.title: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Because the most closely related forms compete most severely, each new variety or species, while forming, presses hardest on its nearest relatives and tends to exterminate them.

claims.title: Divergence of character maximises the life an area supports
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: The greatest amount of life can be supported in an area by great diversification of structure among its inhabitants.

claims.title: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Where organisms compete most closely, as on a small patch of ground, the advantages of diversification mean that the coexisting inhabitants generally belong to different genera and orders.

claims.title: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Floras gain far more new genera than new species from naturalised plants, relative to the native numbers of genera and species, so naturalised plants tend to differ from the natives at the genus level.

claims.title: Intermediate forms and parent species tend to go extinct
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: In a fully stocked country, improved descendants of a species tend to supplant their predecessors, so the intermediate forms between earlier and later states, and the original parent species itself, generally tend to become extinct.

claims.title: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Extinct species, though generally in the same orders, families or genera as living ones, are often somewhat intermediate in character between existing groups, because they lived when the branching lines of descent had diverged less.

claims.title: Differences between varieties grow into differences between species and genera
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Through natural selection and divergence of character, the small differences between varieties of a species steadily increase until they equal the larger differences between species of the same genus, or even between genera.

claims.title: Very few species of past periods have living descendants
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection
claims.statement: Like a tree in which only a few early twigs grew into surviving branches, very few of the species that lived in long-past geological periods now have living modified descendants, and many whole orders, families and genera have died out entirely.

claims.title: Variability is induced by changed conditions acting on the reproductive system
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Deviations of structure arise in some way from the conditions of life to which parents and their ancestors have been exposed over several generations, acting chiefly by disturbing the reproductive system; hence variability is greater under domestication or cultivation than in nature.

claims.title: Direct effects of climate and food on organisms are small
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: The direct effect of differences in climate, food and similar conditions on an organism's structure is very small in animals and perhaps somewhat larger in plants, and cannot account for the complex co-adaptations between organisms.

claims.title: Flightlessness of birds on predator-free oceanic islands is caused by disuse
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: The nearly wingless condition of several birds living on oceanic islands that lack beasts of prey has been caused by disuse of the wings.

claims.title: Wingless Madeira beetles result mainly from selection against being blown to sea
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: The high proportion of flightless beetles on windswept islands such as Madeira is mainly due to natural selection favouring individuals that fly least and so avoid being blown out to sea, probably combined with disuse.

claims.title: Blindness in cave animals results from disuse
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Because useless eyes are unlikely to be harmful in total darkness, the loss of eyes in most cave-dwelling animals is due to disuse alone rather than to natural selection.

claims.title: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Blind cave animals of America should be most closely allied to other inhabitants of America, and those of Europe to inhabitants of Europe, rather than the cave faunas of the two continents being specially similar to each other.

claims.title: Species ranges are limited by competition as much as by climate
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Species in nature are limited in their geographic ranges by competition with other organisms at least as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.

claims.title: Homologous parts tend to vary together
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Parts of the body that are homologous and alike early in embryonic development, such as left and right sides or fore and hind limbs, tend to vary in a correlated way.

claims.title: Taxonomically important characters may be useless products of correlated growth
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Structural differences that systematists treat as highly important, such as differences between outer and inner seeds of Umbelliferae, may arise entirely from unknown laws of correlated growth without being of any use to the species.

claims.title: Natural selection reduces superfluous parts without compensatory enlargement
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Natural selection will in the long run reduce any part of the organisation once it becomes superfluous, saving nutriment, without necessarily causing another part to enlarge; and it can enlarge an organ without requiring reduction of an adjoining part.

claims.title: Parts repeated many times in an individual are variable in number
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: When a part or organ is repeated many times in one individual, such as snake vertebrae or stamens of polyandrous flowers, its number is variable, whereas parts present in small numbers are constant in number.

claims.title: Parts unusually developed relative to congeners are highly variable
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: A part developed to an extraordinary degree or in an extraordinary manner in one species, compared with the same part in closely allied species, tends to be highly variable within that species; the rule does not apply when the unusual part is shared by a whole group.

claims.title: Specific characters are more variable than generic characters
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Characters that distinguish species within a genus are more variable within species than characters shared by all species of the genus, because the former have varied since the species branched from a common progenitor.

claims.title: Congeners differ more in secondary sexual characters than in other parts
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Secondary sexual characters are highly variable, and species of the same group differ from one another more in their secondary sexual characters than in other parts of their organisation.

claims.title: Long-lost characters reappear through a tendency transmitted each generation
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: When a character lost in a breed reappears after many generations, the cause is a tendency to produce that character transmitted in every generation which at last prevails under favourable conditions, not a sudden resemblance to a distant ancestor.

claims.title: Horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra descend from a striped common ancestor
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: The domestic horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra are descended from a common ancestor that was striped like a zebra, which explains the occasional appearance of stripes in horses, asses and their hybrids.

claims.title: Related species with shared constitution produce analogous variations
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation
claims.statement: Species that inherit nearly the same constitution from a common parent and are exposed to similar influences tend to produce analogous variations, so that a variety of one species may resemble another species of the same genus.

claims.title: Formation of a new form exterminates its parent and transitional varieties
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Because each new form tends in a fully stocked country to supplant and exterminate its less improved parent and other competing forms, the parent and all transitional varieties are generally exterminated by the process that forms the new species.

claims.title: Zones of overlap between representative species are narrow
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Where closely allied or representative species replace each other over a continuous area, the neutral territory between them is generally narrow compared with the territory occupied by each, and species become somewhat abruptly rarer towards their range limits.

claims.title: Intermediate varieties are numerically rarer than the forms they connect
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Where varieties intermediate between two other forms occur in nature, they are generally much rarer numerically than the forms they connect, because they inhabit narrower intermediate zones.

claims.title: Common forms improve faster and supplant rare intermediate forms
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Forms existing in larger numbers have a better chance in any given period of presenting favourable variations for natural selection, so they are improved faster and supplant the less numerous intermediate varieties between them.

claims.title: Bat flight arose from an apparatus for gliding
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Bats were derived from gliding animals, and the wing membrane extending to the tail and hind legs in some bats is a trace of an apparatus originally built for gliding rather than flight.

claims.title: Habits can change without corresponding change of structure
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Species sometimes have habits that do not match their structure, such as upland geese with webbed feet that rarely enter water or ground-living woodpeckers, showing that habits can change before structure changes.

claims.title: Complex eyes can be built by selection through graded useful steps
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Natural selection could have converted a simple optic nerve coated with pigment and covered by transparent membrane into a highly perfect eye through a series of graded steps, each useful to its possessor, as shown by the graduated diversity of eyes in living crustaceans.

claims.title: Theory fails if a complex organ could not arise by slight steps
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: If any complex organ were shown to exist that could not possibly have been formed by numerous, successive, slight modifications, the theory of natural selection would break down; no such case is known.

claims.title: Lung-bearing vertebrates descend from an ancestor with a swimbladder
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: All vertebrates with true lungs have descended from an ancient ancestor that had a swimbladder used for flotation, which natural selection converted into a lung.

claims.title: Selection can independently produce similar organs in distantly related beings
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Natural selection, acting on analogous variations, has sometimes modified parts in nearly the same way in two distantly related organisms, as with electric organs in unrelated fishes, so that similar organs need not be inherited from a common ancestor.

claims.title: Few organs lack any known transitional grade
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Despite the small proportion of living and known forms relative to extinct and unknown ones, it is rare to find an organ toward which no transitional grade is known to lead.

claims.title: Most of an organism's structure is due to inheritance, not current use
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: The chief part of each organism's structure is simply inherited, so that many structures, such as the shared bones of monkey arm, horse leg, bat wing and seal flipper, have no direct relation to the species' present habits of life.

claims.title: No structure exists solely for the good of another species
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Natural selection cannot produce any structure in one species exclusively for the good of another species, though it can produce structures that harm other species; proof of such a structure would refute the theory.

claims.title: Selection makes organisms only as perfect as their local competitors
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Natural selection only makes each organism as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of its own country, so endemic species of a region such as New Zealand may yield to species introduced from a larger region.

claims.title: Traits from laws of growth are later co-opted by descendants
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: Many modifications arose wholly from laws of growth and were at first of no advantage to a species, but were later taken advantage of by its further modified descendants, as skull sutures that arose in egg-laying animals were later used in mammalian birth.

claims.title: Nature makes no leaps when past as well as present forms are included
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: The rule that nature makes no leaps is not strictly true of living organisms alone, but if all past organisms are included it must be strictly true.

claims.title: Unity of type is explained by unity of descent
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory
claims.statement: The fundamental agreement in structure among organisms of the same class, independent of their habits of life, is explained by their common descent.

claims.title: Instincts arise mainly by selection of accidental variations, not inherited habit
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: Complex instincts originate chiefly through natural selection preserving and accumulating slight accidental variations of instinct; the inherited effects of habit play only a subordinate role.

claims.title: Complex instincts are reached by gradations visible in related species
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: Complex instincts are built up by slow, gradual steps, so gradations leading to them should be found among the instincts of related species in collateral lines of descent; instincts, like bodily organs, do not change by leaps.

claims.title: No instinct exists for the exclusive good of another species
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: No animal performs an instinctive action solely for the benefit of another species, although each species takes advantage of the instincts of others.

claims.title: Instincts vary within species in a state of nature
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: Instincts vary within species under natural conditions, for example the migratory instinct varies in extent and direction and may be lost entirely, and nest construction varies between regions.

claims.title: Fear of man is acquired slowly by animals exposed to human persecution
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: Fear of humans is slowly acquired by animal populations persecuted by man, so animals on uninhabited islands are tame and heavily hunted large birds are wilder than small ones.

claims.title: Domestic instincts arise from habit and from human selection of chance variations
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: Under domestication new instincts have been acquired and natural instincts lost partly through inherited habit and partly through human selection, methodical or unconscious, of chance mental peculiarities, usually with both acting together.

claims.title: Cuckoo brood parasitism evolved from occasional laying in other birds’ nests
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: The brood-parasitic instinct of the European cuckoo was generated by natural selection from an ancestor that built its own nest but occasionally laid eggs in other birds’ nests, where the fostered young fared better.

claims.title: Slave-making in ants arose from capturing pupae as food
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: The slave-making instinct of ants arose when pupae of other species, originally collected as food, were reared and proved useful as workers, and natural selection strengthened this habit until some species became wholly dependent on slaves.

claims.title: Hive-bee comb building evolved by gradual modification of simpler bee instincts
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: The cell-making instinct of the hive-bee was acquired through natural selection by slight successive modifications of simpler instincts, of the kind seen in a graded series from humble-bees through Melipona to the hive-bee.

claims.title: Hive-bee cells form by bees sweeping equal spheres and building at intersections
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: Hexagonal hive-bee cells result from many bees standing at equal distances from one another, each excavating equal spherical hollows, and building up or leaving unexcavated the planes where these spheres would intersect.

claims.title: The hive-bee comb is maximally economical of wax
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: The comb of the hive-bee is absolutely perfect in economising wax, so natural selection, driven by the saving of wax, could carry comb architecture no further.

claims.title: Selection on the family explains traits of sterile social-insect workers
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: Traits of sterile workers in social insects can evolve because selection acts on the family: fertile parents whose colonies produce sterile members with a useful modification flourish and transmit the tendency to produce such members.

claims.title: Neuter insects of one nest should show graded structural differences
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: If worker modifications spread gradually through selection of fertile parents, sterile workers of the same species in the same nest should sometimes show gradations of structure, and such gradations are in fact often found.

claims.title: Discrete worker castes arose by selection eliminating intermediate forms
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: Distinct castes of sterile workers in one nest arose when a graduated series of workers was first formed and then selection on the fertile parents favoured production of the most useful extreme forms until intermediates were no longer produced.

claims.title: Allied species in distant regions retain nearly the same instincts
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct
claims.statement: Closely allied but distinct species living in distant parts of the world under different conditions often retain nearly the same instincts, which is explained by inheritance from a common ancestor.

claims.title: Sterility of first crosses differs from sterility of hybrids
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: The sterility of first crosses between pure species, whose reproductive organs are perfect, is a different phenomenon from the sterility of their hybrids, whose reproductive organs are functionally impotent.

claims.title: Close interbreeding lowers fertility while occasional crossing raises it
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: Close interbreeding lessens fertility, while an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases it; this explains much of the declining fertility of hybrids kept for successive generations.

claims.title: Hybrid sterility can be removed under domestication
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: Because many domestic animals are believed to descend from two or more distinct species that are now fully fertile together, sterility between species is not indelible but can be removed by domestication.

claims.title: Some sterility in crosses between species is very general but not universal
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: Some degree of sterility in first crosses between species and in their hybrids is an extremely general result, but it is not absolutely universal.

claims.title: Difficulty of first cross and sterility of hybrids correspond only loosely
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: Species that are hard to cross generally produce very sterile hybrids, but the correspondence between the difficulty of a first cross and the sterility of the resulting hybrids is by no means strict.

claims.title: Cross fertility is largely governed by systematic affinity
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: The fertility of first crosses between species and of their hybrids is largely, though not strictly, governed by systematic affinity, so that species of distinct families never produce hybrids while closely allied species generally cross easily.

claims.title: Reciprocal crosses between the same two species often differ greatly in success
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: The ease of crossing two species often differs greatly depending on which species is the father and which the mother, showing that crossing capacity depends on imperceptible differences confined to the reproductive system.

claims.title: Cross sterility is incidental on reproductive differences, not specially endowed
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: The sterility of first crosses and of hybrids is not a quality specially endowed to keep species distinct but is incidental on unknown differences, chiefly in the reproductive systems, of the species crossed.

claims.title: Early embryo death is a frequent cause of sterility in first crosses
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: A very frequent cause of sterility in first crosses between species is the early death of the embryo, which may be exposed to unsuitable conditions within the mother or the egg or seed.

claims.title: Hybrid sterility resembles sterility caused by unnatural conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: The sterility of hybrids closely resembles the sterility induced in pure species by unnatural conditions of life: in both cases the reproductive system is disturbed independently of general health, by disturbed conditions in one case and by two organisations compounded into one in the other.

claims.title: Slight changes of conditions and slight crosses both increase vigour and fertility
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: Slight changes in conditions of life benefit organisms, and crosses between slightly different members of the same species give vigour and fertility to offspring, whereas greater changes and wider crosses tend to cause sterility.

claims.title: Fertility of crossed varieties is not universal nor a species criterion
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: The fertility of varieties when crossed is very general but cannot be shown to be universal, so it does not form a fundamental distinction between varieties and species; some varieties, such as certain maize and Verbascum varieties, are partly sterile together.

claims.title: Hybrids vary little in the first generation but greatly in later generations
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: Hybrids are only slightly variable in the first generation but extremely variable in succeeding generations, because the reproductive system of the hybrids themselves is disturbed.

claims.title: Apart from fertility, offspring of crossed species and crossed varieties are alike
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: Apart from fertility, the offspring of crossed species and of crossed varieties are closely similar in their variability, prepotency, reversion and resemblance to their parents.

claims.title: No fundamental distinction exists between species and varieties
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism
claims.statement: The facts of hybridism do not oppose, and rather support, the view that there is no fundamental distinction between species and varieties.

claims.title: Extinct intermediates connect each species to a common progenitor, not to each other
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: The extinct intermediate forms required by descent with modification link each species to a common, usually unknown, progenitor, and that progenitor will generally have differed in some respects from all of its modified descendants, so forms directly intermediate between two living species should not be expected.

claims.title: The number of past intermediate and transitional links was inconceivably great
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: Because all living species are connected through extinct parent-species back to the common ancestor of each great class by steps no greater than those between varieties, the number of intermediate and transitional forms that have lived on earth must have been inconceivably great.

claims.title: Denudation of the Weald implies roughly 300 million years since the late Chalk
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: Assuming sea erosion of about one inch per century on a 500-foot cliff, the denudation of the Weald required about 300 million years, so far more than 300 million years have elapsed since the latter part of the Secondary period.

claims.title: Soft-bodied organisms and remains on non-depositing sea floor are not preserved
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: Wholly soft-bodied organisms are not preserved as fossils, and shells and bones decay and disappear where they lie on parts of the sea floor where sediment is not accumulating, so the fossil record is strongly biased.

claims.title: Successive formations are separated by wide intervals of unrecorded time
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: The chief cause of the imperfection of the geological record is that successive geological formations are separated from each other by wide intervals of time during which no record was left.

claims.title: Thick fossil-rich formations accumulate during subsidence
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: Fossiliferous formations thick and extensive enough to survive later erosion are formed in shallow seas during periods of slow subsidence in which the supply of sediment roughly keeps pace with sinking.

claims.title: Speciation peaks during elevation, but fossil deposits form mainly during subsidence
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: Periods of land elevation favour the formation of new varieties and species but leave little geological record, whereas periods of subsidence bring much extinction and fewer new species yet produce most fossil-rich deposits, so transitional forms are seldom recorded.

claims.title: A single formation is likely shorter than the time needed to transform a species
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: Although each geological formation represents a long lapse of years, each is probably short compared with the time required to change one species into another, so a single formation should rarely contain a full graded series between species.

claims.title: First appearance of a species in a formation usually marks immigration
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: When a marine species first appears partway through a formation, the most probable explanation is that it immigrated into that area at that time rather than originated there.

claims.title: Only a few transitional links should be found, and these will be ranked as species
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: Given the imperfect record, one should expect to find in geological formations only a few transitional links of varying closeness between species, and even close links found in different stages of one formation will be ranked as distinct species by palaeontologists.

claims.title: Apparent sudden origin of groups reflects missing earlier records
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: The apparently sudden appearance of whole groups of allied species in a formation is generally an artefact: such groups existed and multiplied earlier, elsewhere or during unrecorded intervals, so older fossils of them should continue to be found.

claims.title: After a key new way of life is acquired, many divergent forms arise quickly
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: Adapting an organism to a new and peculiar way of life such as flight may take a long time, but once a few species have gained that advantage, many divergent forms can be produced in a comparatively short time and spread widely.

claims.title: Long ages of abundant life preceded the lowest Silurian strata
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: If descent with modification is true, periods at least as long as the whole time from the Silurian to the present must have passed before the lowest Silurian strata were laid down, and during them the world swarmed with living creatures.

claims.title: Oceans and continents have kept roughly their present positions since the Silurian
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record
claims.statement: Since no oceanic island bears Palaeozoic or Secondary formations, oceans have probably occupied their present areas, and continents theirs, since the earliest Silurian period, though the arrangement may have differed long before.

claims.title: New species have appeared slowly and successively on land and in the sea
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: New species have appeared very slowly and one after another, both on land and in the waters, rather than in simultaneous batches.

claims.title: Species of different genera and classes change at different rates
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Species of different genera and classes have not changed at the same rate or to the same degree through geological time.

claims.title: Land organisms change faster than marine organisms
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Terrestrial organisms appear to change at a faster rate through geological time than marine organisms.

claims.title: A species that has gone extinct never reappears
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Once a species has disappeared from the earth, the identical form never reappears, because any replacement would inherit different characters from its different progenitors.

claims.title: A group's existence is continuous and it never reappears after disappearing
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Genera and families, like species, exist continuously from their first to last appearance and do not reappear after they have once disappeared, since their members must form an unbroken succession of generations.

claims.title: Groups rise gradually in species number to a maximum, then gradually decline
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: The number of species in a genus, or genera in a family, generally increases gradually through time to a maximum and then, sooner or later, gradually decreases to extinction.

claims.title: Species and groups disappear gradually, place by place, not by global catastrophes
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Species and groups of species generally become extinct gradually, one after another, disappearing first from one place, then another, and finally from the world, rather than being swept away together by catastrophes.

claims.title: The extinction of a group is generally slower than its origination
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: The complete extinction of the species of a group generally takes longer than their production, so a group's diversity tapers more gradually at its end than at its beginning, though some groups such as ammonites ended suddenly.

claims.title: Rarity precedes extinction
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Species generally become rare before they become extinct, as seen in recent Tertiary formations and in animals exterminated by humans.

claims.title: In later geological periods new species have roughly balanced extinctions
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: The number of species has not increased indefinitely, at least in the later geological periods, so the production of new forms has caused the extinction of about the same number of old forms.

claims.title: New descendants mainly exterminate their parent species and closest relatives
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Because competition is most severe between the most similar forms, the improved descendants of a species generally cause the extinction of the parent species and of its nearest allies in the same genus.

claims.title: Marine forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: The forms of marine life change almost simultaneously, in a broad geological sense, throughout the world, so that formations in distant regions under different climates can be correlated by their fossils.

claims.title: The more ancient a form, the more it differs from living forms
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: As a general rule, the older a fossil form is, the more it differs from living forms.

claims.title: Extinct forms fill gaps between existing genera, families and orders
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: All fossils can be classed in existing groups or between them, and extinct forms fill up the wide intervals between existing genera, families and orders, forming with living forms one natural system.

claims.title: Older members of distinct groups differ less from each other than living members
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Groups that have changed much over known geological periods should, in older formations, approach each other slightly, so that their older members differ from each other in fewer characters than their living members do.

claims.title: Fossils from consecutive formations are more alike than those from remote ones
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Fossils from two consecutive formations are far more closely related to each other than fossils from two formations widely separated in time, and the fauna of each period is broadly intermediate between those before and after it.

claims.title: Later faunas would outcompete earlier faunas under similar conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Because each new species arose by having some advantage over preceding forms, a more recent fauna or flora would beat and exterminate an older one if they were placed in competition under a similar climate, and in this sense recent forms are higher.

claims.title: Each region's fossils are succeeded by allied living forms in the same region
claims.chapter: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings
claims.statement: Within the same continent or area, the extinct forms of the later Tertiary are closely allied to the living inhabitants (e.g. fossil and living marsupials in Australia, edentates in South America), because each area's inhabitants leave modified descendants there.

claims.title: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of different regions can be explained by their climate and other physical conditions; regions with closely parallel conditions (e.g. Australia, South Africa and western South America at 25°–35° S) have utterly different faunas and floras.

claims.title: Barriers to migration correspond closely to differences between regional biotas
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Barriers of any kind that obstruct free migration (oceans, isthmuses, mountain ranges, deserts, large rivers) are closely related to the differences between the inhabitants of different regions, and the more impassable and long-standing the barrier, the greater the difference.

claims.title: Species of the same continent or sea are related despite differing stations
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: The inhabitants of the same continent or sea show a pervasive affinity to one another, so that distinct but related species replace one another from place to place and across different habitats, rather than being replaced by forms from other continents living under similar conditions.

claims.title: The bond linking inhabitants of the same area through space and time is inheritance
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: The deep affinity uniting the living and extinct inhabitants of the same area, independent of physical conditions, is due to inheritance from common ancestors, while the differences among regions arise mainly from modification through natural selection and only subordinately from the direct influence of physical condit

claims.title: Migration or isolation alone does not cause modification
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Migration and isolation do not by themselves cause modification; a group of competing species that migrates together into a new, isolated country will be little modified, because modification is driven by organisms being brought into new relations with one another.

claims.title: Many genera are confined to one region and the most natural genera are local
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Some families, many sub-families, very many genera and still more sections of genera are confined to a single region, and the most natural genera (those whose species are most closely related) are generally confined to one area.

claims.title: Each species arose in a single area and spread from there
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Each species was first produced in one area only and subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence allowed under past and present conditions, rather than arising independently at several points.

claims.title: Continents and oceanic islands were not united by land in the recent period
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Although continents have undergone great oscillations of level, separate continents have not been continuously joined to each other and to the existing oceanic islands within the period of existing species, contrary to the land-bridge hypotheses of Forbes and others.

claims.title: About a tenth of a flora's seeds could survive sea-drift across 900 miles
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Based on flotation and germination experiments, the seeds of roughly 10 per cent of the plants of a flora, after drying, could be floated by sea currents across about 900 miles of sea and still germinate.

claims.title: Occasional transport bridges hundreds of miles but not distant continents
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Occasional means of transport (sea currents, birds, drift timber, icebergs) suffice to carry organisms across a few hundred miles of sea, between islands or from a continent to a nearby island, but not between distant continents, so the floras of distant continents remain distinct.

claims.title: Identical alpine species on distant mountains are relicts of the Glacial period
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: The same arctic and alpine species on widely separated mountain summits and in arctic regions are relicts of populations that spread across the intervening lowlands during the Glacial period and were stranded on mountains and in the far north as the climate warmed.

claims.title: North American and European temperate biotas share ancestry from Pliocene circumpolar land
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: The relationship, with very little identity, between the temperate inhabitants of North America and Europe arises because a common biota inhabited the nearly continuous circumpolar land in warmer Pliocene times and then migrated southward, becoming separated and modified on each continent.

claims.title: The Glacial period was simultaneous across the whole world
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: The Glacial period, which lasted a very long time at each place, was at least in part simultaneous across the whole world, or at least along broad longitudinal belts from pole to pole, so that global temperature was lower at the same time.

claims.title: Plants of high mountains and temperate lowlands worldwide are identical or closely related
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Throughout the world, plants growing on high mountains (including tropical ones) and on the temperate lowlands of the northern and southern hemispheres are sometimes identical species but much more often distinct yet closely related species.

claims.title: Glacial interchange ran mainly north to south because northern forms were more dominant
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Many more identical and allied plant forms migrated from north to south during the Glacial period than in the reverse direction, because the greater land area of the north and the larger populations there had made northern forms more advanced and dominant through natural selection and competition.

claims.title: Northern species naturalise far more often in the south than the reverse
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: At the present day many European species have become naturalised and partly displaced the natives in La Plata and to a lesser degree in Australia, whereas extremely few southern-hemisphere species have become naturalised anywhere in Europe.

claims.title: Distinct southern genera spread from a once-vegetated Antarctica before the Glacial period
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: Geographical Distribution
claims.statement: Distinct species of genera confined to the southern hemisphere spread in radiating lines from the antarctic lands, which supported a peculiar flora during a warmer period before the Glacial period, reaching southern America, Australia and New Zealand by occasional transport and former islands.

claims.title: Fresh-water species range widely and allied species occur worldwide
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Despite being separated by land and sea barriers, many fresh-water species of quite different classes have enormous ranges, and allied fresh-water species prevail throughout the world.

claims.title: Fresh-water fish species are not shared between distant continents
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: The same species of fresh-water fish never occur in the fresh waters of distant continents, although within a continent fish species often range widely and irregularly, different river systems sharing some species but not others.

claims.title: Water birds disperse seeds and eggs, explaining wide ranges of fresh-water life
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: The wide distribution of fresh-water plants and lower fresh-water animals depends mainly on the transport of their seeds and eggs by animals, especially wide-flying fresh-water birds that move between often distant bodies of water.

claims.title: Oceanic islands have fewer species than equal continental areas
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Oceanic islands are inhabited by far fewer species of all kinds than continental areas of equal size, a difference not explained by physical conditions.

claims.title: Oceanic islands have a very high proportion of endemic species
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Although oceanic islands have few species, the proportion of their species that are endemic (found nowhere else) is often extremely large relative to their area, as expected if occasional colonists arriving in a new isolated district are especially liable to modification.

claims.title: Island endemism is low in groups that arrive easily and in numbers
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Within one island, some groups are almost wholly endemic while others are not, because groups that immigrate readily and in a body (e.g. marine birds, sea-shells, regularly visiting land-birds) keep their mutual relations undisturbed and so are little modified.

claims.title: Natural selection turns island herbaceous plants into shrubs and trees
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Because trees rarely reach distant oceanic islands, herbaceous plants that colonise them gain an advantage by growing taller, so natural selection often converts insular herbaceous plants first into bushes and then into trees, explaining why islands have trees in orders that are elsewhere herbaceous.

claims.title: Frogs, toads and newts are absent from oceanic islands
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Batrachians (frogs, toads and newts) are naturally absent from oceanic islands, not because conditions there are unsuitable (introduced frogs thrive) but because they and their spawn are killed by sea-water and so cannot cross the sea.

claims.title: No native terrestrial mammals on islands more than 300 miles from a continent
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: No native terrestrial mammal inhabits any island more than about 300 miles from a continent or large continental island, even though small mammals thrive when introduced there, because terrestrial mammals cannot cross wide stretches of sea.

claims.title: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Although terrestrial mammals are absent from oceanic islands, bats occur on almost every island, and remote islands often have their own endemic bat species, because bats can fly across wide spaces of sea and are then modified in their new homes.

claims.title: Sea depth between island and mainland predicts their mammalian affinity
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Somewhat independently of distance, the depth of sea separating an island from the neighbouring mainland is related to whether they share the same or allied mammal species: islands separated by shallow channels have the same or very similar mammals, those across deep water have distinct species and genera.

claims.title: Island endemics are related to species of the nearest continent
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: It is an almost universal rule that the endemic species of islands are related to those of the nearest continent or other nearby islands, even when the islands' physical conditions resemble those of a different, more distant region (e.g. Galapagos to America, Cape Verde to Africa).

claims.title: Species on islands of one archipelago are closest relatives of each other
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: The distinct species inhabiting the separate islands of an archipelago are far more closely related to one another than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world, because the islands received immigrants from the same source or from each other.

claims.title: Naturalised species are usually not closely allied to the natives they join
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Species that become naturalised in new countries are generally not closely allied to the native inhabitants but are very distinct, often belonging to genera absent from the region, whereas closely allied species equally well fitted to their places tend to keep separate.

claims.title: Inhabitants of any area are modified colonists from the most accessible source
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: The inhabitants of any area (oceanic islands, mountains, lakes, marshes, caves), where not identical, are plainly related to those of the region from which colonists could most readily have come, the colonists having since been modified and better fitted to their new homes.

claims.title: Regions sharing many allied species will also share some identical species
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Wherever two regions, however distant, contain many closely allied or representative species, they will also contain some identical species and many doubtful forms ranked variously as species or varieties, showing past migration between them.

claims.title: The lower a group of organisms, the more widely it tends to range
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Organisms lower in the scale of nature tend to range more widely than higher ones, because they change more slowly and their seeds and eggs are minute and suited to distant transport.

claims.title: Closer relatives tend to be closer together in time and space
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: Geographical Distribution, continued
claims.statement: Because forms within each class are connected by ordinary generation, the more closely two forms are related by descent, the nearer they will generally be to each other in time and in geographic space.

claims.title: Descent with divergence and extinction produces groups subordinate to groups
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: The nested arrangement of organisms into groups within groups (species within genera, genera within families, and so on) results from the modified descendants of a single progenitor diverging in character while less divergent forms are exterminated.

claims.title: The Natural System expresses propinquity of descent
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: The 'something more' than mere resemblance that naturalists seek in the Natural System is closeness of descent, which is the only known cause of similarity among organisms and is partially revealed by classifications.

claims.title: Characters least modified by adaptation are most constant and useful in classification
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: The value of a character for classification depends on its constancy across large groups of species, and characters are constant when they have been little changed in adapting species to their conditions of life; hence parts least concerned with special habits are generally the most useful for classification.

claims.title: Higher taxonomic ranks are almost arbitrary
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: The relative value of groups such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families and genera is, at least at present, almost arbitrary, as shown by groups being raised in rank merely because more allied species were discovered.

claims.title: Branches equally related by descent can differ greatly in amount of modification
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: A natural arrangement of groups must be strictly genealogical, but branches that are equally closely related to a common progenitor may differ greatly in how much they have been modified, and these differing amounts of difference are what is expressed by ranking them as different genera, families or orders.

claims.title: Varieties form nested groups for the same reason species do
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Domestic and natural varieties fall into groups subordinate to groups (sub-varieties under varieties under species) for the same reason species do, namely closeness of descent combined with various degrees of modification.

claims.title: Characters shared across species with very different habits indicate common inheritance
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: However trifling a character, if it occurs throughout many species with very different habits of life it can be explained only by inheritance from a common parent, and so has high value for classification; for the same reason rudimentary structures can be as useful as other parts.

claims.title: Distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
