claims.statement: Animals from very distinct lines of descent can become adapted to similar conditions and so acquire a close external resemblance; such analogical or adaptive resemblances conceal rather than reveal blood-relationship, so they are almost worthless for classification between groups, although the same characters can indic

claims.title: Expanding dominant groups explain why all life falls into a few great classes
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Larger and more dominant groups tend to keep increasing in size and to supplant smaller, feebler groups, which is why all organisms, recent and extinct, fall into a few great orders, still fewer classes, and a single natural system.

claims.title: Aberrant groups are species-poor relicts of extinction
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Aberrant or osculant groups are the surviving remnants of failing groups that suffered heavy extinction; consequently they are generally represented by very few species, and those species are usually very distinct from each other.

claims.title: Affinities of one group to another are usually general, not to any single species
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: When a member of one group shows a real affinity to a quite distinct group, the affinity is usually general rather than to any particular species, because it retains characters of an ancient common progenitor of both groups.

claims.title: Gaps between groups, even whole classes, are due to extinction of connecting forms
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Extinction has defined and widened the intervals between groups; even the distinctness of whole classes, such as birds from other vertebrates, results from the loss of many ancient forms that once connected their early progenitors.

claims.title: Homologous parts change shape and size but keep the same relative connexions
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Within a class, homologous parts may change to almost any extent in form and size but always remain connected in the same order; for example, the bones of the arm and forearm are never transposed.

claims.title: Unity of type reflects a common progenitor's pattern modified by slight steps
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: The shared pattern of homologous organs within a class is explained by descent from an ancient progenitor (an archetype) that already had that pattern, which natural selection then modified by slight successive steps for different uses without transposing parts.

claims.title: Serially homologous parts derive from many repeated similar elements in progenitors
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Serial homologies within one individual (skull and vertebrae, jaws and legs of crustaceans, floral parts and leaves) arise because the progenitors of vertebrates, articulates and flowering plants had many repeated similar parts, which natural selection adapted to diverse purposes while inheritance retained a fundamenta

claims.title: Embryos of different animals in the same class are strikingly similar
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Embryos of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar, more so than the adults, and the points of resemblance often have no direct relation to their conditions of existence.

claims.title: Active larvae are adapted to their own conditions as fully as adults
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Whenever an embryo or larva becomes active and must provide for itself, it is as perfectly adapted to its conditions of life as the adult, and such adaptations can make the larvae of allied species differ as much as or more than their adults, though most larvae still follow the law of embryonic resemblance.

claims.title: Young of domestic breeds differ much less than adults
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: The characteristic differences between domestic breeds produced by man's selection (in dogs, horses and pigeons) generally do not appear early in life and are inherited at a corresponding later age, so that the young of different breeds differ far less in proportions than the adults, with occasional exceptions such as

claims.title: Community of embryonic structure reveals community of descent
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Because the embryo is the animal in a less modified state that partly reveals the structure of its progenitor, two groups that pass through the same or similar embryonic stages are descended from the same or similar parents, however different their adults; this is why embryonic characters are the most valuable for clas

claims.title: Ancient extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Since embryos partly show the structure of less modified ancient progenitors, ancient and extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants, though this may be obscured by early-appearing variations and may be undemonstrable because the geological record does not reach back far enough.

claims.title: Embryological facts follow from late-appearing variations inherited at corresponding ages
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: The leading facts of embryology are explained because, in the descendants of a common progenitor, successive slight modifications generally do not appear at a very early period of life (though they may be caused earlier) and are inherited at a corresponding later age, leaving embryos little modified.

claims.title: Rudimentary organs are extremely common throughout nature
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Rudimentary, atrophied or aborted organs that bear the stamp of uselessness are extremely common in animals and plants.

claims.title: Rudimentary organs are highly variable
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Rudimentary organs vary greatly in development among individuals of the same species, and the degree of reduction of the same organ can differ much between closely allied species; because they are useless, their variations are not checked by natural selection.

claims.title: Rudimentary organs are relatively larger in the embryo than in the adult
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: As a universal rule, a rudimentary part is relatively larger compared with adjoining parts in the embryo than in the adult, and some rudiments (such as the teeth of whales and ruminants) appear in the embryo and then wholly disappear.

claims.title: Disuse is the main cause of rudimentary organs
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.statement: Disuse over successive generations has been the main agency reducing organs to rudiments (as with eyes of cave animals and wings of island birds), aided by natural selection where an organ becomes injurious; because reduction occurs at maturity and is inherited at a corresponding age, rudiments remain relatively larger

claims.title: Descent with modification embraces all members of each class
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: Because all members of whole classes are linked by chains of affinities, fossils fill wide gaps between orders, rudiments imply fully developed ancestral organs, and structures within a class share one pattern and similar embryos, descent with modification embraces all members of the same class.

claims.title: Animals from at most four or five progenitors, plants from as many or fewer
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: All animals have descended from at most four or five progenitors, and all plants from an equal or smaller number.

claims.title: All living things share chemical composition, cell structure and laws of growth
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: All living things have much in common in their chemical composition, germinal vesicles, cellular structure, and laws of growth and reproduction, as shown even by the same poison often affecting plants and animals similarly.

claims.title: Probably all organisms descend from one primordial form
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: By analogy, probably all organisms that have ever lived on earth have descended from a single primordial form.

claims.title: Species differ from varieties only in their intermediates having existed formerly
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: The only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is that varieties are known or believed to be connected by intermediate gradations at present, whereas species were connected by them in the past; species should therefore be treated, like genera, as combinations made for convenience.

claims.title: Organism-to-organism relations are the most important cause of organic change
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: The most important cause of organic change is the mutual relation of organism to organism, in which the improvement of one form causes the improvement or extermination of others; this is almost independent of changes, even sudden ones, in physical conditions.

claims.title: Amount of fossil change between formations measures elapsed time
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: Because species are produced and exterminated by slow, still-acting causes, the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations is probably a fair, though imperfect, measure of the time elapsed, and can be used to estimate the length of the blank intervals between formations.

claims.title: Rate of organic change was slower early in life's history
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: In early periods of earth's history, when forms of life were fewer and simpler, the rate of organic change was probably slower, and at the first dawn of life it may have been extremely slow.

claims.title: Known geological history is a fragment of the time since the first organism
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: The whole history of the world as known from geology is only a small fragment of the time that has elapsed since the first organism, the progenitor of all later forms, came into existence.

claims.title: Every mental power was acquired by gradation
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: Each mental power and capacity must have been acquired gradually, so psychology will rest on this foundation, and light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history.

claims.title: Few living species will leave descendants; common species of dominant groups will prevail
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: Very few living species will leave descendants in the far future, and those that will prevail and give rise to new dominant species will be the common, widespread species of the larger, dominant groups.

claims.title: Succession by generation has never been broken by a world-wide cataclysm
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: Since all living forms are lineal descendants of forms that lived long before the Silurian epoch, the ordinary succession by generation has never once been broken and no cataclysm has ever desolated the whole world.

claims.title: Natural selection makes endowments tend towards perfection
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: Because natural selection works solely by and for the good of each being, all bodily and mental endowments will tend to progress towards perfection.

claims.title: The 'entangled bank' laws produce the diversity of living forms
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: Recapitulation and Conclusion
claims.statement: The varied and interdependent forms of life were produced by laws still acting: growth with reproduction; inheritance; variability caused by external conditions and by use and disuse; a rate of increase high enough to cause a struggle for life and so natural selection, which in turn causes divergence of character and e

claims.title: Reliance on chance variation and natural selection stalls inquiry into physical causes
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.statement: As long as fortuitous variation and the survival of the fittest are accepted as sufficient explanations in biology, they will tend to hold back careful investigation of the real physical causes of organic form.

claims.title: Cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves and flowers are shaped by the laws of physics
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.statement: The material parts of living things (cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves, flowers) are portions of matter whose particles have been moved, moulded and shaped in obedience to the laws of physics.

claims.title: Problems of organic form are mathematical and problems of growth are physical
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.statement: The problems of the form of living things are, in the first instance, mathematical problems and their problems of growth are essentially physical problems, so morphology is a branch of physical science.

claims.title: No known physical law is transgressed by the bodily mechanism
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.statement: However complex living processes are, no physical law (including those of chemistry, surface action and osmosis) is known to be broken by the working of the body.

claims.title: The form of an object is a diagram of the forces acting or that have acted on it
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.statement: The form of any portion of matter, living or dead, can be read as a diagram of forces: from the shape of a solid one can deduce the forces that produced and maintain it, and from the shape of a fluid the forces currently acting on it, so an organism's conformation is explained by a balance of forces.

claims.title: Surface tension at a cell's boundary strongly affects its form
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.statement: Like other fluid bodies, the surface of a cell such as an Amoeba carries a surface tension that depends on the substance it touches, and this surface tension strongly affects the cell's form.

claims.title: Protoplasm behaves as a highly viscous fluid that changes shape under force
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.statement: The protoplasm of an Amoeba deforms and flows under the slightest pressure, so it is a fluid, but it is far more viscous than water, like treacle, and this viscosity slows its changes of shape.

claims.title: Vital phenomena cannot be cleanly divided into physical and non-physical ones
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.statement: There is no clear rule for deciding what is 'vital', and the properties of organisms cannot be clearly split into those of physical origin and those peculiar to living things, so physical analysis must proceed piece by piece.

claims.title: Nuclei, chromosomes and germ-plasm act only as seats of energy and centres of force
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.statement: In development, variation and inheritance, material elements such as the spermatozoon, nucleus, chromosomes or germ-plasm never act as matter alone, but only as seats of energy and centres of force.

claims.title: Changes in the length-weight constant k reveal changes of form during growth
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Weight varies as the cube of length (W = kL³) in an animal of unchanging form and density, so tracking whether k stays constant or varies with length shows whether the animal's general form changes as it grows; such changes are likely as long as growth continues.

claims.title: Tree trunk diameter must grow as the 3/2 power of height
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: For a tree to stand without buckling under its own weight, its diameter must increase as the 3/2 power of its height, which explains why young trees are slender and old large ones stunted, and sets a theoretical maximum tree height (about 300 ft for a Kew-flagstaff pine).

claims.title: Gravity sets an upper limit on the size of terrestrial animals
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Because the strength of muscles and the crushing resistance of bones vary as their cross-section (the square of linear size) while body weight varies as the cube, there is a definite upper limit to the size of an animal living under gravity; the elephant, with disproportionately thick limb bones and reduced agility, is

claims.title: Buoyancy removes the physical barrier to size in fully aquatic animals
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: An animal wholly immersed in water whose density about matches the water, like a whale, has its weight counterpoised, so there is no longer a physical barrier to its indefinite growth in size.

claims.title: Larger fish can sprint faster but cover similar distances and tire more slowly
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Since muscular work available scales as the cube of linear size while the rate of energy supply, depending on respiratory surface, scales only as the square, a larger fish should achieve a much higher burst speed than a smaller one but travel a similar distance over a year, and smaller individuals should fatigue faster

claims.title: Power needed for flight grows as length^3.5 while muscle power grows as length^3
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: A bird of fixed proportions must fly at a minimum speed proportional to the square root of its linear size, so the work needed for flight varies as the 3½ power of linear size while the work its muscles can supply varies only as the cube; flight thus becomes harder as birds get larger (about 1.4 times harder per doubli

claims.title: Ostrich and moa have passed the size at which muscular flight is possible
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: The ostrich probably, and the moa certainly, reached a size at which flight by muscular action with ordinary bird anatomy became physiologically impossible, and a bird as large as a man could not fly.

claims.title: Giant Carboniferous insects and pterodactyls imply a denser ancient atmosphere
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: The giant wingspans of Carboniferous dragonflies and the small bodies and huge wings of pterodactyls, which seem beyond present mechanical limits, can be explained if the Carboniferous and Jurassic atmosphere was notably denser, for example through more carbonic acid.

claims.title: Similarly built animals should jump to the same absolute height regardless of size
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Because the impulse of a leap is proportional to muscle volume and so to body mass, the take-off velocity is independent of size, and similarly built animals should jump to the same actual height rather than the same relative height; longer levers in larger animals give them some advantage.

claims.title: Speed varies as the square root of linear size in swimming, flight and walking
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Leaving aside differences in mechanical construction, swimming (Froude's law), flight (minimum stable speed) and walking (the leg swinging as a pendulum) all give the same result: an animal's velocity tends to vary as the square root of its linear dimensions.

claims.title: Doubling gravity would make terrestrial animals short-legged or serpent-like
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: The form and actions of terrestrial animals are conditioned by the strength of gravity: if it were doubled, bipedal form would fail and most land animals would resemble short-legged saurians or serpents; if halved, animals would be lighter, more active and need less heart, lungs and blood.

claims.title: Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Throughout morphology, surface tends to keep pace with volume through changes of form, such as intestinal villi and folds, the shark's spiral valve, and brain convolutions whose complexity is correlated with animal size, so that a roughly constant ratio of surface to mass is maintained.

claims.title: Form of small organisms is set by surface tension, not gravity, favouring spheres
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: The form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity and mainly due to surface tension, acting either now or at an earlier stage before the form was made rigid, so small organisms tend strongly toward spherical and other simple surface-tension forms that do not occur in the external form of large animals.

claims.title: Form follows growth rates in large organisms but not in minute ones
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Large and small organisms differ in kind in how form arises: in large organisms form is the direct result of unequal growth rates in different directions, but in minute organisms and individual cells intermolecular forces outweigh gravity and form is not simply correlated with growth.

claims.title: Cell division restores the ratio of surface to mass
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Cell division keeps the ratio between a cell's surface and its mass approximately constant and restores the balance of surface energy with the cell's other energies; cleavage of an egg increases surface without increasing volume or mass.

claims.title: Cells of each kind vary little about a mean size, whatever the body size
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Cells of each kind vary little about a characteristic mean size and have absolute size limits, so dwarf and giant individuals of a species (e.g. Crepidula, sea-urchin larvae) differ in cell number rather than cell size.

claims.title: Ganglion-cell size varies little; larger species have ganglia with more cells
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Across animals large and small, ganglion (nerve) cells vary in size only within narrow limits, and smaller species have simpler ganglia containing fewer cells than larger species.

claims.title: The smallest organisms approach molecular size, so they cannot be much smaller
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.statement: Because a micrococcus 0.15 µm across contains only some tens of thousands of protein molecules, the smallest known organisms approach molecular dimensions, and organisms cannot be subdivided indefinitely or be much smaller than those already discovered.

claims.title: External form results from the ratio of growth rates in different directions
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Except for certain very minute organisms whose form is set directly by molecular forces, the external form of an organism is accounted for by the ratio between its rates of growth in different directions.

claims.title: Constant growth-rate ratios preserve form; changing ratios produce development
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: When the ratio between growth rates in different directions stays constant, an organism grows in bulk with little or no change of form; such constancy seldom lasts more than a season, and when the ratio alters the organism undergoes development, a steady and persistent change of form.

claims.title: Embryonic folds arise from local differences in growth rate of a uniform sheet
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: The foldings of the blastoderm that produce the neural and amniotic folds result from unequal rates of growth, local accelerations and retardations, in what is at first an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue, in the way that a sheet buckles when parts of it expand or contract.

claims.title: Differences between related forms emerge gradually and are small in the young
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Because form differences are attained by growth at specific velocities over long periods, differences between any two related individuals or species must appear gradually and be little apparent in the young, and animals of very different adult size differ less and less in size and form when traced back through foetal s

claims.title: Human stature grows fast in infancy, steadily in childhood, then quickens in the teens
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: The human curve of growth in stature shows rapid increase in infancy, a long period of slower, nearly steady growth in early boyhood, a marked quickening in the early teens, and finally a gradual arrest as full height is reached.

claims.title: Adult human stature declines well before fifty and markedly by old age
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Full adult stature in man lasts only for a time: it begins to decrease well before fifty, is notably lessened by sixty, and is much reduced in extreme old age, so that growth takes a negative value.

claims.title: Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Whatever the law of increase in a linear dimension, volume and therefore weight tend to vary as the cube of linear dimensions, which mainly (though not wholly) explains why the human weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve.

claims.title: Boys and girls share a growth-velocity curve differing mainly in phase
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: The curves of growth velocity in boys and girls are of very similar shape but differ in amplitude and especially in phase, the girl's adolescent acceleration beginning and ending earlier than the boy's.

claims.title: All animals pass through the same phases of growth: slow start, early peak, slowdown
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: In long-lived and short-lived animals alike, growth begins slowly, reaches its maximum velocity early, and then slows down (with temporary accelerations) toward a point where it ceases.

claims.title: Cold-blooded animals approach a maximal size only asymptotically
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: In cold-blooded animals such as fishes the slowing of growth is greatly protracted, so that size seems never to reach a maximum but only to approach a limit asymptotically.

claims.title: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: The size an animal finally attains results from both its rate and its duration of growth: some species are larger because they grow faster (rabbit versus guinea-pig), others because they grow for longer (man versus rabbit).

claims.title: Human length growth peaks in velocity around the fifth month before birth
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: The human curve of growth in length has a point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: before it growth velocity continually increases, and after it, though growth remains rapid, velocity falls away.

claims.title: Variability of stature and weight tracks the rate of growth
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: The coefficient of variability of human stature and weight falls when the rate of growth diminishes and rises again during the adolescent acceleration, so that variability is a function of the rate of growth.

claims.title: Growth rate is interrupted at physiological epochs such as birth, puberty, metamorphosis
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Curves of growth show well-marked interruptions or changes of rate at physiological epochs such as birth and puberty, in man and in other animals, and most strikingly in animals that undergo a regular metamorphosis.

claims.title: Metamorphosis is often, perhaps always, accompanied by loss of bulk and weight
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Negative growth, an actual loss of bulk and weight, often and perhaps always accompanies metamorphosis, as in the eel, the silkworm before pupation and the frog tadpole.

claims.title: Organ size bears no constant ratio to body size through life, especially the brain
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: There is no simple and constant relation, holding throughout life, between the size of the whole body and that of organs such as brain, heart and liver; the brain in particular falls from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at twenty-five.

claims.title: Plaice weight-length coefficient peaks near the size of sexual maturity
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: In plaice the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 is not constant but rises to a maximum and then slowly declines with increasing size, the maximum falling near 30 cm, about the size at which sexual maturity begins.

claims.title: Seasonal cycle in fish weight at fixed length is caused by spawning
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: In plaice of fixed length, weight falls from about November to March or April and is restored between May or June and November, a periodic change caused wholly by spawning and the subsequent rebuilding of tissues and gonads, so that the spawning season can be determined from length and weight alone.

claims.title: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: A large part of an organism's specific morphology depends on there being, besides an aggregate rate of growth of the whole, a characteristic specific rate of growth for each part or organ, so that small changes in these local rates soon produce striking differences of form.

claims.title: Common temperate plants share a growth optimum near 26 °C
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: The optimum temperature for growth is much the same, about 26 °C, for the common plants of temperate climates, and considerably higher for plants of warmer regions such as melon and maize.

claims.title: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).

claims.title: Optimum temperature curves arise from acceleration combined with cumulative damage
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Growth rate has an optimum temperature because temperature both accelerates growth according to van’t Hoff’s law and progressively damages or fatigues the organism, so the optimum curve is a complex resultant rather than a primary phenomenon.

claims.title: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.

claims.title: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.

claims.title: Growth rate depends largely on water uptake (turgor) as well as metabolism
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: A large part of growth, in animals and more conspicuously in plants, depends on turgor and osmotic conditions: the velocity of growth depends largely on the amount of water taken into the cells as well as on chemical metabolism.

claims.title: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.

claims.title: The organic curve of growth resembles the velocity curve of chemical autocatalysis
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: The normal curve of growth of an organism closely resembles the velocity curve of an autocatalytic chemical reaction, with a phase of increasing acceleration, a phase in which limiting conditions reduce acceleration, and usually a final phase of retardation and loss of mass; but only a resemblance, not an identity, can

claims.title: Internal secretions and other substances accelerate growth and alter proportions
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Substances inside and outside the organism, such as thyroid and pituitary secretions or iodine compounds, can accelerate growth in a way that changes not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.

claims.title: Natural selection removes forms rather than originating them
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Since forms, including exaggerated ones such as the great Secondary reptiles and Tertiary mammals, can arise from changes in growth, natural selection is needed to explain their disappearance rather than their appearance; in general its function is not to originate but to remove.

claims.title: Velocity of regenerative growth varies inversely as about the square of time
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: After its early maximum, the velocity of regenerative growth (tadpole tails) falls off inversely as some power of the time since injury, approximately as 1/T^2, so that V T^2 is nearly constant.

claims.title: Regeneration is ordinary growth, with the same curve as growth from zero
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Regeneration is a particular case of growth obeying the same laws; the regeneration curve (short latent period, rapid rise to a maximum velocity, then slow decline) only appears different because ordinary growth curves start at birth, and a complete growth curve from zero has the same essential features.

claims.title: Claw reversal after amputation depends on regeneration versus growth rates
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Whether an amputated large crustacean claw regenerates as the large claw, or the claws exchange roles, depends on the ratio between the regenerative growth rate of the amputated claw and the growth rate of the uninjured claw, since claw form follows claw size.

claims.title: Reproduction by fission is a physical tendency to segment plus regeneration
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Reproduction by fission in worm-like animals consists essentially of the physical tendency of a long semi-fluid tube to break into segments, combined with ordinary regeneration, which explains its occurrence in zoologically unrelated animals and its absence in some close relatives.

claims.title: Growth velocity peaks and falls because surface resistance suddenly increases
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: The abrupt change from increasing to decreasing growth velocity is more likely due to a sudden increase of resistance, such as the formation of a comparatively firm skin during histological differentiation, than to a decline of internal growth forces; the later slowing reflects waning growth forces against rising super

claims.title: Form changes follow the same route in individual development and racial history
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.statement: Changes of form produced by varying rates of growth are the same phenomenon in individual development and in the differences between species; a transformation from one form to another follows the same course whether it happens within a lifetime or over ancestral history, which accounts for much of von Baer's law of rec

claims.title: Cell structure matters only as the visible expression of forces and energy
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: The study of visible cell structure has little value except as part of a dynamical investigation, because the activities of a cell are due to energy and forces, not to particular material particles or structures as such.

claims.title: Mitotic figures require a polarised force like magnetism, not mechanical traction
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: The spindle and asters of dividing cells are lines of force of a bipolar field made visible by more permeable particles, like iron filings between magnet poles, and they cannot be explained by mere mechanical traction on a protoplasmic web but require some polarised and polarising force analogous to magnetism or electr

claims.title: The nucleus is spherical because it is an immiscible fluid drop under uniform tension
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: The nucleus is almost always spherical because its fluid substance does not mix with the surrounding protoplasm, so it is bounded by a film of uniform surface tension and immersed in a medium transmitting uniform fluid pressure; where the cytoplasm becomes more solid (as in muscle cells or mucus-laden epithelial cells)

claims.title: Morphological polarity of the cell is the outward sign of a dynamical polarity
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: The visible polarity of a cell (symmetry of structure about an axis, such as nucleus–centrosome or free–attached surface) is the outward expression of a real polarised distribution of forces, whose lines of force are made visible where particles of matter become strung together under those forces.

claims.title: The alveolar meshwork of nucleus and cytoplasm is a surface-tension froth
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: The alveolar 'reticulum' seen in the nucleus and cytoplasm is a froth or foam produced by the interacting surface tensions of two intermixed fluids of similar density striving to separate, and is not inherent in the nature of protoplasm.

claims.title: Fine internal networks and granules seen in fixed cells are largely artefacts
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: Fixation preserves the general outward form of small organisms and cells, but the minute internal networks and granules described as the structure of protoplasm are to a large extent artefacts of coagulating fixatives, although larger structures such as nucleus, vacuoles, centrosomes and the spindle are really present

claims.title: Chromatin behaves as a diamagnetic body and moves to the equatorial plane
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: In the bipolar field between the centrosomes the nucleus as a whole behaves as a body more permeable than the cytoplasm and is drawn in between the poles, whereas its chromatin, once broken up, behaves like a diamagnetic body, is repelled to the weaker parts of the field, and so collects in a peripheral circle on the e

claims.title: Differences of electric potential play a great part in cell division
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: Differences of electric potential between cell constituents, and between parts of the egg, play a great part in cell division; the potential difference between animal and vegetative poles of a fertilised egg fluctuates or reverses at successive segmentations, and the electrical difference of chromatin is greatest at mi

claims.title: Every cell division results from conflict between surface tension and opposing forces
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: In all cells the mechanical process of division must be explained as the result of a conflict between surface tension and its opposing forces, the division plane being set in the equatorial plane of the polar field.

claims.title: Entry of the first spermatozoon raises the surface tension of the egg
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: Because later spermatozoa fail to enter the egg after the first, an immediate consequence of sperm entry is an increase in the surface tension of the egg.

claims.title: The pronuclei travel curved paths and meet before reaching the centre of the egg
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: Given an attraction between the male and female pronuclei and a force drawing them toward the egg centre, their paths lie within the triangle formed by the two bodies and the centre, are curved (convex toward the line joining them) unless they start on a diameter, and the pronuclei meet a little before the centre and t

claims.title: Mitotic phenomena follow from simple physical assumptions and have secondary significance
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: Most if not all of the intracellular phenomena of mitosis follow inevitably from very simple assumptions about the physical constitution of the cell and a simple distribution of polarised forces within it, and are likely to prove of only remote and secondary biological significance.

claims.title: Chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: Although chromosome number is constant within a species, the range of numbers across plants and animals is small: few organisms have fewer than six chromosomes in the germ-nuclei and fewer still have more than sixteen.

claims.title: Details of mitosis vary among close relatives and are not specific to the organism
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: The details of mitosis (presence of visible caryokinesis, position of the field of force, number of chromosome groups, chromosome form and arrangement) vary greatly even among closely related organisms or within one species, and are not specifically related to the organism in which they occur.

claims.title: Early embryological categories seldom coincide with phylogenetic classification
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: Early embryological data, up to and well beyond segmentation, are a subject for physiological and physical investigation, and their categories (yolk content, chromosome form and number, radial, bilateral or spiral cleavage) will only seldom and accidentally coincide with the natural or phylogenetic classification of th

claims.title: Surface tension gives the cell its outline and morphological individuality
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: The cell is a sphere of action of localised forces, of which surface tension gives the cell its outline and individuality; partial versus total segmentation of eggs, and unicellular versus multicellular organisation, differ in whether surface tensions succeed in forming visible separations between cells.

claims.title: The centrosome is essentially a centre of force, not necessarily a material body
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: The centrosome is essentially a dynamic centre of force, which may or may not consist of a visible concentration of matter but tends to produce one, as shown by cells that live without visible centrosomes and centrosomes that disappear and form anew.

claims.title: A continuous field of force shapes the whole organism regardless of its cells
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.statement: The multicellular organism is not a colony of independent cells: a continuous field of force runs through the entire organism, not restricted to protoplasmic continuity, and shapes it independently of the number, size and form of its cells.

claims.title: Fluid protoplasm growing by imbibition produces rounded rather than plane surfaces
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Because protoplasm is fluid and grows by imbibition (intussusception) rather than by deposition of particles on a surface, freely growing organisms tend to have swelling, rounded contours, and plane surfaces are rare in them unless produced by pressure.

claims.title: Surface tension is probably the paramount force determining cell form
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Of the physical forces that determine the forms of cells, solitary or in contact, surface tension is of great and probably paramount importance, usually acting together with gravity, mechanical pressure and osmosis.

claims.title: Organic symmetry reflects equilibrium and is absent without it, as in amoeba
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Symmetry is highly characteristic of organic forms because they are figures of equilibrium governed by a principle of minimal energy, as in liquid films; symmetry is lacking only where equilibrium is lacking, as in the amoeba.

claims.title: Rounding off of protoplasm is due to surface tension, not vital contractility
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: When a drop of protoplasm, or the tip of an amoeba's pseudopodium, rounds itself off, this is a simple consequence of surface tension and not of any special vital contractility.

claims.title: Plasmodial taxes towards moisture, warmth and food parallel surface-tension phenomena
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The movements of a plasmodium (Aethalium) towards damp, warm or nutritious spots and away from sugar or salt solutions can each be accounted for by local changes of surface tension, as in inanimate drops moving on a warmed or chemically altered surface.

claims.title: Resting cells are spherical; the amoeboid phase is one of activity and unequal tensions
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: In naked protoplasmic cells the amoeboid form marks a phase of activity with unequal surface tensions, whereas the spherical form marks a phase of rest when internal homogeneity and minimal potential energy are attained, at which time the cell also becomes encysted.

claims.title: A yeast bud arises where surface tension locally and suddenly diminishes
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: A bud appears on a yeast cell because the surface tension diminishes at one part of the cell surface, so that this area expands, after which the bud's own surface tension rounds it into a roughly spherical form.

claims.title: Each new foraminiferal chamber is a surface-tension figure; the whole shell is not
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: In multichambered organisms such as the foraminifera Globigerina or Rotalia, and in desmids, each newly formed bud or chamber is a figure of equilibrium shaped by surface tension while still fluid, and is then solidified onto earlier chambers, so the whole organism is not itself a figure of minimal area.

claims.title: Surface tension governs the forms of small organisms and cells, not large organisms
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Surface tension governs form only where surface energy is a large fraction of total energy, so it determines the forms of minute organisms and of the small cells of larger organisms, while the general forms of large organisms are due to other, non-molecular forces.

claims.title: Spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest unicellular forms
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Of the six surfaces of revolution with constant mean curvature (plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid), spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest forms of small unicellular organisms and of cells in simple aggregates, and transitions between them are frequent during growth, reproduction and devel

claims.title: A cylindrical cell's end cap has twice the cylinder's radius and height about 0.27R
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Where a cylindrical cell of uniform wall tension is capped by part of a sphere, the sphere's radius is twice the cylinder's radius, the cap subtends a cone of 60°, and its height is about 0.27 of the cylinder radius (a little more than one-eighth of the diameter), proportions seen in the free end cells of Spirogyra.

claims.title: Viscid spider-thread coating breaks into beads at the cylinder stability limit
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The sticky fluid coating of a spider's spiral thread, being a liquid cylinder, becomes unstable when its length exceeds its circumference and breaks up into equal, equally spaced beads (often with smaller beads between), the spacing being somewhat greater than theory owing to viscosity and drag on the core thread.

claims.title: Notched hydroid cups and annulated stems are both due to surface tension
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The notching of the rim of hydroid calycles and the annular constrictions of their cylindrical stems are phenomena of the same order, both produced by surface tension acting on the structures while they are still fluid or semifluid films, as in the beaded rim of a splash.

claims.title: Freely growing cylindrical cells owe their form to an anisotropic wall
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: A cylindrical cell such as Spirogyra that grows without external restraint takes its form because its developing membrane is anisotropic, extending more easily in one direction; a slight inequality of tension in two directions gives an ellipsoidal cell and a great inequality a cylindrical one.

claims.title: Small organisms show a limited range of forms because molecular forces control them
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Because protozoa, bacteria and other minute cells are of a size at which form is mainly controlled by molecular forces, they exhibit only a limited range of forms, which vary with physical conditions.

claims.title: Bacterial form is too plastic to serve for species identification
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Bacteria and micrococci change shape so much with life stage, circumstances and preparation that their specific identity can seldom be recognised by form, so they have a physiological rather than morphological specificity.

claims.title: Vorticella bells form a graded series of unduloids
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The bells of the various species of Vorticella, like many other Infusoria, are unduloids or partial unduloids spanning every gradation from nearly cylindrical to nearly spherical, bounded by the stalk attachment and the ciliary ring as by two unequal supporting rings, and the species differ only in ratio or degree.

claims.title: Protozoan loricas form by adsorption into least-area surfaces, not for protection
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The membranous cups (loricas) of Salpingoeca, Tintinnus and similar protozoa arise inevitably from substances adsorbed in the surface layer of the protoplasm, and molecular forces make the resulting pellicle a surface of least possible area under the circumstances, here an unduloid; this efficient cause, rather than a

claims.title: Shared form in simple organisms need not imply common descent
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The assumption that similar or identical forms indicate genealogical relationship is far less well founded for minute organisms with few, simple characters whose form is largely produced directly by a physical force, so identical forms of such organisms in different times or places need not indicate unbroken descent or

claims.title: The unduloid Lagena shell is formed while hanging vertically in the sea
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The flask-shaped (unduloid) shell of Lagena is formed while the organism hangs vertically, in a position of symmetry about its vertical axis, like a hanging drop; flattened or winged forms are those formed when this symmetry of position was absent and the shell lay horizontally.

claims.title: Thin walls flute longitudinally; thick narrow necks pleat transversely
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Small tension changes in a thin-walled elongated cell produce wrinkling in the plane of greatest curvature, hence longitudinal fluting, especially near the ends; where the wall is thick relative to diameter, as in the narrow neck of Lagena or tubular hydroid gonangia, bending stiffness makes folding transverse instead.

claims.title: Symmetrical surface-tension pull sets heliozoan filaments radially
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: Fluid surface protoplasm creeps up the stiff axial filaments of a heliozoan such as Actinophrys, and because this surface-tension pull is symmetrical around each filament the filaments are set normal to the cell surface, radiating from the centre; closely spaced filaments produce honeycomb-like depressions between them

claims.title: The trypanosome undulating membrane is a liquid film drawn up along a flagellum
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The undulating membrane of trypanosomes and related flagellates forms when the flagellum lies near and parallel to the body and the fluid surface protoplasm is drawn up as a film along it, as a soap-film would be; the membrane is thus a liquid film of constant mean curvature whose undulations are produced by molecular

claims.title: The biconcave red blood corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The biconcave mammalian red blood corpuscle is not a surface of constant mean curvature and so cannot be a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone; some other force, possibly osmotic inequilibrium or fluid-crystal forces of its cholesterin-like constituents, must maintain its shape, which changes to a sph

claims.title: Decapod sperm-cell shape is an intermediate phase of osmotic shrinkage
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The normal form of decapod crustacean sperm-cells is one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage from a spherical form, caused by osmotic withdrawal of fluid without a matching reduction of surface area, so that equivalent shapes are produced by salt solutions of equivalent (molecular-weight-proportional) concentratio

claims.title: Elastic fibrillae act as a microscopic skeleton shaping spiral cells
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.statement: The spiral and other peculiar forms of decapod sperm-cells and of many Infusoria are produced by more or less elastic fibrillae in the cell, which restrain and modify the surface forces like the wire frames and coils in Plateau's experiments, acting as a microscopic skeleton.

claims.title: Cell-wall secretion is adsorption of constituents at the surface
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.statement: The so-called secretion of a cell-wall or membrane is the adsorption of certain constituents of the cell, which lower surface tension, to its surface (as formulated by the Gibbs-Thomson law), where they also increase viscosity and rigidity; the formation of a cell membrane is thus a chemico-physical phenomenon.

claims.title: Spicules are deposited at interfaces between cells or vacuoles
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.statement: Skeletal spicules, as in sponges and radiolaria, are characteristically deposited in the interfacial boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and their form is in many cases regulated by the arrangement of these boundaries.

claims.title: Membranes and cysts form only after protoplasm rounds up with positive surface tension
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.statement: Because adsorption requires a surface tension greater than zero, films or threads of creeping protoplasm do not form an encysting membrane, and an organism forms its cyst or cell-wall only when its protoplasm has developed a positive surface tension and gathered into a roughly spherical body.

claims.title: Winter encystment and winter-egg shells relate to temperature effects on adsorption
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.statement: Since a rise of temperature reduces adsorbability (and surface tension), lower temperature favours adsorption and membrane formation, which probably accounts for the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter and the strong shells or capsules of winter eggs.

claims.title: Chondriosomes and similar fibrils are surface-tension clumps drawn along the cell axis
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.statement: The mitochondria, chondriosomes and similar granules and fibrils of cells are not special entities with specific functions but clumps of heterogeneous cell contents gathered by surface tension and drawn out along the cell axis by osmotic currents arising from surface energy and adsorption, revealing a field of force an

claims.title: Potassium salts concentrate where cell-surface tension is weak
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.statement: Potassium salts, like inorganic substances generally, raise surface tension and therefore concentrate at those parts of a cell surface where the tension is weak, so their localised accumulation (shown by Macallum's cobalt-nitrite method) indicates inequalities of surface tension.

claims.title: Conjugation outgrowths and root-hairs arise at sites of potassium concentration
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.statement: The bulges that begin conjugation in algae such as Pleurocarpus and Mesocarpus, and the root-hair outgrowth of Equisetum spores, arise where surface tension is weakened, and these sites coincide with heavy concentrations of potassium salts, which disperse when the cell becomes symmetrical again.

claims.title: Potassium accumulates at the bases of cilia and flagella
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.statement: Ciliate and flagellate cells show a characteristic accumulation of potassium at and near the base of their cilia, which accounts (through weakened surface tension) for the small protuberance where a flagellum arises and the ridge at the base of a row of cilia.

claims.title: Unicellular forms and their asymmetries follow surface molecular forces
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption
claims.statement: In unicellular organisms not only the general configuration but also the departures from symmetry can be correlated with molecular forces, especially local variations of surface tension, acting in their fluid or semifluid surfaces.

claims.title: Forms of cell-aggregates are shaped chiefly by surface tension toward minimal areas
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: The forms of cells in contact with one another, and ultimately of tissues, are determined especially by surface tension, which shows itself in the production of surfaces of (relatively) minimal area.

claims.title: Right-angled cell walls arise because older walls solidify before new partitions form
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: Plant cell walls often meet at right angles (Sachs’s Rule) because an earlier wall has usually become solid and rigid before a later partition joins it, so the fluid partition sets itself at equal angles, i.e. perpendicular, to the rigid wall.

claims.title: Shape of paired cells depends on relative tensions at outer surface and partition
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: Whether two adjacent cells in a filament (as in Nostoc and its allies) are separated by flat partitions, are hemispherical, or are each more than a hemisphere depends on the relative magnitudes of the tension at the outer cell surface and at the boundary between the cells.

claims.title: Tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120°, regardless of cell size
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: In sections of tissues such as plant parenchyma, as in a froth of soap-bubbles, cell walls meet three at a time at angles of 120° whatever the sizes of the cells, while the relative sizes of neighbouring cells determine only the curvature of the walls.

claims.title: Four cells of a segmenting egg never meet in a point; a polar furrow is always present
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: In the four-celled stage of a segmenting egg whose cells are in full fluid contact, the four cells cannot meet in a single point; a short intermediate partition (the polar furrow) must be present, and reports of four cells meeting in a simple cross are due to error or imperfect observation.

claims.title: Strong cell–cell tension relative to cell–medium tension makes cells round off
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: Where the tension at cell–cell contacts exceeds that at cell–medium surfaces, the external angle between neighbouring cells is less than 120°, and if the cell–cell tension equals or exceeds the sum of the other two the cells touch only at a point, which explains rounded-off blastomeres separated by spaces.

claims.title: An epidermis’s physical characters follow simply from its lying on the outside
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: The fundamental character of an epidermis is that it lies on the outside of the cell mass, and its main physical features (flattened, rectangular cells meeting partitions at near right angles) follow from that position through unequal and consolidated tensions in its outer walls.

claims.title: Hexagons are regular only where cells are equal in size and forces uniform
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: Perfectly regular hexagonal cell patterns occur only where the cells are uniform in size and subject to uniform forces, as in the retinal pigment epithelium; where cell sizes vary (intestinal epithelium, parenchyma) or growth adds directional traction, the hexagons become irregular or elongated.

claims.title: Cylinders or spheres pressed into full surface contact form hexagons
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: Whenever cylinders or spheres of similar size are brought into complete surface contact by any uniform force (surface tension, growth pressure or external pressure), they tend to form a pattern of hexagons in section or surface view, each meeting six neighbours with 120° angles.

claims.title: Close-packed corallites of varying size are on average hexagonal
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: In colonial corals whose corallites are in close contact, the corallites are squeezed into hexagonal prisms; where their sizes vary irregularly they are hexagonal on average, some having fewer and some more than six sides, while loosely bundled corallites stay cylindrical.

claims.title: The bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism capped by rhombic-dodecahedral facets
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: The hive-bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism closed at one end by three rhombic facets of a rhombic dodecahedron meeting at about 109° 28′, the configuration that encloses a given volume with the least surface.

claims.title: Comb geometry arises from surface tension in semi-fluid wax, not bee design
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: The regular hexagonal and pyramidal geometry of the bee’s comb is produced automatically by surface tension acting on the cell walls while the wax (or the wasp’s paper pulp) is still semi-fluid, the insects merely building thin tubular cells packed closely together; it is not due to the bee seeking to economise wax.

claims.title: Parenchyma cells are generally rhombic dodecahedra, ideal froths tetrakaidecahedra
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: A perfectly fluid froth of equal cells is divided into Kelvin’s fourteen-sided tetrakaidecahedra, but in plant parenchyma, given restraint and imperfect fluidity, the cells generally take the rhombic dodecahedral form even under symmetrical conditions.

claims.title: Physical laws govern the whole configuration of later-stage segmenting eggs
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: The whole configuration of an egg in advanced stages of segmentation is determined by simple physical laws just as in the two- and four-celled stages, even though the mathematics becomes too difficult to follow.

claims.title: Polar-furrow arrangements follow relative cell sizes, not species identity
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: Small changes in the relative sizes of the four cells carry the median partition and its polar furrows through all their possible arrangements, which correspond to those observed in various embryos; these arrangements are physical phenomena distributed without relation to zoological classification, not species characte

claims.title: No evidence that physical forces give way to unknown vital agencies in development
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates
claims.statement: Although forces other than surface tension act in a growing embryo, there is no evidence at any stage that physical forces cease to govern its material form and are replaced by agencies unknown to physics.

claims.title: Minimal bisecting walls cut the longest axis and alternate at right angles
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: For a rectangular cell to be divided equally by a partition of least area, the partition must cut across its longest axis, and in successive bisections each new partition must be at right angles to the one before.

claims.title: A new cell wall has the least area that can enclose the given volume (Errera)
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: The fundamental rule of cell division is that the incipient partition of a dividing cell takes the least possible area that can divide the given volume; Sachs’s rule of successive divisions at right angles is a subordinate case of this principle.

claims.title: A cell cutting off under ~3/10 of its volume uses a curved corner wall, not a plane
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: When a cubical or rectangular cell divides unequally and the smaller part is less than about three-tenths of the whole, the minimal partition is a quarter-cylinder cutting off one corner rather than a plane wall; below about 0.15 of the volume a spherical octant in a corner is smaller still.

claims.title: A quadrant-shaped flat cell divides by a curved anticlinal wall about 3:7 along its side
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: A flattened cell shaped like a quadrant of a circle divides into equal halves by a circular-arc anticlinal wall meeting the side and periphery at right angles, cutting off about 55° 22′ of the arc and starting about three-tenths of the radius from the centre, since this is the shortest bisecting wall.

claims.title: Sector cells divide anticlinally only between 62½° and 90°, otherwise periclinally
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: A sector-shaped (triangular) cell is likely to divide by an anticlinal wall only when its angle of arc lies between about 62½° and 90°; narrower, more tapering cells divide by a periclinal wall, which then has the smaller area.

claims.title: Uniform growth of a disc makes its daughter cells divide at different times
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: Uniform, symmetrical growth of a flattened disc does not imply uniform growth of its cells: after a quadrant divides into triangular and quadrilateral halves, the triangular cell gains area faster and reaches division size first (at about 1.345 times the radius, against about 1.517 for the quadrilateral).

claims.title: Successive minimal-area divisions leave quadrilateral cells forming an epidermis
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: Successive minimal-area divisions of a disc soon leave only quadrilateral cells at the periphery, which divide radially, producing a superficial layer of parallel-sided cells (an epidermis) contrasting with the irregular cells beneath.

claims.title: The arrangement of the first eight cells is not a constant character of a species
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: A particular arrangement of cell partitions at the eight-celled stage is not a specific or constant character of an organism; within a single species such as the frog, several essentially different arrangements occur.

claims.title: All surface groupings of eight cells belong to one of thirteen types
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: Because n cells sharing a common outer boundary and meeting three at a time need n − 3 intermediate partitions, every possible grouping of eight cells all reaching the surface belongs to one of thirteen topological types, so all drawings of such eight-celled structures represent one of these types.

claims.title: Most stable cell groupings spread contacts evenly; unstable ones concentrate them
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: Among the possible arrangements of a small group of cells, the most stable (and therefore commonest) are those in which the cell-to-cell contacts are most evenly divided among the cells, and the least stable are those in which one cell has a predominant number of contacts.

claims.title: Few partition patterns recur across organisms regardless of classification
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: Because a closed surface divided into a small number of faces admits only a small number of arrangements, the same few configurations of cells (and of parts and organs) recur in all kinds of plants and animals with no relation to biological classification.

claims.title: A coral fossula reflects space-partitioning, not higher bilateral organisation
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: The asymmetrical chamber (fossula) of corals such as Heterophyllia and Zaphrentis arises as one of the possible arrangements of septa meeting three at a time, and gives no grounds for interpreting it as a sign of bilaterality or a higher grade of organisation.

claims.title: Stomata lie in rows on oblong-celled leaves and scattered on polygonal-celled ones
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: Because the stomatal mother cell is cut off by a minimal partition whose form depends on epidermal cell shape, stomata are arranged in regular rows where epidermal cells are oblong (as in hyacinth) and irregularly where they are polygonal (as in Sedum).

claims.title: Pollen-grain shape depends on whether walls harden before the tetrad separates
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: Pollen grains and spores formed as tetrahedral tetrads keep the plane facets and sharp angles of the tetrad if their walls solidify before the grains separate, but become spherical if they separate while still soft.

claims.title: Outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: Because quadrangular cells subdivide by periclinal walls that strengthen the boundary while triangular cells divide by oblique anticlines, outward growth is greater over triangular cells, so buds and outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells, as is widely seen in cryptogams.

claims.title: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: A growing cell divides according to the shape it has reached, set by the ratio of its growth rate to its division frequency: if markedly oblong it divides transversely, if a little more than a hemisphere obliquely, and if less than a hemisphere by a vertical wall along its axis.

claims.title: Cell division pattern is the result, not the cause, of the form of the growing mass
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)
claims.statement: The form of a growing organism regulates the form and number of the cells that compose it: the cell network is the result, not the cause, of the overall configuration, which is caused by whatever processes make growth faster in one direction than another.

claims.title: Skeletal salts precipitate in dead or inactive matrix, not living protoplasm
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: Calcareous and other skeletal deposits are, as a rule, precipitated not within actively living protoplasm but in dead or inactive formed material, such as the intercellular matrix or the cell-wall, so their form is not directly shaped by the living cells.

claims.title: Sea-urchin larvae reared without lime develop healthily but lack skeletal rods and arms
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: Sea-urchin eggs reared in lime-free sea-water develop into apparently healthy larvae that lack the calcareous skeletal rods, and the long larval arms normally supported by those rods are suppressed; the organism can live without the material of its skeleton.

claims.title: Biological molecular asymmetry may originate from circularly polarised sunlight
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: The one-handed molecular asymmetry of organic products need not be a prerogative of life; it may have started from a non-vital asymmetric force, such as sunlight circularly polarised by reflection from the sea, which acts unequally on right- and left-handed molecules.

claims.title: Pearls and bony-fish otoliths share the structure of artificial calcospherites
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: The concentrically zoned, radiate structure of pearls and of the otoliths of molluscs and bony fishes is essentially the same as that of the calcospherites formed artificially when calcium carbonate is precipitated in albumin, implying the same physico-chemical mode of formation.

claims.title: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: Because rhythmic Liesegang precipitation arises from diffusion within the system itself, concentric zones in fish scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains cannot be assumed to record periodic external conditions such as seasons or day and night.

claims.title: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: Albumin increases the solubility of calcium carbonate and phosphate, whereas its breakdown products dissolve them much less; hence skeletal calcium salts are thrown down when proteins are broken down in metabolism, not by direct action of carbonic acid on a more soluble salt.

claims.title: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: Skeletal elements comparable in size to a single cell (sponge spicules, radiolarian and foraminiferal skeletons) are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, whereas massive skeletons such as vertebrate bones are shaped by gravity, muscle action and mechanical loads, so scale produces essential differences i

claims.title: A straight-growing spicule confined to a cell surface grows along a geodetic
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: A spicule tending to grow in a straight line but confined within or against a cell wall grows along a geodetic of the cell surface, so in a spherical or ellipsoidal cell it becomes a circular arc, an elliptic arc or, most often, a portion of a spiral in space, as in C- and S-shaped sponge spicules.

claims.title: Like spicules in silica and calcite show form is set by external forces, not chemistry
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
