claims.statement: Holothurian spicules of calcium carbonate reproduce, often indistinguishably, the forms of siliceous sponge spicules, which shows that such spicule forms are determined by the external forces acting during growth (cell confinement), not by the chemical nature or molecular structure of the material.

claims.title: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: Skeletal material deposited between cells or within their partitions takes the shape of the cell junctions: in a layer of equal cells, where partitions meet in threes at 120°, it forms triradiate spicules with rays at 120°, and in a solid aggregate of four cells it forms tetrahedral four-rayed spicules with rays at abo

claims.title: Six-rayed hexactinellid spicules reflect cubic, not closest, packing of vesicles
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: The six-rayed spicules of hexactinellid sponges form because the vesicles that mould them are arranged in linear series (cubic packing) rather than closest packing, so the spicules follow the angles and edges of a system of cubes instead of hexagons or dodecahedra.

claims.title: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: Radiolarian species show vague distributions in space and time: many occur worldwide without specific geographic limits, families and genera appear unchanged since the Cambrian, and a small sample of sediment typically contains scores or hundreds of forms with no local predominance of one species.

claims.title: Agglutinated protist shells form by surface energy, not choice or skill
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: The building of agglutinated shells from sand-grains, spicules or diatom frustules by rhizopods such as Difflugia is a purely physical consequence of foreign particles being trapped in the surface film by surface energy, with selectivity explained by specific surface-energies rather than volition.

claims.title: Hexagonal lattice shells form as silica collects in grooves between surface vesicles
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: When the outer surface of a radiolarian is covered by a layer of nearly equal froth-like vesicles, silica secreted or adsorbed at the surface collects in the grooves between them, producing a spherical shell of rods in a regular hexagonal network; less regular vesicles give less regular meshes, and repeated layers give

claims.title: Lattice-shell form is independent of the material, being moulded on vesicles
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: Spherical hexagonal lattice shells are equally regular whether made of silica (oceanic Radiolaria), strontium sulphate (Acantharia) or an organic chitin-like substance (Clathrulina), showing that their form comes from moulding on an underlying vesicular structure, not from the material.

claims.title: Callimitra's skeleton is formed on the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of four cells
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: The skeleton of the nassellarian Callimitra reproduces the interfacial film system of four soap-bubbles in tetrahedral contact (six plane interfaces meeting in threes at 120°, edges meeting near 109°), so it must have been formed at the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of cells.

claims.title: Regular dodecahedral radiolarian shells cannot arise by crystal-like space partitioning
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: Radiolaria show all five regular polyhedra, including the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron which cannot occur in crystals; therefore the regular radiolarian dodecahedron is not produced by the space-partitioning principles that govern crystallisation.

claims.title: Twenty-spined Radiolaria have hexagonal symmetry, not Müller's arrangement
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: In twenty-spined Radiolaria the spines pass through the facets of a modified hexagonal prism, giving a true hexagonal symmetry of two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two whorls of six intermediate spines; Müller's law of five four-spined circles with no polar spine does not properly apply to any case.

claims.title: Radiolarian axial polarity arises in the central protoplasm, unexplained by mechanics
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons
claims.statement: The polar symmetry of the radial spines in Radiolaria cannot be explained by any obvious mechanical forces of the peripheral froth; it arises in the central living protoplasm, and may reflect obscure but still physical directive forces analogous to Lehmann's 'Gestaltungskraft' in fluid crystals.

claims.title: Annular, longitudinal and spiral wall thickenings of plant cells are cylinder geodetics
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.statement: The three kinds of geodetic on a cylinder (parallel rings, straight longitudinal lines and helical spirals) are all realised in the local wall thickenings of cylindrical plant cells and vessels, and the helical geodetic in the spiral coils of insect tracheae and tracheids.

claims.title: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.statement: On a right cone the spiral geodetic coils more and more closely as the cone narrows, and the sutural line and parallel striations of a turreted spiral shell such as Turritella are geodetics of this kind.

claims.title: Two crossing systems of geodetic spirals are a common source of reticulated patterns
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.statement: In organic structures two opposite systems of geodetic spirals often coexist and interfere, forming a criss-cross arrangement, and this is a very common source of reticulated patterns.

claims.title: Muscle fibres on hollow organs arrange themselves along geodesic curves
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.statement: A contractile fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface first pulls itself into the shortest path on that surface before it can constrict the organ, so the muscle fibres of hollow organs such as the heart, stomach, arteries and intestine automatically lie along geodesics (annular and longitudinal in a simple tube).

claims.title: Heart and stomach fibres stay geodetic after the twisting of the primitive tube
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.statement: The heart and stomach develop from simple tubes by dilatation and twisting; their originally circular and longitudinal fibres remain geodetic on the distorted surface, new geodetic systems (such as the oblique stomach fibres) appear on new pouches, and the heart contracts effectively only because its fibres run the sho

claims.title: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics
claims.statement: Small ciliated and flagellated organisms cannot steer, but by rotating about their long axis while swimming they convert a constant body-fixed swerve into a continually changing direction in space, so they travel along a helix around a nearly straight axis rather than in a circle.

claims.title: Horns, molluscan shells, foraminifera and sunflower florets follow the logarithmic spiral
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The permanent spiral forms found in organisms, such as the horns of ruminants, molluscan and foraminiferal shells and the arrangement of florets in the sunflower, are all logarithmic spirals; the outline of a cordate leaf is the one spiral-like organic outline that is not.

claims.title: A spiral needs a deflecting force carried by the growing body, not an external one
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: A deflecting force of constant direction acting from outside, such as wind or gravity, can only bend a growing structure towards a limiting direction and never into a spiral; a spiral arises only when the deflecting force is intrinsic to the growing body and turns with the direction of growth, as the columellar muscle

claims.title: A constant ratio of longitudinal to transverse growth rates yields a logarithmic spiral
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: In a tubular structure whose growth is unequal on its two sides, a constant ratio between the rates of growth in the longitudinal and transverse directions generally produces a logarithmic spiral, the value of the ratio fixing the spiral's constant angle, with the circle and the straight line as limiting cases.

claims.title: The scorpioid cyme traces a true logarithmic spiral
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: In a scorpioid cyme, where each shoot arises from the last on the same side at an equal angle and successive shoots diminish in length in a constant ratio, the shoots are tangents to a true logarithmic spiral; in the helicoid cyme the same spiral is present but hidden by a superimposed twist.

claims.title: The shell grows in size without changing its shape
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: A spiral shell, like the animal within it, increases in size without changing its shape, even though it grows at one end only; this constant similarity of form under terminal growth is the defining property of the logarithmic spiral and of no other curve.

claims.title: Each increment of a spirally grown structure is a gnomon to the whole before it
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: In horns, shells and all other organic forms showing a logarithmic spiral, the existing structure is partly old and partly new, and each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the whole pre-existing structure, that is, an addition that leaves the enlarged whole similar to what it was before.

claims.title: Logarithmic spirals occur in accreted hard parts, not in simultaneously formed soft parts
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The logarithmic spiral should not be found in structures whose parts are produced simultaneously, such as the margin of a leaf or the contour of a fish, but in hard parts built of successive, permanently retained increments, such as shell, tusk, horn and claw, where it is usually accompanied by lines of growth.

claims.title: Whorl breadths of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod shells form a geometric progression
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: Careful measurement shows that the breadths of successive whorls along a radius of the Nautilus shell, and of spiral ammonitoid and gastropod shells generally, are in geometric progression, so that these shells are logarithmic spirals (for Nautilus each whorl is about three times as broad as the one before).

claims.title: All differences of form between shells are differences of degree in a few growth ratios
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The form of any turbinate shell is fixed by a small set of factors (shape of the generating curve, its rate of growth, its rate of rotation about the pole, its rate of translation along the axis, and its inclination), and all differences of form between one shell and another are differences of degree in the relative ma

claims.title: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is about 80° in Nautilus, where each whorl is about three times as broad as its predecessor, and in ordinary ammonitoid and typical spiral gastropod shells is seldom below 80° and usually between 80° and 85°.

claims.title: Separation or overlap of whorls reflects the growth-rate ratio of outer to inner border
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: Whether the whorls of a spiral shell stand apart, just touch, or overlap (up to complete involution, as in Nautilus pompilius versus N. umbilicatus) depends only on the ratio of the rate of growth of the outer border of the tube to that of its inner border.

claims.title: Spiral constants of shells give no valid evidence of ancestry
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The constant angle of a shell's spiral, like its size, is no evidence of which form is more primitive or ancestral, nor does an intermediate angle show that a shell is intermediate in time or descent; phylogenetic series built from straight, loosely coiled and closely coiled cephalopod shells are not supported by the m

claims.title: Mathematical morphology can reveal orthogenetic series and warn of convergence
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: Progressive change of growth ratios along a series of allied forms (orthogenesis) is real in some lineages, and the mathematical study of form can detect such series where they are not obvious, while also showing that strong resemblances of form may arise independently as numerical coincidences.

claims.title: Ontogenetic change in spiral angle explains narrowing-whorled and uncoiling ammonites
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: In some ammonoids the spiral angle changes progressively during growth: where it increases the whorls become narrower (as in Oekotraustes), and where it diminishes towards zero the coil opens out into an almost straight curve (as in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites).

claims.title: Dissimilar turbinate shells share similar spiral angles and differ mainly in apical angle
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: Shells as different in appearance as Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis differ very little in their spiral angle (the ratio of radial to tangential growth) and differ in form mainly in the apical angle of the enveloping cone, which is set by the rate of translation along the axis relative to growth.

claims.title: Bivalve growth lines are coaxial curves set by direction-dependent growth rate
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The lines of growth on bivalve shells are not concentric but coaxial curves through the umbo, and they arise because the rate of growth varies as a simple function of direction; in the simplest case the lines are coaxial circles (as in Anomia), and with more complex functions they are coaxial ellipses or other figures

claims.title: Incomplete moulting gives Estheria a mollusc-like spiral shell with growth lines
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The bivalved carapace of the crustacean Estheria resembles a lamellibranch shell, with lines of growth and a logarithmic spiral of small angle, because its moult is incomplete: each old carapace is retained and the new one grows beneath it and projects beyond its edge.

claims.title: Brachiopod spiral arm direction follows shell shape through spatial constraint
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The form and direction of brachiopod spiral arms (brachidia) are determined by their initial curvature and the space and pressures within the shell, so that long outwardly directed spirals should go with transversely elongated shells such as Spirifer, inwardly directed spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and di

claims.title: Ammonite shell and aptychus are two parts of a once united split cone
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The shell and the aptychus of ammonites are probably the ventral and dorsal portions of a once united conical shell split by unequal growth, as in pteropods; other cephalopods retain only one of the two, the ventral one as the shell of Nautilus and the dorsal one as the shell of Sepia or Spirula.

claims.title: Cephalopod septa take the form of minimal surfaces like soap films
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: Because a septum is first laid down as an elastic membrane under uniform pressure, it takes the shape of a soap film with the same boundary, a surface of minimal area: spherical in a straight cone with a perpendicular attachment, ellipsoidal with an oblique attachment, and saddle-shaped where the line of attachment is

claims.title: The fine frilling of ammonite sutures is a surface-tension phenomenon
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: The minutely branched, arborescent outline superposed on the lobes and saddles of some ammonite sutures, with branches ending in rounded arcs, is a surface-tension phenomenon of the same kind as the patterns made by milk on a greasy plate or oil on an alkaline solution.

claims.title: The same spiral shell forms recur across unrelated groups, all ages and all seas
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: Spiral shell forms appear with little relation to the kind of animal producing them, recurring in gastropods, cephalopods, foraminifera and tube worms, and mathematically identical forms recur in every geological period and are found mixed together regardless of climate or local conditions.

claims.title: Natural Selection plays no necessary part in producing spiral shell forms
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral
claims.statement: Natural Selection, in any strictly biological sense, has no necessary share in producing the varied forms of spiral shells, which arise from differences in growth rates and ratios.

claims.title: Single-chambered foraminiferal shells take the form of fluid drops under surface tension
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: The form of a single-chambered foraminiferal shell is explained by the laws of surface tension: the protoplasm behaves as a fluid drop whose equilibrium shape is fixed when it acquires its solid covering.

claims.title: Foraminifera are spiral because they grow by permanent increments added outside
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Foraminiferal shells tend towards a spiral form because they grow by successive increments added to the exterior, each of which becomes a permanent, rigid part of the structure.

claims.title: Septa are convex outwards in Foraminifera and concave in Nautilus because of pressure side
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Foraminiferal septa are convex outwards and those of Nautilus concave outwards because the pressure each membrane resisted when it set lay on opposite sides; in both cases the septum tends to a surface of minimal area.

claims.title: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, large shells similar to small ones
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, recognisable by continued similarity: the large many-chambered shell has the same shape as the smaller, younger shell.

claims.title: Fusulina whorls increase in ratio 1:1.5, a spiral of constant angle about 86°
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: In Fusulina the breadths of successive whorls stand in the nearly constant ratio 1 : 1.5, which corresponds to a logarithmic spiral with a constant angle of about 86°, like that of ammonites.

claims.title: Constant chamber-size ratio follows from growth proportional to existing mass
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Each foraminiferal chamber bears a constant ratio of size to the next because the rate of increase at each instant is proportional to the whole existing mass of the homogeneous organism.

claims.title: Minimum potential energy plus proportional growth yields the logarithmic spiral
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Each new protoplasmic drop settles in a position of minimum potential energy (including minimal area), which makes each chamber similar to the last; proportional growth of size then gives the series the form of a logarithmic spiral. Rhumbler's specific 'law of the constant angle' of contact is too narrow an explanation

claims.title: Attached Foraminifera form plane spirals with whorls flattened on the attached side
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Most spiral Foraminifera are plane (discoid) spirals because some force keeps the chambers in a plane, especially in forms that live attached to rock or seaweed, whose whorls are flattened on the attached surface; freely floating forms such as Globigerina tend towards helicoid spirals.

claims.title: Many foraminiferal species and genera may be temporary manifestations of variability
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Because very slight changes in surface energies could turn one foraminiferal form into another, many forms distinguished as separate species and even genera may be no more than temporary manifestations of variability, as in Peneroplis.

claims.title: Foraminiferal forms follow such simple laws that none is fitter than another to survive
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Foraminiferal shells grow by laws so simple and so in harmony with their material and the forces acting on them that no form is better, fitter or less fit to survive than another, which accounts for the great diversity of types and their persistence since the Cretaceous.

claims.title: Identical foraminiferal forms may have arisen independently again and again
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: The possible lines of variation in Foraminifera may be so narrow and determinate that identical forms have arisen independently many times.

claims.title: Increased shell strength is not an advantage driving foraminiferal evolution
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Against Rhumbler, niceties of shell form have little effect on survival: delicate foraminiferal shells survive unbroken in vast numbers, so breakage is not a constant danger and increased strength is not a selective advantage guiding their evolution.

claims.title: Foraminifera are absent from coarse gravels because of hydraulic sorting by currents
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Foraminiferal shells are absent from coarse sands and gravels not because they avoid concussion but because light shells are sorted by currents like any other graded sediment, settling where water is still.

claims.title: Forms set by physical forces undermine inference of kinship from similarity
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera
claims.statement: Insofar as forms depend on physical forces and their variations on simple quantitative changes in those forces, similarity of form cannot safely be taken as evidence of consanguinity, and the link between classification and phylogeny must be revised.

claims.title: Rhinoceros horn is a plane logarithmic spiral from constant front-to-back growth ratio
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: The rhinoceros horn grows faster anteriorly than posteriorly in a constant ratio, so it curves as a logarithmic spiral; lying in the median plane, it has no lateral twist and forms a plane spiral.

claims.title: Paired horns of ruminants are conjugate, mirror-image spirals
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: The paired horns of hollow-horned ruminants are conjugate spirals, the left horn being the mirror image of the right.

claims.title: Most horns are logarithmic spirals from constant unequal growth on opposite sides
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: In the great majority of horns the curve is a continuous logarithmic spiral, caused by unequal rates of growth parallel to the axis on opposite sides of the horn, the inequality keeping a constant ratio throughout growth.

claims.title: Goat and sheep horns form a series of homologous spirals of increasing angle
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: Horns of wild goats and sheep form a series of homologous logarithmic spirals with increasing constant angle: under 40° in Oryx, under 70° in the Scinde wild goat, about 75° in Ovis ammon and a little more in the Highland ram.

claims.title: Argali horns share a spiral angle but differ in their shearing (helical) component
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: Among closely allied wild sheep (Argali) the constant angle of the horn's logarithmic spiral is nearly the same, and the species differ chiefly in the helical shearing component.

claims.title: A horn is a plane spiral only if fastest and slowest growth lie diametrically opposite
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: If the maximal and minimal growth rates around the basal growth zone of a horn lie diametrically opposite, the horn is a plane spiral; otherwise it is a spiral in space with a helical component, which is the usual case because the horn's field of force has no such plane of symmetry.

claims.title: Uneven adhesion of the horn sheath to its bony core can itself produce the spiral
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: Unequal retardation of the growing horn sheath by its adhesion to the bony core can produce the same spiral as unequal growth, and is probably a very important and sometimes the chief factor in horn curvature.

claims.title: The thicker the horn, the greater its spiral curvature
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: On the whole, thicker horns are more strongly spirally curved than slender ones, because a larger cross-section allows greater differences in growth or retardation between opposite sides.

claims.title: Sinuous growth lines on non-cylindrical horns result from torsional strain
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: Horns that grow as curves of double curvature undergo torsional strain, because the sheath is attached to the core, and this strain warps the rings into the sinuous growth lines predicted by St Venant for a twisted non-circular prism; such lines are absent from cylindrical ox horns.

claims.title: Twining of climbing stems results from unequal growth on different sides
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: The revolving nutation of twining plants, like the helicoid growth of an antelope horn, is caused by unequal rates of growth on different sides of the stem, the difference being that in the stem growth occurs along its whole length.

claims.title: Stem torsion on rough supports is a mechanical couple from adhesion, not an adaptation
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: Twining stems become twisted on rough supports but not on smooth ones because adhesion to the rough support sets up a mechanical couple, so Darwin's adaptive explanation (gaining rigidity) is unnecessary.

claims.title: A pair of antlers is confined to a single smooth spheroidal surface
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: The branches of a pair of deer antlers are confined to a single, more or less spheroidal or ellipsoidal curved surface, the two antlers forming one mirror-symmetric surface whose tine tips lie on a continuous curve; the antler is essentially a surface, whereas a horn is an axial rod.

claims.title: Claws, beaks and teeth grown by unequal permanent accretion are logarithmic spirals
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: Wherever a structure grows by permanent increments with unequal longitudinal growth about its axis, as in nails, claws, beaks and teeth, it always tends to the form of a logarithmic spiral, which becomes conspicuous only when the structure is long.

claims.title: Elephant and American mastodon tusks are the same spiral as the mammoth's, only shorter
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion
claims.statement: The tusks of living elephants and American mastodons follow essentially the same logarithmic spiral as the mammoth's great spiral tusks and differ only in size, so that if they grew long enough they would become equally spiral.

claims.title: Spirals of sunflower, thistle and cone are deformations of helices on a stem
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: The logarithmic spirals of flat or convex inflorescences and the helices on elongated stems are one phenomenon: the fir-cone, teasel, thistle and sunflower heads are successive geometric deformations of a long, nearly cylindrical stem, on which the same arrangement appears as helices.

claims.title: Sunflower spirals intersect isogonally, rarely orthogonally
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: Against Church, the spirals in a sunflower disc intersect isogonally (at a constant angle), and orthogonal intersection is only a particular and probably infrequent case.

claims.title: Phyllotactic spirals follow inevitably from similar parts produced at regular intervals
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: There is no subtle mystery in phyllotaxis: the steady production of similar parts, similarly placed, at similar successive intervals of time necessarily produces symmetrical patterns (helices on a cylinder, logarithmic spirals on a surface containing the pole), which are a secondary mathematical result rather than a pr

claims.title: Parastichy counts on fir-cones are nearly constant within a species
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: The numbers of conspicuous parastichies on fir-cones are on the whole very constant within a species, e.g. 5 and 3 in the Norway spruce and 8 and 5 in the common larch.

claims.title: Parastichy numbers change when the structure varies greatly in size
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: Phyllotactic parastichy numbers vary with the size of the whole structure, as in sunflower discs where one species may show 34/55, 55/89 or even 89/144 rows.

claims.title: Right- and left-handed parastichy directions occur about equally often
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: Within a species, cones with a given parastichy arrangement are nearly equally divided between right-handed and left-handed spiral directions (e.g. 224 versus 243 among 467 Norway spruce cones).

claims.title: One Fibonacci parastichy pair necessarily entails all the lower pairs
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: Following Tait, if a single genetic spiral exists and one pair of parastichy numbers from the series 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… is present, all the lower pairs of the series are necessarily present in the same system.

claims.title: Most phyllotaxis has between two and three leaves per turn of the genetic spiral
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: The prevalence of Fibonacci parastichy numbers arises because in the great majority of fir-cones and other phyllotactic systems there are more than two but fewer than three leaves in one turn of the genetic spiral (t = 2); other observed series correspond to t = 3, 4, 5.

claims.title: Which parastichies are conspicuous depends on leaf proportions, not on divergence
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: Which of the implicit spiral families is conspicuous does not depend on the angle of divergence but on the proportions of the leaves or scales, strictly on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboid circumscribing each leaf-area.

claims.title: Convergence of phyllotactic ratios to the golden mean has no biological significance
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: That the phyllotactic fractions 1/2, 2/3, 3/5… converge to 0.618…, the golden mean, is a mathematical coincidence without biological significance; the precise divergence angle and orthostichies are likewise unimportant.

claims.title: Close approximations to the golden mean are rare; poor ones like 2/3 are common
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: Against the 'ideal angle' theory, phyllotactic arrangements that closely approximate the golden mean (8/13, 13/21, 34/55 and higher) are comparatively rare, while poorer approximations such as 3/5, 2/3 and 1/2 are extremely common.

claims.title: Leaf exposure is changed far more by internode length than by divergence angle
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: If leaves benefit from being spread apart for exposure to air, lengthening the axis to separate them vertically has a far greater effect than any adjustment of the divergence angle, so the azimuthal 'ideal angle' cannot be the plant's means of optimising exposure.

claims.title: The Fibonacci series has no adaptive role introduced by natural selection
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis
claims.statement: The Fibonacci series in phyllotaxis, its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis that natural selection introduced it into plant structure have no place in the study of botanical phenomena.

claims.title: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: Hard-shelled eggs, while often pointed, are never flattened or discoidal: they are prolate, never oblate, solids of revolution.

claims.title: The most pointed eggs are those largest relative to the parent bird
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: As a very common rule, the most asymmetrical, posteriorly tapered eggs are those that are large relative to the parent bird (guillemot, curlews, sandpipers, terns), because they are under the greatest pressure in the oviduct; relatively large but symmetrical eggs (apteryx) imply a relatively large oviduct.

claims.title: A pullet's first eggs are smaller and rounder than its later ones
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: In the domestic fowl egg size and shape are directly related: a young pullet's first eggs are smaller and more nearly spherical than later ones, and breeds laying relatively smaller eggs lay rounder eggs.

claims.title: Peristaltic pressure behind the egg's middle makes the front blunt and rear pointed
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: Peristaltic contraction of the oviduct applies greatest pressure behind the middle of the forming egg, making the anterior end broader and the posterior narrower; the resulting tapered form also favours movement down the oviduct blunt end first.

claims.title: Egg shape is caused by radial pressure of the oviduct before the shell hardens
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: The essential cause of the form and variation of form of an egg is the regularly varying, largely radial pressure applied by successive rings of the oviduct before the shell solidifies, not adaptation to nesting circumstances.

claims.title: Egg form obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P, the equation of all eggs
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: The shape of an egg, as an extensible membrane filled with incompressible fluid under external pressure, obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P (external normal pressure plus membrane tension times total curvature equals internal pressure), which Thompson calls the equation of all eggs.

claims.title: Membrane tension peaks at the small end, where abnormal eggs are irregular
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: In conical eggs with spherical ends, the tension of the envelope is greatest at and near the small end, so that is where eggs are most likely to be distorted or to burst and where abnormal eggs most often show irregularities.

claims.title: Lateral spine of Schistosoma eggs is moulded in the ootype, not a species mark
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: Following Looss, the lateral spine of some Schistosoma eggs is moulded mechanically in a funnel-shaped part of the uterus, so lateral- and terminal-spined eggs are mechanical variants of one thing and do not show the existence of a separate species, S. mansoni.

claims.title: Sea-urchin shell outlines match liquid drops flattened by gravity
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: The vertical outlines of regular sea-urchin shells are the forms of liquid drops depressed by gravity (with the pull of the tube-feet), their degree of flattening varying with the tension or strength of the shell: strong shells (Palaeechinus) stay nearly spherical, soft flexible ones (Phormosoma) are most flattened.

claims.title: Vessel wall thickness tracks radius in large arteries but falls off in small ones
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: Under constant pressure the wall thickness of a blood-vessel should vary as its radius (P = T/R); because pressure falls with friction from large to small arteries, wall thickness is proportional to vessel size in larger vessels but becomes disproportionately thin in small arteries and capillaries.

claims.title: Heart wall thickness varies inversely with the mean curvature of the chamber
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: Within each cavity of the heart, where pressure is uniform, wall thickness t varies inversely as the mean curvature, t(1/r + 1/r′) = C, so the highly curved apex of the left ventricle is thinnest.

claims.title: Left ventricle wall is 6–7 times right's, matching the pressure ratio
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: The left ventricle requires six to seven times the dilating pressure of the right, and its wall thickness is greater in the same proportion.

claims.title: Blood-vessels are arranged for minimum effort and minimum wall-surface
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: The form and arrangement of blood-vessels are such that circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort and a minimum of wall-surface (and hence of friction).

claims.title: Small arterial branches leave at large angles, large branches at small angles
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: Small arterial branches come off the main stem at large angles (about 70°–90° for the smallest) and large branches at small angles, with equal branches diverging at equal angles, as Roux's rules state.

claims.title: Optimal branching angle has cosine equal to ratio of energy loss in trunk and branch
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures
claims.statement: The most favourable angle at which an arterial branch leaves its trunk is that whose cosine equals the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the main vessel to that in the branch (cos x = L/L′).

claims.title: Mechanical adaptations of form are demonstrable, unlike colour adaptations
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Unlike explanations of colouration as cryptic, warning or mimetic, which cannot be demonstrated, the fitness of organic form for mechanical functions such as swimming or flight can be analysed and established in detail by statics and dynamics.

claims.title: Bone is nearly as strong in tension as in compression
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Fresh bone resists tearing almost as well as it resists crushing (tensile strength about 9–12 and crushing strength about 13–16 kg per sq. mm), which makes it an economical structural material that can serve equally as tie or strut.

claims.title: Structures that must resist bending are built as hollow tubes
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Where stiffness against bending in all directions is required, organisms use a hollow cylindrical construction with little or no material in the core, as in the thin-walled, almost empty wing bones of long-winged birds such as the albatross, quills, and hollow stems of reeds and straw.

claims.title: Femoral wall thickness follows the bending-moment distribution along the shaft
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Because bending strain is greatest at mid-length of a bent column, the walls of a long bone such as the femur are thickest in the middle of the shaft and thin gradually towards the ends, so that wall thickness forms a graph of the bending moments along the bone.

claims.title: Trabeculae of cancellous bone follow the lines of compressive and tensile stress
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: The trabeculae of cancellous bone, as in the head of the femur, are arranged along the principal lines of compressive and tensile stress of the loaded bone, crossing one another at right angles, exactly as in the engineer's stress diagram of a comparable structure such as a crane-head.

claims.title: Shear removes obliquely laid trabeculae, leaving those aligned with stress lines
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Trabecular alignment arises because a trabecula laid down along a pressure or tension line is undisturbed, since there is no shear along those lines, whereas one lying obliquely is acted on by shearing force and displaced until it comes into line with the stress.

claims.title: Trabecular architecture remodels to new force patterns after malunited fracture
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Trabecular arrangement is produced by the forces acting on the bone, not by heredity: when a fracture heals with the parts displaced so that the stress lines are redistributed, the trabecular system is entirely remodelled within weeks to align with the new forces, even at a distance from the injury.

claims.title: Mechanical strain directly stimulates growth
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: A state of strain produced by stress is a direct stimulus to growth, so that tissues under increased load grow stronger or thicker, as when the fibula of a puppy whose tibia was excised grew as thick as or thicker than the normal tibia.

claims.title: The quadruped backbone is a double-armed cantilever girder, not an arch
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Because the jointed legs cannot resist the horizontal thrust of an arch and there is no tie between its ends, the backbone of a standing quadruped is not an arch, tied arch or bowstring girder but is mechanically comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.

claims.title: Height of vertebral spines is proportional to the local bending moment
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: In the vertebral girder, ligaments form the upper tension member, vertebral bodies the lower compression member and the spines the web, and the height of the vertebral spines at each point along the back is proportional to the bending moment at that point.

claims.title: Quadrupeds carry more of their weight on the fore-legs than on the hind-legs
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: In large quadrupeds the fore-legs carry considerably more of the body weight than the hind-legs (about 55–58% in horses and elephants and about two-thirds in camels and llamas).

claims.title: Heavy heads give tall withers spines; heavy tails give tall lumbar-sacral spines
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Animals whose head and neck form a large fraction of body weight have large bending moments over the fore-legs and correspondingly tall spines over the withers, whereas animals with light heads and heavy tails (anteaters, Diplodocus) or that are bipedal (kangaroo, Iguanodon) have their tallest spines over the loins and

claims.title: Aquatic mammals lack the tall withers and haunch spines of land quadrupeds
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Because buoyancy neutralises gravity so that there are no piers or cantilevers, all aquatic mammals (whales, seals, sea-cows) have lost the high arched vertebral spines over the withers and haunches, and aquatic birds have a weak, straight pelvis compared with terrestrial birds.

claims.title: Fish vertebral processes are set at about 120° to one another for uniform stiffness
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: In ordinary fishes such as cod and haddock (and partly in whales), the backbone is stiffened by three series of ligament-connected processes, dorsal and two transverse, arranged at nearly equal angles of 120°, which gives the greatest and most uniform strength possible for such a system.

claims.title: Backbone girders are shallower than engineers would build because flexibility is needed
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: The vertebral girder of large animals such as Diplodocus or Stegosaurus is shallower than an engineer's cantilever of comparable load, because a deeper girder would increase rigidity, and an animal's backbone must combine strength with flexibility.

claims.title: Skeletal form is largely a diagram of mechanical stress
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Skeletal form, as produced by growth, is to a very large extent determined by mechanical stress: material is laid down along the lines of stress so as to avoid shear, from the trabeculae within each bone to the arrangement of the bones in the whole skeleton.

claims.title: Mechanically shaped single bones are unreliable guides to phylogenetic affinity
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: Because the form of bones such as the scapula or vertebrae reflects the mechanical stresses of an animal's mode of life, resemblance or difference in a single such bone is no reliable evidence for or against blood-relationship, as in comparing Zeuglodon with whales.

claims.title: New mechanical forces modify many correlated parts together, not isolated bones
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency
claims.statement: When altered environment and habits introduce new forces, the resulting modifications of form appear not as isolated changes in single parts but as slow, general, graded modifications spread over many correlated parts or the whole body.

claims.title: Organic forms depart from mathematical ideals only as inanimate forms do
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: There is no essential difference between organic and inorganic form: living forms depart from ideal mathematical figures only because secondary forces act alongside the main one, just as no chain hangs as a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere.

claims.title: Specific differences in form are mainly differences of relative magnitude
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: The essential differences in form between species of the same group are differences of proportion or relative magnitude (Aristotle's 'excess and defect'), and these are the main cause of specific differences.

claims.title: Evolution varies the whole body in correlation, not character by character
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: Because dissimilar related fishes can be referred as wholes to the same figure in different coordinate systems, variation has proceeded on definite and orderly lines under a comprehensive law of growth affecting the whole structure, rather than by independent variation of separate parts as the usual conception of natur

claims.title: Related organisms differ by simple, symmetrical Cartesian transformations
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: The forms of related organisms can, as a general rule, be mapped onto one another by a simple and symmetrical deformation of a Cartesian coordinate grid, such as would result from a slight and simple change in the system of forces acting on the growing organism.

claims.title: Shear-deformed fossils are often mistaken for distinct species
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: Fossils in folded and inclined strata are often symmetrically deformed, usually by simple shear, so that they have been described as distinct species and occasionally even as new genera.

claims.title: Cannon-bones of ox, sheep and giraffe differ by a simple one-axis stretch
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: The cannon-bones of the ox, sheep and giraffe differ essentially only in relative length and breadth: at equal length, the sheep's bone is about two-thirds and the giraffe's about one-third as broad as the ox's.

claims.title: Ratio of radial to tangential growth about a node yields lanceolate, ovate, cordate leaves
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: Dicotyledon leaf shapes arise from growth radial to and transverse to radii about a node of no growth at the leaf base; increasing the ratio of tangential to radial growth carries the outline successively from lanceolate to ovate to cordate.

claims.title: The lopsided begonia leaf reflects unequal, not asymmetrical, growth
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: The two halves of a begonia leaf, one ovate and the other cordate, are mathematically similar figures produced by unequal growth on either side of the midrib, so that angles to equal radii on the two sides are in constant proportion.

claims.title: Organisms grow along stream lines definable by a mathematical transformation
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: The law of growth implied by representing related forms as orthogonal coordinate transformations is that the organism grows along stream lines definable by a suitable mathematical transformation; departures from orthogonality reflect the organism not being homogeneous and isotropic.

claims.title: Many organic forms arise from uniform expansive growth limited by local constraints
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: Many developmental changes of form are produced by local trammels or lines of constraint acting on otherwise uniform and symmetrical expansive growth, as a ligature turns a gourd into two globes or a muscular band makes the stomach a lopsided bubble.

claims.title: One transformation accounts for the differences between porcupine-fish and sunfish
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: Deforming the coordinate grid of Diodon (concentric circles and approximately hyperbolic curves) yields the outline of the sunfish Orthagoriscus, so that a single integral transformation accounts for all their apparently separate external differences while leaving the head region nearly unchanged.

claims.title: One harmonious deformation accounts for all skull differences among crocodilians
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: Across most crocodilian genera, the skull contours and even the shapes and sizes of individual bones and vacuities can be derived from one another by a single simple coordinate transformation, so that the skull of Notosuchus can be reconstructed bone for bone from that of Crocodilus.

claims.title: Perissodactyls are more closely related to hares and rabbits than to other ungulates
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: Since the rabbit's skull is derived from that of a primitive rhinoceros by a simple uniform downward flexure, the Perissodactyla are more closely related to the Leporidae than to other ungulates, and the Leporidae more closely to Perissodactyla than to other rodents.

claims.title: Fossil horse skulls match interpolated stages between Hyracotherium and Equus
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: Skulls interpolated by coordinate transformation between Hyracotherium (Eohippus) and Equus coincide closely with actual fossil skulls of Mesohippus and Protohippus, which therefore lie on the transformation series from Eohippus to the horse.

claims.title: Parahippus is a divergent offshoot, not on the direct line to Equus
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: Because the skull of Parahippus fits the interpolated transformation series from Eohippus to Equus poorly, Parahippus is not in the direct line of descent but represents a divergent branch of the Equidae.

claims.title: Ape and human skull differences form one continuous, roughly logarithmic transformation
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: The differences between the human skull and the skulls of the chimpanzee and baboon form one continuous integral deformation in which corresponding areas of the grid increase approximately logarithmically downwards and forwards, rather than separate modifications of jaws, braincase and face.

claims.title: Human and anthropoid skulls show divergent rather than linear evolutionary change
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: No continuous transformation series passes through known fossil and living human and anthropoid skulls (Mesopithecus, Pithecanthropus, Neanderthal, modern man), indicating that there is no single straight line of descent and that their variation has been divergent.

claims.title: Depth expansion and lateral compression vary inversely, conserving fish volume
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms
claims.statement: In related fishes, expansion in one transverse dimension tends to be compensated by compression in the other, so that volume at a given length changes less than linear dimensions; the plaice is about twice as deep and half as thick as the haddock and has almost the same length-weight coefficient k = W/L^3.

claims.title: A mathematical approach is essential to the study of organic form
claims.chapter: Ch. Epilogue: Epilogue
claims.statement: A mathematical aspect of morphology, largely neglected by morphologists, is interwoven with their problems, complementary to description, and essential to the proper understanding of form.

claims.title: Mathematical regularity and usefulness coincide in living forms
claims.chapter: Ch. Epilogue: Epilogue
claims.statement: What is most beautiful and regular in natural form, as in the bee's cell, is also found to be most useful and excellent.

claims.title: Living and non-living things are bound alike by physical and mathematical law
claims.chapter: Ch. Epilogue: Epilogue
claims.statement: Living and non-living things alike are governed by the same physical and mathematical laws.

claims.title: Rules governing nature need not be those of traditional mathematics
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: Although theoretical science requires that the systems it studies follow definite rules, those rules need not be the equation-based rules of traditional mathematics; the more general rules embodied in simple computer programs are equally candidates for describing the natural world.

claims.title: Programs with very simple rules often behave in complex ways
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: When simple computer programs are enumerated and run systematically, their behavior is often far from simple, and some of the very simplest programs produce behavior as complex as any known.

claims.title: Natural complexity arises because natural systems behave like typical programs
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: The great complexity seen across physical, biological and other natural systems is explained by those systems operating like typical simple programs, which commonly produce complex behavior, rather than by any special or supernatural source of complexity.

claims.title: Equation-based descriptions work for simple behavior but fail for complex behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: Describing behavior with mathematical equations succeeds for fairly simple behavior such as planetary motion but almost inevitably fails when behavior is more complex, and descriptions based on natural selection share this limitation; thinking in terms of programs allows meaningful statements about highly complex behav

claims.title: The same basic forms of behavior recur in simple programs regardless of details
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: Across the world of simple programs the same basic forms of behavior occur repeatedly almost independently of the underlying details of the rules, suggesting universal principles of overall behavior that should also apply to systems throughout nature.

claims.title: Simple programs yield a straightforward explanation of thermodynamic behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: The long-standing difficulty in understanding how thermodynamic behavior, including the Second Law of Thermodynamics, arises in physics can be resolved by a straightforward explanation drawn from the behavior of simple programs.

claims.title: Universal computation is possible in systems with one-sentence rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: Contrary to the assumption that computational universality requires elaborate systems like electronic computers, there exist systems whose rules can be stated in a single sentence that are nevertheless universal, able to perform any possible computation.

claims.title: Most systems with non-simple behavior are computationally irreducible
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: Predicting a system's outcome by a mathematical shortcut is normally possible only for special systems with simple behavior; other systems are computationally irreducible, so their behavior can be found only by tracing each step with roughly as much computational effort as the system itself expends.

claims.title: Computational irreducibility explains free will despite deterministic rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: Computational irreducibility provides an explanation of how humans, even if they follow definite underlying rules, can meaningfully be said to have free will.

claims.title: Complexity of simple abstract systems imposes fundamental limits on proof
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: The complexity found in simple abstract systems leads to fundamental limitations on mathematical proof, of the kind hinted at by Gödel's Theorem, and these limitations are relevant well beyond the narrow scope of current mathematics.

claims.title: Simple programs capture how genetic programs generate biological forms
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: Simple programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms and appear to capture essential mechanisms by which genetic programs generate observed biological forms, enabling new models and general abstract theories in biology.

claims.title: Sophisticated tasks need only extremely simple underlying rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: Contrary to engineering experience, performing sophisticated tasks does not require correspondingly complicated basic rules; extremely simple underlying rules, potentially implementable directly at the atomic scale, are often sufficient.

claims.title: Natural selection tends to oppose rather than generate complexity
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science
claims.statement: Darwinian natural selection does not clearly imply the generation of complexity and in many respects tends to oppose it; a different mechanism, the intrinsic complexity of simple programs, is responsible for most great complexity in biology.

claims.title: A rule-90-type cellular automaton produces a nested self-similar pattern
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: A one-dimensional cellular automaton in which each cell becomes black when exactly one of its two neighbors was black (rule 90), started from a single black cell, produces an intricate but regular nested pattern made of triangular pieces that are smaller copies of the whole.

claims.title: Rule 30 from a single black cell produces an irregular, complex pattern
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: The elementary cellular automaton rule 30, started from a single black cell, produces a highly irregular and complex pattern with almost no overall regularity, rather than a uniform, repetitive or nested one.

claims.title: Simple rules with simple initial conditions can yield highly complex behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: As a general phenomenon, a system with simple underlying rules started from simple initial conditions can nevertheless show highly complex behavior.

claims.title: Complexity from simple rules accounts for most complexity in nature
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: The generation of complex behavior from simple rules and simple initial conditions is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity seen in nature.

claims.title: Rule 30's center column shows no deviation from randomness over a million steps
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: The sequence of cell colors directly below the initial black cell in rule 30 does not repeat in its first million steps, and statistical tests show no meaningful deviation from perfect randomness.

claims.title: Some cellular automata make even average properties hard to predict
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Some simple cellular automata, such as rule 110, are more complex than random-looking ones like rule 30: they mix regular regions with interacting localized structures, so that even average properties of their behavior become very difficult to predict.

claims.title: Rule 110's fate can be determined only by running it
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Whether the localized structures in rule 110 eventually annihilate into a regular pattern or proliferate into randomness apparently cannot be determined in advance; the only reliable method is to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as needed.

claims.title: Rule 110 from one black cell becomes periodic with period 240 after about 2780 steps
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Rule 110 started from a single black cell resolves after about 2780 steps: one localized structure survives and interacts with periodic stripes from the left to give behavior that repeats every 240 steps.

claims.title: Identical cell rules yield diverse behaviors through different configurations
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Even though every cell of a cellular automaton follows the same rule, different configurations of cell colors can collectively produce many different kinds of behavior, such as regular backgrounds and distinct localized structures.

claims.title: Intuition that complex results need complex plans comes from engineering
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: The intuition that complex objects require complex construction plans fails because it derives from engineering, where designers restrict themselves to systems whose behavior they can understand and predict, a constraint nature does not share.

claims.title: Systems with simple rules and complex behavior are very common in nature
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Because nature is not constrained to predictable designs, systems whose simple rules produce complex behavior, like rule 30 and rule 110, are very common in nature.

claims.title: Complex cellular-automaton-like patterns are absent from historical ornament
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Historical ornamental art contains many repetitive patterns and some nested ones, but the more complicated patterns produced by simple cellular automata such as rule 30 never appear to have been used.

claims.title: Computers enable discoveries beyond working out mathematical equations
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Computers are not limited to computing the consequences of mathematical equations; directly studying the behavior of even the simplest computer programs yields fundamental scientific discoveries.

claims.title: Unknown phenomena are found only by systematic, preconception-free experiments
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Phenomena not already known to exist can be found only by very systematic and general experiments whose results are examined with as few preconceptions as possible.

claims.title: Lack of adequate computers delayed discovery of complexity from simple rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: A main reason that complexity from simple programs was not discovered before the 1980s is that computer technology powerful enough for the required large-scale exploratory experiments did not yet exist, together with a lack of intuition drawn from practical computing.

claims.title: It is usually very hard to foresee what even a simple program will do
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Practical computing shows that it is usually very difficult to foresee the behavior of even a simple program, which is why software bugs are so common; the simple structure of cellular automaton rules likewise does not make their behavior easy to predict.

claims.title: Primes follow simple generating rules yet are distributed seemingly randomly
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: The prime numbers, though generated by simple rules, have a distribution that seems in many respects random, an early instance of complexity from simple rules that mathematics largely neglected in favor of proving regularities.

claims.title: Complexity from simple programs was never discovered before despite many hints
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment
claims.statement: Although there were many hints over several centuries, including primes, digits of pi, iterated maps and the Game of Life, the basic phenomenon of simple programs producing complex behavior was never identified before Wolfram's work.

claims.title: Overall behavior types are similar across all kinds of simple programs
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Whatever kind of underlying rules a simple program uses (cellular automata, mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, register machines, symbolic systems), the overall behavior that emerges falls into the same few basic types first seen in elementary cellular automata.

claims.title: Most elementary cellular automata give fixed-size patterns from a single black cell
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Among the 256 elementary (two-color, nearest-neighbor) cellular automata started from a single black cell, about two-thirds produce patterns that stay of fixed size and about one-third produce patterns that grow forever, with about 14% yielding patterns more complicated than repetition.

claims.title: Ten of the 256 elementary cellular automata produce apparent randomness
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Of the 256 elementary cellular automata started from a single black cell, 10 produce patterns that seem in many respects random, falling into three basic forms, while 24 produce nested patterns falling into only three fundamentally different forms.

claims.title: Beyond a threshold, more complex rules do not give more complex behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: At least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules of a system does not lead to more complex overall behavior; in cellular automata, all the ingredients for the most complex behavior already exist in the elementary two-color rules.

claims.title: About 85% of three-color totalistic cellular automata behave regularly
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: About 85% of the 2187 three-color nearest-neighbor totalistic cellular automata produce behavior that is ultimately quite regular, while the remainder include rules with seemingly random behavior and rules with interacting localized structures like rule 110.

claims.title: No basic mobile automaton shows behavior beyond repetition or nesting
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: None of the 65,536 two-color mobile automata whose rule updates only the active cell shows behavior more complex than repetition or nesting; complex behavior appears only when the rule can also update the active cell's neighbors, and even then it is rare.

claims.title: Complex behavior correlates with many cells being active at once
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: In generalized mobile automata, complex behavior almost never occurs unless many cells are active simultaneously, and this correlation between overall activity and complexity helps explain why complexity is much more common in cellular automata than in mobile automata.

claims.title: Two- and three-state two-color Turing machines give only repetition or nesting
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: All 4096 two-state, two-color Turing machines, and all of the roughly three million three-state, two-color Turing machines started on a blank tape, ultimately produce only repetitive or nested patterns.

claims.title: Four head states suffice for random-looking Turing machine behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Two-color Turing machines with four head states can produce seemingly random behavior (about five in every million such rules), and allowing more than four states makes apparent randomness only slightly more common without changing the kinds of behavior seen.

claims.title: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only produce nested patterns
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Substitution systems in which each element is replaced according to its own color alone always produce nested patterns, so obtaining behavior more complicated than nesting requires rules that depend on at least one neighboring element.

claims.title: Substitution systems with deletion need three or more colors for complexity
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Among two-color substitution systems that allow elements to be destroyed, those with slow growth produce only simple repetitive patterns, but allowing three or four colors immediately makes patterns as random-looking as those of cellular automata possible.

claims.title: Text-editor-like search-and-replace rules can generate great complexity
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Sequential substitution systems, which repeatedly apply the first matching search-and-replace rule like a text editor, give only simple behavior with two replacements and two elements, but with three replacements about one in 10,000 random rules produces seemingly random behavior.

claims.title: One-element-deletion tag systems reduce to neighbor-independent substitution
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: A tag system that removes only one element per step always acts as a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system and so produces only repetitive or nested patterns, whereas removing two elements per step can yield very complicated behavior.

claims.title: Simple cyclic tag systems show random fluctuations in sequence growth
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Some cyclic tag systems with two alternating blocks, started from a single black element, produce sequences whose average growth is steady but whose fluctuations about that growth are in many respects random.

claims.title: Register machines need eight instructions to show complex behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Among two-register machines with increment and decrement-jump instructions, all programs of up to four instructions behave repetitively, only two five-instruction programs give nesting, none up to seven instructions is substantially more complicated, and 126 of the 11,019,960,576 eight-instruction programs show complex

claims.title: Short programs in ordinary low-level languages can behave randomly
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Because register machines idealize programs in low-level languages such as C, Basic, Java or assembler, searching many millions of short programs in such languages typically yields at least a few with complex, seemingly random behavior.

claims.title: Combinator-like symbolic rewriting systems can behave randomly
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Symbolic systems that repeatedly apply a single rewrite rule of the form e[x_][y_] → (expression in x and y) to nested expressions can, like other simple programs, produce behavior that is complex and seemingly random rather than stabilizing.

claims.title: Complexity does not depend on the special features of cellular automata
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Removing the special features of cellular automata, such as a rigid array of cells and parallel updating, does not prevent complex behavior from simple rules, so the phenomenon of complexity is universal and independent of the details of particular systems.

claims.title: The rule-complexity threshold for complex behavior is very low
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Systems with sufficiently simple rules show only repetition, slightly more complicated rules often add nesting, and complex behavior requires crossing a threshold in rule complexity, but in every kind of system studied this threshold is extremely low.

claims.title: Repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures dominate everywhere
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: The four themes of repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures are the dominant types of behavior across a vast range of systems, and these overall behavior types are almost independent of the details of the underlying rules.

claims.title: Overall behavior of natural systems can be inferred without knowing their details
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Because the typical types of behavior are independent of rule details, one can make fundamental statements about the overall behavior of a natural system without knowing its internal details, and its important features will usually be ones already seen in very simple programs.

claims.title: Computer experiments let one discover phenomena not anticipated in advance
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: A methodology based on computer experiments, in which one runs precisely specified programs and observes their behavior, can discover genuinely unexpected phenomena that a traditional approach of constructing examples of predefined behavior would miss, while giving results as precise as mathematical statements.

claims.title: One can never start a computer experiment with too simple a system
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs
claims.statement: Computer experiments should study the simplest possible systems with the simplest possible procedures, because simple systems already show complex behavior, and the most common mistake is studying systems far more complicated than necessary.

claims.title: Number systems fully solvable by analysis show only simple behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Systems based on numbers that traditional mathematics (e.g. calculus) can analyze completely end up showing only fairly simple behavior; textbook systems are selected for analyzability and therefore are simple.

claims.title: Simple arithmetic systems can produce highly complex behavior
