claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: When systems based on numbers are studied by computer experiment rather than by mathematical analysis, even very simple ones turn out to produce highly complex behavior.

claims.title: Base-2 digits of powers of 3 look random beyond small-scale structure
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Successive powers of 3 written in base 2 form a pattern that, apart from some small-scale structure, appears random for all practical purposes, even though it comes from repeated multiplication by 3.

claims.title: Fractional parts of powers of 3/2 are complex and apparently random
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: The fractional parts of successive powers of 3/2, a base-independent measure of size, show the same complexity and apparent randomness that appears in their digit sequences.

claims.title: Simple whole-number rules can yield complex sizes, not just complex digits
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Simple rules acting only on whole numbers (such as multiplying by 5/2 when even and adding 1 then halving when odd) can produce sequences whose overall sizes fluctuate in a complex, apparently random way with no sign of repetition, so complexity is not just an artifact of looking at digits.

claims.title: Non-local arithmetic rules still behave like local cellular automata
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Although arithmetic operations are non-local in digits (carries can propagate arbitrarily far) while cellular automaton rules are local, the overall behavior of number-based systems is very similar to that of cellular automata, so the details of underlying rules do not crucially affect the kinds of behavior that occur.

claims.title: Reverse-and-add in base 2 shows localized structures and never repeats
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: The base-2 reverse-and-add process (add a number to its digit-reversal) started from 512 produces localized structures like those in cellular automata, and its overall pattern never appears to become simply repetitive.

claims.title: Recursive sequences using only addition and subtraction can be complex
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Recursive integer sequences whose rule refers back a variable distance (e.g. f[n - f[n - 1]]) and uses only addition and subtraction can produce fluctuations that are complex and in many respects random.

claims.title: The sequence of primes is in many respects random
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Even though the primes are generated by a simple sieving rule, the sequence of primes appears in many respects remarkably random.

claims.title: Complexity in number-theoretic sequences arises from their generating rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Sequences defined by simple properties of numbers (primes, divisor sums, representations as sums of squares or primes) show complexity that persists despite centuries of number theory, and this complexity arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules generating them, just as in other simple programs.

claims.title: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Despite pi's simple definition, its digit sequence shows no significant regularity in all computed digits and appears for practical purposes completely random.

claims.title: Square roots of non-square integers have random-looking digits
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: As far as can be determined, the square root of every whole number that is not a perfect square has a digit sequence that appears completely random.

claims.title: Cube roots, logarithms and exponentials also have random-looking digits
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Beyond square roots, almost all cube roots, fourth roots, logarithms and exponentials of simple numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.

claims.title: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Every rational number p/q has a digit sequence that eventually repeats (with period at most q - 1), and rational numbers are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences.

claims.title: Roots never have nested digit sequences
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Nested digit sequences, such as those produced by substitution systems, never correspond to numbers obtainable by taking roots (square roots, cube roots, and so on).

claims.title: Continued fractions of pi and higher roots look random
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: In continued fraction representation, square roots are purely repetitive and e shows definite regularity, but pi, cube roots, fourth roots and similar numbers have continued fraction terms that seem essentially random.

claims.title: Numbers from simple operations are intrinsically complex in any representation
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: For any representation of numbers in which recovering the value takes comparable effort for all numbers, some numbers look simple but others produced by simple mathematical operations look random, so such numbers are often intrinsically complex independent of representation.

claims.title: Axis crossings of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] follow a continued-fraction substitution system
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: For a sum of two sine functions Sin[x] + Sin[a x], the arrangement of axis crossings is generated by a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from successive continued fraction terms of (a - 1)/(a + 1), giving nested patterns when a is a quadratic irrational.

claims.title: The shift map only transcribes randomness from its initial condition
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: The shift map (doubling modulo 1) generates no randomness of its own: it just moves digits of the initial number leftward, so its output is random only if the initial number's digit sequence was already random.

claims.title: Some simple iterated maps generate randomness intrinsically from simple seeds
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Some simple iterated maps, such as taking the fractional part of 3x/2, produce behavior that looks random even when started from very simple initial numbers like 1/2, so they intrinsically generate randomness rather than transcribing it from initial conditions.

claims.title: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not itself produce randomness
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (the chaos phenomenon) only amplifies differences already present in initial conditions, so on its own it contributes nothing to the ultimate production of randomness, even in systems that also show intrinsic randomness.

claims.title: Continuous cellular automata show the same complexity as discrete ones
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Cellular automata whose cells take a continuous range of gray levels, updated by simple maps of the neighborhood average, show the same kind of complexity as ordinary discrete cellular automata, and can even show localized structures.

claims.title: Nature does not fundamentally follow continuous differential equations
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Although almost all traditional models in physics (Maxwell, Einstein, Schrödinger equations) are partial differential equations, nature does not fundamentally follow these continuous mathematical abstractions.

claims.title: Partial differential equations predominate largely by historical accident
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: The dominance of partial differential equations as models in science is in many respects a historical accident of their being solvable by explicit formulas before computers; had computers come earlier, scientific modeling would probably be very different.

claims.title: Simple partial differential equations can show complex behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Complex behavior of the kind seen in simple programs is not restricted to discrete systems: some fairly simple partial differential equations, found by searching, produce highly complex patterns, even with apparently discrete patches.

claims.title: Complexity is not rarer in continuous systems, only harder to detect
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Complexity is probably not fundamentally rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones; it was much easier to discover in discrete systems because they can be studied directly by computer experiment without approximation artifacts.

claims.title: Phenomena seen in discrete simple programs also occur in simple continuous systems
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers
claims.statement: Essentially all of the phenomena observed in discrete simple programs can also be found in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.

claims.title: Adding dimensions does not fundamentally change the occurrence of complexity
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Contrary to what traditional science suggests, going from one to two or more dimensions produces some specific new effects but does not fundamentally change the overall behavior or the occurrence of complexity in simple programs.

claims.title: Slices of 2D cellular automata resemble 1D cellular automata
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: The complexity inside patterns generated by two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata is very similar to that of one-dimensional cellular automata: a one-dimensional slice through the 2D pattern evolves much like an ordinary 1D cellular automaton.

claims.title: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Some simple two-dimensional cellular automata on a square grid grow patterns whose overall shape closely approximates a perfect circle, despite the grid's square symmetry.

claims.title: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: A simple 2D cellular automaton (a cell turns black when exactly three of its eight neighbors are black, otherwise unchanged) can grow patterns whose overall shapes keep changing with no simple form, so complexity can appear in a pattern's overall shape as well as in its interior.

claims.title: Three-dimensional cellular automata show the same basic kinds of behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Three-dimensional cellular automata show some new specific phenomena but the same basic kinds of behavior as one- and two-dimensional ones, so the phenomenon of complexity does not depend crucially on dimensionality.

claims.title: Complex behavior in 2D Turing machines is as rare as in 1D
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Two-dimensional Turing machines behave much like one-dimensional ones: with two or three head states only repetitive and nested behavior normally occurs, and with four states complex behavior is possible but rare (a few rules per million).

claims.title: Neighbor-independent geometric replacement rules always give nested fractals
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Substitution systems and geometric replacement rules in which each element is replaced independently of other elements, including those of traditional fractal geometry, inevitably produce purely nested patterns.

claims.title: Fractal geometry misses complexity by excluding interactions between elements
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Traditional fractal geometry does not consider interactions between elements, which is why all patterns it produces are purely nested; allowing replacements to depend on neighbors on a grid readily yields complicated, non-nested patterns.

claims.title: Networks of identical two-connection nodes can form arrays of any dimension
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Networks in which every node is identical and has exactly two outgoing connections can, purely by the pattern of connections, form structures equivalent to arrays of any number of dimensions, as well as trees and nested structures.

claims.title: Network rules depending on distance-two neighborhoods can give random growth
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Network systems whose rewiring rules depend only on whether a node's two connections lead to the same node always grow in an essentially repetitive way, but when rules depend on nodes up to two connections away, even the number of nodes can vary in an apparently random way (in about one in 10,000 rules).

claims.title: Network systems may underlie the structure of space and spacetime
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Some network systems will likely turn out to be closely related to the basic structure of space and spacetime in our universe.

claims.title: Most multiway systems grow exponentially or not at all
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Most multiway systems (which keep all sequences produced by all possible replacements at each step) either grow exponentially fast or do not grow at all; slow growth is rare.

claims.title: Slowly growing multiway systems eventually become repetitive
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Even when slowly growing multiway systems show early apparent randomness in their state counts, they typically end up showing some form of repetition (sometimes with long periods, such as 1071 steps).

claims.title: Multiway systems build their own network of connections in time
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Because each sequence in a multiway system always leads to the same successors, the evolution can be represented as a network of which state leads to which, so multiway systems build up their own, often complicated, pattern of connections in time.

claims.title: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: In one dimension, any set of local constraints on cell colors that can be satisfied at all can be satisfied by a simple, purely repetitive arrangement, so simple 1D constraints cannot force complex patterns.

claims.title: All satisfiable 2D nearest-neighbor template constraints allow repetitive patterns
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Of all 4,294,967,296 two-dimensional constraints defined by allowed templates of a cell and its four neighbors, 766,979,044 cannot be satisfied, and every one of the rest can be satisfied by a repetitive pattern, with 171 repetitive patterns sufficing for all.

claims.title: Constraint systems require going outside the system to find their patterns
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Unlike rule-based systems, which can be run directly, systems defined by constraints offer no direct procedure for finding the patterns they allow; one must search from outside the system, which can take enormous computational effort.

claims.title: The simplest constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern forces a nested one
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Among 2D template constraints that also require one template to appear somewhere, systematic search over more than 18 million constraints finds that the first constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern (number 18762389) forces a unique nested pattern.

claims.title: No tested simple template constraint forces more than nested behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Of the 137,438,953,472 template constraints with a required-template condition, none of the millions tested forces anything more complicated than nested behavior.

claims.title: 3x3 template constraints can force a rule 30–like random pattern
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Constraints on 3×3 blocks of cells can be constructed to force complex patterns: a set of 56 allowed templates forces a unique, largely random pattern equivalent to the evolution of the rule 30 cellular automaton.

claims.title: Simple constraints rarely force complex behavior, unlike simple rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Unlike simple evolution rules, almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns; complex behavior forced by constraints is rare.

claims.title: Constraint-like equations helped hide complexity from traditional science
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond
claims.statement: Because describing complex behavior with constraints requires fairly complicated constraints, the traditional focus of science and mathematics on equations that act like constraints is another reason they failed to identify the phenomenon of complexity.

claims.title: Simple systems self-organize from random initial conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Many simple-rule systems such as cellular automata, when started from completely random initial conditions, spontaneously organize themselves and produce behavior with many distinctly non-random features.

claims.title: Cellular automaton behavior falls into four basic classes
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Despite differing in detail for almost every rule, the patterns produced by cellular automata of all kinds from random initial conditions can almost always be easily assigned to one of just four classes: uniform final state (class 1), simple stable or periodic structures (class 2), apparently random behavior (class 3),

claims.title: Class 4 consists of simple localized structures interacting in complex ways
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Class 4 cellular automata mix order and randomness: they produce localized structures that are individually fairly simple, but which move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.

claims.title: Detailed cellular automaton properties correlate with the four classes
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Most detailed properties of cellular automata correlate closely with the four visually defined classes, so that knowing a cellular automaton's class is often enough to predict its detailed properties.

claims.title: A cellular automaton's class usually cannot be read off its rule
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: For most cellular automata there is no easy way to determine from the underlying rule which class of behavior it will produce; one generally has to run it and see, though some rule forms can be shown to give only class 1 or 2 behavior.

claims.title: Class 4 lies between class 2 and class 3 in activity
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Although class 4 is the most complex in appearance, in terms of overall activity it is intermediate between class 2 and class 3, and in sequences of rules it commonly appears at the transition between class 2 and class 3 rules.

claims.title: Continuous cellular automata show the same four classes
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Cellular automata whose cells take continuous gray-level values show essentially the same four classes of behavior as discrete cellular automata, with class 4 behavior and its discrete localized structures typically appearing at transitions as the rule parameter is varied.

claims.title: Two-dimensional cellular automata show the same four classes
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Two-dimensional cellular automata exhibit the same four classes of behavior as one-dimensional ones, which becomes evident when one-dimensional slices through their evolution are examined; class 4 behavior, as in the Game of Life, occurs even on a white background with slightly more complicated rules.

claims.title: The four classes respond differently to small changes in initial conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Changing one cell of the initial condition has characteristically different effects by class: in class 1 the change dies out, in class 2 it stays localized, in class 3 it spreads at a uniform rate to affect the whole system, and in class 4 it spreads only sporadically.

claims.title: Natural systems can be understood by how they handle information
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Some of the most important features of natural systems can often be understood just by identifying which cellular automaton class their handling of information (forgetting, localized retention, long-range communication) corresponds to.

claims.title: Class 2 repetitiveness stems from lack of long-range communication
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Class 2 cellular automata are always eventually repetitive because their lack of long-range communication makes each part behave as an independent system of limited size, typically only a few cells across, and hence with short repetition periods.

claims.title: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Any system of limited size made of discrete elements and following definite rules must eventually exhibit repetitive behavior, with repetition period at most equal to its total number of possible states.

claims.title: Repetition periods of class 3 rules grow rapidly with system size
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: In cellular automata on a finite cyclic lattice, a rapid increase of repetition period with lattice size is characteristic of class 3 behavior, with large fluctuations as size changes; among elementary rules only rule 45 appears to give periods always near the maximum possible.

claims.title: Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: The randomness of class 3 systems is not merely inherited from random initial conditions: random behavior can be generated even when the initial conditions contain no randomness at all.

claims.title: Additive rule 90 only transmits randomness from its initial conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Because rule 90 is additive, its patterns are superpositions of the single-cell nested pattern, so it cannot generate randomness intrinsically; any randomness it shows comes from the initial conditions, and deviations such as a low initial density persist forever, unlike in rule 22.

claims.title: Intrinsic randomness generation makes large-scale behavior stable
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Systems that intrinsically generate randomness, like rule 22 or rule 30, produce the same overall random behavior with the same large-scale properties whatever their initial conditions, giving them a fundamental stability that he says underlies the apparent stability of many systems in nature.

claims.title: Spatially periodic initial conditions always give repetitive behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: In any cellular automaton, an initial condition consisting of a fixed block of n cells repeated forever leads to repetitive behavior with period at most 2^n, since each block evolves like a finite cyclic system.

claims.title: Special initial conditions often make one cellular automaton emulate another
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: It is common for a cellular automaton to have special initial conditions under which it behaves exactly like some other cellular automaton; for example rule 126 behaves like rule 90 when started from paired-cell blocks, and class 3 rules can thereby act like class 2 rules.

claims.title: Nested patterns arise from rules that emulate themselves
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: A cellular automaton whose blocks of cells evolve by the same rule as individual cells must produce patterns that are either essentially uniform or nested; this self-emulation is why rule 90 and rules that emulate it produce nested patterns.

claims.title: Additive rules self-emulate; rules 90 and 150 are the only elementary ones
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Every additive cellular automaton rule can emulate itself and therefore yields nested patterns, and among two-color nearest-neighbor rules the only fundamentally different additive rules are rules 90 and 150; self-emulation is otherwise rare, though non-additive examples such as rule 184 exist.

claims.title: Allowed-sequence networks grow fast for class 3 and 4, slowly for 1 and 2
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: As cellular automata evolve, the set of cell sequences that can occur generally becomes progressively restricted; the finite networks describing these sets stay simple (about t^2 nodes after t steps) for class 1 and 2 rules but grow at least exponentially for most class 3 and 4 rules, apart from surjective rules starte

claims.title: Class 4 systems always have structures that persist forever
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: A crucial feature of any class 4 cellular automaton is that, although most structures that form eventually die out, there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.

claims.title: Complicated persistent structures imply moving structures exist
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: In class 4 cellular automata, whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found; moving structures are what allow information to travel and complex class 4 behavior to occur.

claims.title: Class 4 automata can mimic many other systems
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Class 4 cellular automata can, with appropriate initial conditions, mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems, including producing unbounded growth of either complex or very simple form.

claims.title: Interactions among simple structures in rule 110 give immense complexity
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness
claims.statement: Although individual persistent structures in class 4 systems such as rule 110 behave fairly repetitively, collisions between them can produce cascades of new structures and outcomes that take very many steps to resolve, yielding behavior of immense complexity from an extremely simple rule.

claims.title: Universal behavior types span simple programs and natural systems
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: The same kinds of overall behavior arise regardless of the details of underlying rules, and this universality holds not only among simple programs but also between simple programs and systems in nature, so idealized cell models and real molecular systems should show the same universal features.

claims.title: Just three basic mechanisms account for randomness
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Apparent randomness in any system arises from one of just three basic mechanisms: continual random input from the environment, randomness transcribed from initial conditions, or intrinsic generation of randomness by the system's own rules with no random input.

claims.title: Intrinsic randomness generation explains most randomness in nature
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: The mechanism in which a system's own deterministic rules generate randomness without any random input is ultimately responsible for a large fraction, and perhaps essentially all, of the randomness seen in the natural world.

claims.title: Hardware noise-based random generators deviate from perfect randomness
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Devices that generate randomness by amplifying microscopic environmental noise (spark gaps, vacuum tubes, semiconductor diodes) have consistently been found to produce output with significant deviations from perfect randomness, because the sampling device relaxes only gradually and because the environment itself has co

claims.title: Randomness from initial conditions lasts only a limited number of steps
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: In physical chaotic systems such as kneading, mirror arrangements or pegboards, randomness can be attributed purely to initial conditions only for a small number of steps (around ten collisions for a pegboard), because amplification quickly reaches atomic scales and environmental perturbations take over; the limit is s

claims.title: Solar system motion should show sensitive dependence over millions of years
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Although planetary motion looks regular on human timescales, sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur in the solar system, producing significant randomness over a few million years that may explain some present-day features of the solar system.

claims.title: Maximal-period linear congruential generators still show strong nonrandomness
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Linear congruential random number generators designed to have maximal repetition period have repeatedly turned out to deviate substantially from perfect randomness (for example, successive outputs plotted as points fall on regular stripes), because the mathematical tractability that guarantees their period also implies

claims.title: Amenability to mathematical analysis implies deviations from randomness
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: The very possibility of detailed mathematical analysis of a system tends to imply that its output has at least some deviations from perfect randomness, whereas simple rules not constrained by the need for such analysis can generate highly random behavior.

claims.title: Rapid production of much randomness indicates intrinsic generation
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be responsible, because it uses every component of a system to produce new randomness and has no length limit, whereas environmental amplification is slow and initial-condition randomness is sh

claims.title: Intrinsically generated randomness is repeatable across experimental runs
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: If randomness in an experiment comes from intrinsic generation, then even the precise details of the random-looking behavior should be repeatable from one run to the next, because such behavior is robust to perturbations below a critical size, whereas randomness from the environment or from initial conditions should sh

claims.title: Detailed visual similarities in organisms imply intrinsic randomness
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Detailed visual similarities between members of the same species, and between the two symmetric sides of a system, in features that look complex and random cannot be attributed to environmental or initial-condition randomness and must come from intrinsic randomness generation.

claims.title: Randomness lets discrete components produce continuous behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Systems made of discrete components appear smooth and continuous on large scales mainly because microscopic randomness averages out the discreteness, and it does not matter whether that randomness comes from outside or from intrinsic generation, as shown by random walks, aggregation models and deterministic cellular au

claims.title: Continuity requires slow features relative to small-scale random changes
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Continuous large-scale behavior can arise in a system with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes; for growth, the random small-scale changes must occur much faster than the overall growth.

claims.title: Density-driven discrete transitions are rare in 1D CAs, common in higher dimensions
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Cellular automata in which a continuous change in initial density of black cells produces a discrete switch in long-time behavior, with whichever color was initially more common taking over the whole system, are fairly rare in one dimension, where domain boundaries often get stuck, but become increasingly common in two

claims.title: Continuous rules can yield discrete behavior, so discrete models often fit
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Even systems governed by continuous equations, such as certain chemical reaction kinetics, commonly have a limited number of stable states with discrete transitions between them, and because discrete overall behavior is often a system's most obvious feature, discrete models like cellular automata are often the most app

claims.title: Complex natural behavior is almost never best explained by constraints
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Almost none of the complex behavior seen in nature is best explained as the satisfaction of constraints, because finding a pattern that satisfies a constraint is usually far too difficult a computation to happen routinely in nature; explicit processes of evolution are the more plausible explanation.

claims.title: Local-improvement procedures get stuck when satisfying discrete constraints
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: For discrete constraint systems the landscape of constraint violations is almost always jagged, so iterative procedures that only move downhill almost invariably get stuck far from a solution, random modifications help only slowly, and no speed-up techniques work well across broad classes of systems; hence natural syst

claims.title: Pushed or jiggled spheres do not reach densest packing
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Unlike identical coins in two dimensions, which readily form the densest hexagonal packing when pushed together, balls in three dimensions pushed together or jiggled almost always get stuck and essentially never reach the densest repetitive packing, which seems obtainable only by careful one-by-one placement.

claims.title: Complex biological forms come from growth rules, not selection-driven constraints
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Natural selection can produce forms determined by constraint satisfaction only when those forms are rather simple; complex biological forms are associated instead with explicit evolution rules, mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.

claims.title: Rule complexity does not determine behavioral complexity
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: There is no direct correspondence between the complexity of a system's underlying rules and the complexity of its behavior: some of the simplest rules yield highly complex behavior, fairly complicated rules often yield simple behavior, and rules differing at a single position can behave very differently.

claims.title: Nesting in nature mostly arises from building up, not splitting down
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Nested patterns can arise either from elements splitting or branching into smaller ones or from larger elements being built up from smaller ones (as in additive cellular automata), and the building-up route is probably the more common origin of nesting in nature.

claims.title: Merging of independently growing domains generically produces nesting
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature
claims.statement: Nesting can arise from random initial conditions through progressive annihilation of randomly placed elements: in essentially any system where domains grow fairly independently and then progressively merge, an overall nested pattern resembling a river-tributary tree forms, even when domain boundaries move as random wal

claims.title: Models of complex systems should first be judged by comparing overall pictures
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: For systems with complex behavior, a model cannot be adequately assessed by matching a few extracted numbers; the best first test is a visual comparison of the model's overall behavior with that of the real system.

claims.title: Snowflake shapes arise from growth inhibition captured by a hexagonal cellular automaton
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The main features of snowflake shapes are reproduced by a hexagonal cellular automaton in which a cell becomes ice only if exactly one neighbor is ice, which represents the inhibition of nearby growth by released latent heat.

claims.title: Growing snowflakes should alternate between tree-like and faceted shapes
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: During the growth of an individual snowflake its shape should alternate between tree-like and faceted forms, as new branches grow and then collide with one another.

claims.title: Randomness in crystal shapes is often intrinsically generated by simple growth rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Apparent randomness in the shapes of crystalline materials often arises intrinsically from simple deterministic growth rules, rather than from randomness in the seed or the growth environment.

claims.title: Randomness of fracture surfaces comes from a material-independent intrinsic mechanism
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The roughness and randomness of fracture paths does not come from random irregularities in a material but from a general mechanism in which deterministic interactions of element displacements around a moving crack intrinsically generate randomness, as in a simple cellular automaton model.

claims.title: Conservation plus microscopic randomness yields universal fluid behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Any system of particles that conserves quantities such as particle number and momentum and has sufficient microscopic randomness will show the same large-scale fluid behavior, so a discrete cellular automaton particle model can reproduce the flow of real fluids.

claims.title: Large-scale fluid flow shows little sensitive dependence on initial conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: In almost all cases, large-scale fluid behavior does not depend discernibly on the detailed initial conditions; small perturbations are damped out by viscosity, so sensitive dependence (chaos) is the exception rather than the rule.

claims.title: Turbulent randomness is intrinsically generated at the level of large-scale fluid motion
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The randomness seen in turbulent fluids is mostly neither inserted from outside nor inherited from molecular randomness, but is intrinsically generated by the dynamics of the large-scale fluid motion itself.

claims.title: Random-looking yet repeatable fluid flows should be producible
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Because turbulent randomness is generated intrinsically by large-scale motion, carefully prepared experiments should produce fluid flows that look random yet are essentially the same on every repeated run.

claims.title: Evolution cannot have found optimal solutions to complex fitness constraints
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Since iterative random search converges only for simple constraints, the roughly trillion generations of life on Earth are insufficient to find optimal solutions to complex constraints, so most features of organisms are merely good-enough solutions rather than optima.

claims.title: Most biological complexity comes from randomly chosen programs, not natural selection
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Most of the complexity seen in biological organisms originates from the abstract fact that many randomly chosen programs produce complex behavior, rather than from adaptation or careful optimization by natural selection.

claims.title: Complexity of individual organism parts has been roughly constant for eons
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The complexity of individual parts of organisms, such as textures and other morphological features, was already present in early fossils and has not changed much in at least several hundred million years.

claims.title: Genetic programs for complex pigment patterns are short
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The genetic programs that generate patterns such as those on mollusc shells are short, as indicated by the large variety of patterns within species, and molecular biology should be able to isolate them and confirm their brevity.

claims.title: Natural selection works meaningfully only on simple behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The power of natural selection is limited: it can systematically optimize only systems or parts of systems whose behavior is simple, and achieves very little when behavior is complex.

claims.title: Natural selection makes organisms simpler and more engineering-like
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Rather than generating complexity, the main effect of natural selection is to make biological systems avoid complexity, favoring simple, somewhat independent components with smoothly adjustable properties, as in engineered systems.

claims.title: Features that change fastest between species are the most complex
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Among related species, the features that differ most rapidly (such as pigmentation and texture patterns) are the ones that show the most obvious complexity, while features under natural selection stay nearly constant.

claims.title: Convergent structures recur because they are common among programs, not optimal
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: When similar complex structures arise independently in very different organisms, this is because those structures are common outputs of programs of certain kinds, not because they are optimal.

claims.title: Natural selection does not inherently drive organisms toward more elaborate structure
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Natural selection does not inevitably produce progressively more elaborate organisms; increases in complexity in the fossil record come from random mutations that add features without fatal flaws, while selection's systematic effect is to simplify.

claims.title: Plant branching patterns come from simple substitution-system growth rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The overall branching patterns of plants, from algae to ferns to trees and flowering plants, are produced by simple growth rules in which each stem tip repeatedly splits into smaller copies of itself at fixed relative lengths and angles.

claims.title: Leaf shapes arise from the same simple branching process as whole plants
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The shapes of leaves, from smooth to prickly to irregular, are produced by the same simple branching growth process that governs overall plant forms, and small changes in its parameters can change leaf shape greatly.

claims.title: The 137.5° phyllotaxis angle results from a simple inhibition growth process
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The near-universal 137.5° (golden-ratio) angle between successive plant organs is not an optimization found by natural selection but the inevitable result of a simple process where each new element forms where a chemical concentration is highest and depletes it nearby.

claims.title: Simple growth-rate models generate essentially all mollusc shell shapes
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Mollusc shell shapes result from secreting material at different rates around the shell opening, and essentially every form produced by a simple growth model with a few parameters is found in some real mollusc.

claims.title: Animal embryos develop hierarchically because of a fixed length scale
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Because regions of tissue a few tenths of a millimeter across subdivide into regions using different sections of the genetic program (controlled by chemical gradients and homeobox genes), embryos necessarily develop hierarchically, e.g. a leg region before a foot region.

claims.title: Shape differences between related animals come from differing growth rates
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Differences in shape among related animals are largely due to different patterns of relative growth rates of their parts, so their shapes are related by simple smooth geometric transformations.

claims.title: Diversity of plant and animal forms comes from different simple rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Most of the diversity and complexity in the forms of plants and animals arises because slightly different, essentially randomly picked simple growth rules lead to very different and often complex behavior.

claims.title: Mollusc shell pigment patterns are generated like one-dimensional cellular automata
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Pigmentation patterns on mollusc shells are produced line by line by pigment-secreting elements whose new states depend on neighbors' previous states, so the range of shell patterns closely matches the patterns of the simplest symmetric one-dimensional cellular automata.

claims.title: Mollusc shell pattern rules are effectively random, not optimized
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The rules generating mollusc shell patterns are effectively chosen at random from the simplest possibilities rather than optimized against predators or for mates, as shown by many species whose patterns are hidden by opaque skin throughout life.

claims.title: Animal coat patterns arise from local activation and longer-range inhibition rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: The few recurring kinds of animal pigmentation patterns (spots, labyrinths, stripes) are produced by a simple rule in which each element tends to match the average color of nearby elements and oppose that of elements further away, as in a two-dimensional cellular automaton.

claims.title: Short-timescale market randomness comes from internal market dynamics
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: Much of the apparent randomness in financial prices, especially on timescales of minutes or seconds, is generated by the internal dynamics of trading entities interacting with one another, not by external news or changes in the value of the asset.

claims.title: Simple cellular automaton markets generate random-looking price series
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems
claims.statement: In a market modelled as a one-dimensional cellular automaton of buy/sell agents reacting to neighbors, any rule that lets information eventually propagate to all agents makes the running buy-minus-sell total show significant randomness.

claims.title: A very simple program may underlie all of physics
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Underneath the known laws of physics there may be a single very simple program from which all known laws, and all the complexity of the universe, emerge.

claims.title: Reversible rules are rare among cellular automata
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Reversibility is rare among simple cellular automaton rules: only 6 of the 256 elementary two-color nearest-neighbor rules are reversible, and only 1800 of the 7,625,597,484,987 three-color nearest-neighbor rules are.

claims.title: Reversible systems can behave as complexly as any other
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Although only a tiny fraction of possible rules are reversible, reversible cellular automata can still produce behavior, including apparent randomness and localized structures, as complex as that of non-reversible systems.

claims.title: Second Law holds because experiments cannot prepare randomness-decreasing states
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is observed to hold because practical experiments can only set up initial conditions that are simple to describe and construct, and finding initial conditions of a reversible system that would lead to decreasing randomness requires computation as great as the system's own evolution.

claims.title: Reversible rule 37R does not obey the Second Law
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: The reversible cellular automaton rule 37R, even as a closed system, shows neither a systematic trend toward increasing randomness nor simple predictable behavior, but fluctuates indefinitely between more and less ordered states, so it does not obey the Second Law for practical purposes.

claims.title: Biological order arises from partitioning into separated compartments
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Biological systems can show increasing order despite the Second Law mainly because they partition into parts (cells, organisms) separated by membrane-like boundaries, within which organized behavior can occur while the boundary survives.

claims.title: The Second Law is general but not universally valid
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is an important and general principle but is not universally valid; many systems in nature behave like rule 37R and do not show a uniform trend toward increasing randomness.

claims.title: Continuum behavior emerges from discrete randomizing conserving rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Smooth continuum behavior, such as diffusion of density, emerges from discrete systems whenever small-scale apparent randomness washes out individual details and conserved quantities constrain overall features, as shown by block cellular automata whose average density follows the diffusion equation.

claims.title: The fundamental rule cannot be found by working backwards from known laws
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: If the ultimate rule for the universe is simple, it cannot realistically be found by engineering it from observed features; the only practical method is to choose a straightforward representation and systematically search through large numbers of candidate rules.

claims.title: Space, gravity and quantum features are generic across many candidate rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Features such as seemingly continuous space and certain aspects of gravitation and quantum mechanics will emerge from many different underlying rules for the universe, whereas properties like the spectrum of particle masses, and perhaps the dimensionality of space, will be specific to particular rules.

claims.title: Most known physical laws are emergent, not fundamental
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Most physical laws discovered so far are not fundamental but are emergent large-scale features of an underlying rule, so their simplicity says little about the simplicity of that rule.

claims.title: Space is discrete below the scales probed by experiment
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Space, though experimentally continuous down to about 10^-20 meters, is very likely made of discrete elements at still smaller scales, just as fluids and other seemingly continuous things have turned out to be.

claims.title: Space and matter should be made of the same stuff
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: In the simplest ultimate model of the universe there is no distinction between space and its contents: matter and everything else are made of the same underlying structure as space, unlike in a cellular automaton.

claims.title: At the lowest level space is a network of nodes
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: At the lowest level, space is most likely a giant network of nodes defined only by their connections (and it suffices to consider nodes with exactly three connections), with ordinary space emerging as a large-scale limit.

claims.title: Network dimension is set by growth of node counts with distance
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: A network corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space exactly when the number of nodes within graph distance r of a node grows in a limiting sense like r^d; tree-like or randomly connected networks correspond to no finite dimension.

claims.title: Observers perceive time only through the causal network of events
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: An observer embedded in a system such as a mobile automaton cannot see its individual update steps; all the observer can perceive is the network of causal relationships between updating events, so perceived time and spacetime derive purely from that causal network, and sequential updating can appear as synchronized par

claims.title: Non-overlapping replacement rules give update-order-independent causal networks
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: A substitution system whose rules replace only blocks that can never overlap themselves or each other always yields the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are applied (the property Wolfram calls causal invariance).

claims.title: The universe's rules likely yield a unique causal network
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Although the universe has no global clock and its rules may be applicable in arbitrary order, its actual rules most likely have the property of always yielding the same causal network, and so a unique perceived history.

claims.title: Small-scale randomness in the network makes space robustly 3D
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: The ultimate rules for the universe will produce networks that look largely random at small scales, and this randomness is what allows a definite and robust dimensionality of 3 to emerge for space.

claims.title: Elementary length and time are tiny and their ratio is light speed
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Each connection in the causal network of the universe corresponds to an identical elementary distance (perhaps about 10^-35 meters) and elementary time (perhaps about 10^-43 seconds), whose ratio is a fixed speed identified with the speed of light.

claims.title: Causal invariance yields special relativity
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: If the underlying rules of the universe are causal invariant, then slices through the causal network at different angles, corresponding to different uniform velocities, are all governed by the same rules, so physics is the same regardless of uniform motion and the standard phenomena of special relativity such as time d

claims.title: Elementary particles are persistent localized structures in the network
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Elementary particles are analogs of the localized structures seen in class 4 cellular automata: persistent structures (such as tangles or non-planar cores) in the network of space, so that the fundamental rules need make no reference to particular particles.

claims.title: Fundamental particle masses may still have simple ratios
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Although observed elementary particle masses are not in simple ratios (unlike electric charges), truly fundamental particle masses may still have simple relations, because observed masses include varying amounts of interaction energy.

claims.title: Network curvature appears in node counts via the Ricci scalar
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: In a large network approximating d-dimensional space, the leading correction to the number of nodes reached within distance r is proportional to the Ricci scalar curvature times r^(d+1), so curvature can be determined purely from network connectivity.

claims.title: Causal invariant dimension-preserving network rules give Einstein equations
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Network replacement rules that are causal invariant and maintain a fixed number of dimensions will almost inevitably produce large-scale behavior close to the vacuum Einstein equations of general relativity, analogous to how Navier–Stokes behavior emerges from cellular automaton fluids.

claims.title: Network-based programs will reproduce the key features of quantum theory
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: Discrete network models of the universe with causal invariance will ultimately turn out to exhibit many if not all of the key features of quantum theory, even though they are not set up in terms of its standard formalism.

claims.title: Network threads let deterministic models produce quantum correlations
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics
claims.statement: The quantum correlations between distant particles usually taken to rule out definite underlying processes can arise in a deterministic network model, because particles created together stay linked by threads of connections that bypass ordinary three-dimensional space.

claims.title: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: The basic mechanisms underlying human perception and scientific analysis, like the mechanisms behind many natural processes, can be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.

claims.title: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Although inferring the generating procedure from observed behavior is fairly easy for the rules of traditional mathematics, for general simple programs it is often extremely difficult, because their complex output shows no obvious trace of its simple origin.

claims.title: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Defining something as random only when no short description of it exists at all is too restrictive and uncomputable (it would mean deterministic rules can never generate randomness), so any useful definition of randomness must refer to how short descriptions are to be found.

claims.title: Something is random if essentially no simple program detects regularities in it
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Since essentially all standard methods of perception and analysis are based on simple programs, something should be considered random whenever essentially no simple program succeeds in detecting regularities in it.

claims.title: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Once a few simple programs corresponding to standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities in some data, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed, so the everyday judgment of randomness is in practice fairly unambiguous.

claims.title: Complexity means our perception and analysis fail to find a short description
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: To call something complex is to say that our methods of perception and analysis have failed to find a short description of the features of it that we are interested in; complexity therefore depends on which features one chooses to capture.

claims.title: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: People tend to lose interest in images with no simple features (such as perfectly random ones), and the images that hold attention and seem most aesthetically pleasing are those in which some features are simple to describe while others have no short description findable by human visual perception.

claims.title: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Structurally different lossless data compression methods (run-length, block/Huffman, pointer-based and two-dimensional schemes) have remarkably similar capabilities: they compress uniform regions, repetitive behavior and to some extent nested behavior, but achieve no substantial compression of more complex behavior eve

claims.title: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Under lossy compression by keeping only some basic forms (as in JPEG-like schemes), the relevant features of both simple and completely random images remain recognizable at high compression, whereas images normally considered complex need much lower compression, and reordering the basic forms does not change this subst

claims.title: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Human perception generally works by cells responding to specific fixed features and ignoring others; in vision, cortical cells act as templates for small local patterns, and textures are distinguished by the densities of such local features, much as colors are distinguished by densities of red, green and blue.

claims.title: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Humans can readily see by eye that a two-dimensional pattern is purely repetitive, but generally cannot tell that a pattern is nested (unless it is dominated by large uniform areas), even though a simple two-dimensional pointer-based encoding recognizes the nesting.

claims.title: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: For sounds generated from sequences with fairly uniform properties, the human auditory system recognizes only exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies; nested or other non-repetitive structure, beyond a few large spectral peaks, is heard as random noise.

claims.title: Best-fit probabilistic models of deterministic data look more random than the data
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: When probabilistic models such as block-frequency, Markov or probabilistic cellular automaton models are fitted to data generated by deterministic cellular automata, they reproduce the statistics used in fitting but their typical behavior is considerably more random and misses most detailed features of the data.

claims.title: Equal block frequencies of all lengths is not a universal randomness test
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Checking that all blocks of all lengths occur with equal frequency does not guarantee absence of regularity: sequences such as linear feedback shift register output or concatenated binary digits of successive integers have accurate block frequencies yet are non-random, as revealed for instance by an abnormally small sp

claims.title: Rule 30 center column and digits of pi pass statistical tests for randomness
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: The center column of the rule 30 cellular automaton and the base 2 digits of pi show no detectable deviation from randomness under block-frequency statistics or under analysis by simple cellular automata, even though both are generated by simple rules.

claims.title: Rule 30 can serve as a cryptographic stream cipher as secure as any known
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Simple rules with complex behavior, such as the rule 30 cellular automaton sampled sparsely to give an encrypting sequence, can be used to build stream ciphers at least as secure against cryptanalysis as any known system, unlike additive cellular automata or linear feedback shift registers, whose keys are easily recove

claims.title: Every nested pattern likely has a formula in generalized hypergeometric functions
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Although most nested patterns have no obvious relation to ordinary mathematical functions, a formula for the color of each cell of any nested pattern can probably be found in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions or similar generalizations of traditional functions.

claims.title: No simple formula describes many steps of rule 30 evolution
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Minimal Boolean formulas (in disjunctive normal form or in Nand operations) for the outcome of rule 30 grow rapidly with the number of steps, unlike those for simple rules such as 90 and 254, indicating that no simple formula describes rule 30 evolution and that, in most cases, cellular automaton patterns have no simpl

claims.title: Human memory works like similarity-preserving hashing by layers of neurons
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Human memory likely retrieves data by a simple hashing-like mechanism in which successive layers of nerve cells, each responding to patterns in fixed random sets of inputs, produce representations that are the same for inputs differing by small changes, allowing retrieval by similarity.

claims.title: Memory retrieval, not logic, underlies almost all of human thinking
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Retrieval from memory on the basis of similarity underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking, including generalization, analogy and intuition, and logical reasoning is not fundamental but is itself carried out by retrieving learned patterns of argument from memory.

claims.title: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Despite the complicated construction of the brain, there is a core to human thinking that is largely independent of neural details and is based on rather simple rules, with nothing fundamentally special about the processes involved.

claims.title: General human-like thinking is easier to reproduce than task-specific versions
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Because complex behavior from simple rules is hard to direct to specific tasks, it will likely be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than a special version of human-like thinking restricted to specific tasks; a recognizably human-like system would also need a human-like base of experience.

claims.title: No method of perception or analysis can recognize all possible regularities
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: No method of perception and analysis, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize all possible regularities and thus tell immediately whether a piece of data can be generated from some simple description, although higher methods could recognize some regularities current methods miss.

claims.title: Practical perception and analysis methods recognize only repetition and nesting
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Essentially all methods of perception and analysis in practical use have similar capabilities, recognizing repetition and sometimes nesting but almost nothing more complex, possibly because only such regularities are both common and quickly recognizable, or because humans choose methods matching their built-in percepti

claims.title: Extraterrestrial signals taken for noise could be meaningful messages
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
claims.statement: Some extraterrestrial radio and other signals that are detected and assumed to be random noise could be meaningful messages encoded in a way recognizable only by higher forms of perception and analysis than those applied so far.

claims.title: Computation is the central organizing idea of the new science
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: The most important idea underlying Wolfram's new kind of science is computation: systems such as cellular automata should be viewed as computations, with initial conditions as input and later states as output, so that systems with entirely different rules can be discussed in a unified, abstract way.

claims.title: Any system can be viewed as performing a computation
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Any system whatsoever, not just a cellular automaton, can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.

claims.title: Universality is crucial for understanding complexity in natural systems
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Although universality has never before been seriously considered in natural science, it is crucial for finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity seen in natural systems.

claims.title: A universal system can produce arbitrarily complex behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Because a universal system can emulate any other system, it can produce behavior as complex as that of any other system, so knowing a system is universal implies it can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.

claims.title: Universality is widespread and occurs in many systems in nature
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Contrary to the assumption that universality is rare and found only in systems specifically constructed to have it, universality is a widespread phenomenon that also occurs in a wide range of important systems found in nature.

claims.title: A fixed universal cellular automaton can emulate any cellular automaton
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: A single cellular automaton with fixed rules (Wolfram's 19-color, next-nearest-neighbor construction) can, given suitable initial conditions, emulate any cellular automaton whatsoever, regardless of how many colors or neighbors its rules involve, including rules more complicated than its own.

claims.title: Cellular automata can emulate nearly all other system types, even computers
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Cellular automata can be set up to emulate almost every type of system considered in the book—mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, sequential substitution and tag systems, register machines, arithmetic systems, logic circuits and random-access memory—and in principle a practical computer in its entir

claims.title: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Unlike mobile automata or Turing machines, substitution systems cannot in general be emulated one step per cellular automaton step, because the number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor each step while a cellular automaton pattern can grow only by a fixed amount per step; progressively m

claims.title: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only generate repetitive or nested patterns, so they cannot emulate cellular automata such as rule 30, whereas neighbor-dependent substitution systems can emulate cellular automata straightforwardly.

claims.title: Any system type that can emulate every cellular automaton has universal members
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Since a universal cellular automaton exists, any type of system shown capable of emulating any cellular automaton—including mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbor-dependent and sequential substitution systems, tag systems, cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines—must contain universal examples.

claims.title: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: A system that repeatedly takes a whole number, computes its remainder modulo a constant and applies an arithmetic operation chosen by that remainder can emulate a register machine, and is therefore universal; given how widespread universality is, arithmetic supporting it is unsurprising.

claims.title: Structurally different systems are computationally equivalent
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Because essentially all the kinds of systems studied (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and others) can emulate each other, a wide variety of systems with very different underlying structures are fundamentally equivalent in the computations they can perform, so computation can

claims.title: Past the threshold of universality, more complex rules add no capability
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: As systems of a given type are given progressively greater computational capabilities they eventually pass a threshold of universality, after which the set of computations they can perform is always the same, so more sophisticated rules gain nothing further and a universal system's capabilities are independent of the d

claims.title: Elementary cellular automaton rule 110 is universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Rule 110, a two-color nearest-neighbor elementary cellular automaton, is universal: by arranging its naturally occurring localized structures as components, it can be made to emulate any cyclic tag system, and hence any Turing machine.

claims.title: Universality should be common, including among very simple rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: The universality of rule 110, one of the simplest possible cellular automaton rules, implies that universality is far more common than previously thought and should occur in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.

claims.title: Complexity of behavior saturates soon after the simplest rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: As rules become progressively more complicated, overall behavior grows more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached, and since that threshold is very low, behavior beyond the very simplest rules of any kind should quickly become as complex as it will ever be—consistent with the Chapter 3 survey.

claims.title: All class 4 cellular automata are expected to be universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Any cellular automaton showing class 4 behavior (localized structures moving and interacting in complicated ways) will, like rule 110, turn out to be universal, because such rules eventually yield localized structures rich enough to support universality.

claims.title: Rule 110 and its reflections are the only clear elementary class 4 rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata, the only clear immediate example of class 4 behavior is rule 110 together with its left-right and black-white equivalents (rules 124, 137 and 193), while class 4 behavior is common once more colors or neighbors are allowed, even for totalistic rules.

claims.title: Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Cellular automata that produce only uniform or repetitive patterns (class 1 and class 2) can never be universal, because they transmit information only over limited distances and so support only processes involving a limited number of cells.

claims.title: Nested-pattern and additive cellular automata cannot be universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Cellular automata whose information transmission is highly constrained so that patterns are essentially nested, and additive rules such as rules 90 and 150 whose states after a power-of-two number of steps are simple superpositions of shifted copies of the initial condition, cannot be universal.

claims.title: Rule 54 shows only repetitive or nested forms in 100 million initial conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Rule 54, a possible class 4 elementary cellular automaton, shows only repetitive or nested behavior in its first hundred million initial conditions, leaving it uncertain whether rule 54 is universal.

claims.title: Any non-repetitive, non-nested system is expected to be universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
