claims.statement: More or less any system whose behavior is not fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal, so there is a close connection between universality and the appearance of complex behavior, though proving it will be far easier for some systems (such as rule 110) than others.

claims.title: Uncontrolled information flow in class 3 rules hinders universality proofs
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Universality proofs proceed by building components from localized structures, which requires controlled transmission of information; in class 3 systems a change to a single cell eventually spreads to all cells, making it very hard to identify definite components and hence to prove universality.

claims.title: Rules 30 and 45 are expected to be universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Although the localized structures found in rules 30 and 45 on repetitive backgrounds all move at the same speed and so cannot interact, preventing a rule 110-style proof, rules 30 and 45 will nevertheless turn out to be universal.

claims.title: Complex elementary rules can emulate one step of every elementary rule
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Using block encodings, elementary rules with complex behavior such as rules 22, 30 and 110 can be made to emulate a single step of all 256 elementary cellular automata, whereas rules with simple behavior such as 90 and 184 can emulate only a few; this supports the idea that complex-looking cellular automata can do arbi

claims.title: Perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Since elementary cellular automata whose behavior looks complex can do computations as sophisticated as desired, they are expected to be universal, so perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal.

claims.title: A 2-state 5-color Turing machine is universal via rule 110
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: A Turing machine with just 2 states and 5 colors, far simpler than the 7-state 4-color machine that had long been the simplest known, is universal because it emulates rule 110 by sweeping back and forth and updating all cells by one rule 110 step per sweep.

claims.title: No 2-state 2-color Turing machine can be universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: All 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors have behavior too simple to support universality.

claims.title: Complex behavior is rare but present in small Turing machine spaces
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Starting from a blank tape, roughly one in 50,000 2-state 4-color Turing machines and one in 200,000 4-state 2-color machines show complex behavior, and 14 essentially equivalent machines among the 2,985,984 with 2 states and 3 colors do so.

claims.title: A complex 2-state 3-color Turing machine is likely the simplest universal one
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: The 2-state 3-color Turing machine numbered 596,440, which yields complicated behavior from a blank tape, is likely universal, and if so would by most measures be the simplest universal Turing machine.

claims.title: All 3-state 2-color Turing machines behave simply from blank tape
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: With blank initial conditions all 2,985,984 Turing machines with 3 states and 2 colors quickly produce simple repetitive or nested behavior, and even with more complicated initial conditions their behavior eventually seems to resolve into a simple form.

claims.title: Combinators show highly complex behavior despite simple rules
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation
claims.statement: Combinators, symbolic systems long known to be universal, show highly complex behavior despite simple rules—for example a length-8 initial expression grows exponentially with seemingly random internal structure—and they can emulate rule 110, suggesting their universality is just associated with general complex behavior

claims.title: Every process, natural or artificial, can be viewed as a computation
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Any process that follows definite rules, including processes in nature governed by physical law as well as processes constructed by humans, can be viewed as a computation, giving a uniform framework for comparing very different processes.

claims.title: Principle of Computational Equivalence: one maximal level of sophistication
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Almost all processes whose behavior is not obviously simple correspond to computations of equivalent sophistication; there is essentially a single highest level of computational sophistication, and almost all such processes reach it regardless of how simple their rules or initial conditions are.

claims.title: No physical system can compute beyond cellular automata and Turing machines
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: As a law of nature, no system that can actually be constructed in our universe can carry out explicit computations more sophisticated than those of universal systems such as cellular automata and Turing machines; imaginable hypercomputers (e.g. with infinite tables of results) cannot be built.

claims.title: An overwhelming fraction of non-simple rules are universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Among all possible rules of a given type (such as cellular automata) whose behavior is not obviously simple, i.e. not repetitive or nested, the overwhelming majority are computationally universal, so universality is extremely common rather than a rare engineered property.

claims.title: Rules occurring in nature are typically not specially selected
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: When no constraint such as engineering design or natural selection forces simple behavior, the rules that operate in nature are effectively selected in no special way apart from tending to be structurally simple, so they behave like randomly chosen rules and are almost always universal when their behavior is not obviou

claims.title: Rule 30 from a single cell contains every possible block
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: The pattern generated by the rule 30 cellular automaton from a single black cell appears to contain every possible block of cells eventually, so that essentially any possible computation exists somewhere within this single pattern.

claims.title: Complicated molecules generally do not reach minimum-energy configurations
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Although simple molecules may settle into minimum-energy configurations, complicated molecules typically do not; they explore configurations by an explicit evolution process, so nature does not actually solve hard constraint-satisfaction problems as traditional models idealize.

claims.title: Continuous systems cannot exceed discrete computation in practice
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Continuous systems, including analog computers, systems described by continuous equations, and even idealized perfectly continuous systems under reasonable assumptions, cannot perform computations fundamentally more sophisticated than discrete systems like cellular automata; continuity is largely an idealization.

claims.title: Equations with trigonometric functions can encode infinite computations
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Whereas solving pure polynomial equations allows no computation beyond that of ordinary discrete systems, once trigonometric functions are allowed one can construct equations whose solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of infinitely many steps of a system like a cellular automaton.

claims.title: Human thinking rests on rather simple computational processes
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: The basic mechanisms of human thinking will turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes, so human thought does not perform computations beyond the level allowed by the Principle of Computational Equivalence.

claims.title: No hidden regularity beyond repetition and nesting in rule-30-like systems
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: There is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems with complex behavior such as rule 30; beyond systems with obvious regularities like repetition and nesting, most systems are universal and computationally equivalent.

claims.title: Complexity arises because observers are computationally equivalent to systems
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Systems with simple rules appear complex because, once a low threshold is passed, their evolution is as computationally sophisticated as any process of perception or analysis used to study them, and this holds for any method of perception and analysis that can actually be used.

claims.title: Computational irreducibility blocks shortcuts to predicting behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: For computationally irreducible systems, even with complete knowledge of rules and initial conditions, there is no way to predict the behavior except by performing almost as many computational steps as the system's own evolution.

claims.title: Only obviously simple behavior is reducible; nearly all else is irreducible
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Behavior that is obviously simple, such as repetitive or nested behavior, is always computationally reducible, while in practically all other cases behavior is computationally irreducible.

claims.title: Traditional theoretical science fails where irreducibility is present
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Traditional theoretical science, including its use of mathematical formulas, relies on computational reducibility, which is the fundamental reason it has made little progress with systems whose behavior is not quite simple and why it has tended to restrict its domain to reducible phenomena.

claims.title: Many common systems can only be understood by explicit simulation
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Computer simulation is not merely a convenient substitute for mathematical formulas: there are many common systems whose behavior can be determined only by something like explicit simulation, and there can be no easy theory for almost any behavior that seems complex.

claims.title: Nested cellular automaton patterns can be computed in logarithmic time
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: For cellular automata with nested behavior such as elementary rules 60 and 188, the color of a cell after t steps can be found in about log2(t) steps from the base-2 digits of its position, rather than by tracing all t steps.

claims.title: Complex-looking yet computationally reducible systems are very rare
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Systems whose behavior looks complex but is nevertheless computationally reducible, such as the cellular automaton that generates digits of powers of 2, are very rare; in the vast majority of cases complex-looking behavior in nature and elsewhere is computationally irreducible.

claims.title: Apparent free will stems from irreducible brain computation
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: The apparent freedom of human will arises because, although brain components follow definite laws, the brain's overall behavior is an irreducible computation whose outcome cannot be found by reasonable laws; no external influence, chaos, or quantum randomness is needed.

claims.title: Undecidability shows up with very simple rules and initial conditions
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Undecidability has obvious effects even in a very simple system: in a 4-color totalistic cellular automaton (code 1004600) started from simple initial conditions, some patterns die out only after over a thousand steps while others are still growing after ten million steps with no indication of their final outcome.

claims.title: Infinite-time questions about complex systems are almost always undecidable
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: For almost any system whose behavior seems complex, almost any non-trivial question about its behavior after infinitely many steps (e.g. whether a pattern dies out, becomes repetitive, or ever produces a given arrangement) is undecidable, and such undecidability should be widespread in nature.

claims.title: Post Correspondence Problem with three pairs is likely undecidable
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Whether a set of upper/lower block pairs can be concatenated to give identical strings (the Post Correspondence Problem) is straightforward for two pairs, but already with three pairs there is computational irreducibility, making the question undecidable in general.

claims.title: Exhaustive search of 2-state 2-color Turing machines finds three growth rates
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Enumerating all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors shows that the maximum number of steps to finish a computation grows with input length only linearly, quadratically, or exponentially, and every exponential case has another such machine computing the same function in bounded steps.

claims.title: Some simple Turing machine computations require exponential effort
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Exhaustive search of all roughly 4 billion 4-state 2-color Turing machines shows certain computations by such machines cannot be sped up by any machine of that size, suggesting that some computations specified by very simple rules require effort growing exponentially with input length.

claims.title: Diverse computational systems emulate each other with comparable step counts
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Almost all the varied systems considered (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution and other systems) can emulate each other in a comparable number of steps, typically with at most polynomial overhead such as t^2 or t^(d+1), so rates of computation do not differ greatly across systems, including presumably thos

claims.title: P is likely different from NP
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: It is likely that in most meaningful senses there is no general way to determine whether any path of a multiway or non-deterministic system yields a given outcome in a number of steps growing only polynomially, i.e. P is not equal to NP.

claims.title: Inverse problems for rule 30 are likely NP-complete
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Even for the rule 30 cellular automaton, deciding whether initial conditions exist that produce a given outcome after t steps (such as a vertical black stripe of a given height in the center column) is expected to be NP-complete, illustrating that simple instances of NP-complete problems are common.

claims.title: Quantum computing's exponential speedups are likely an idealization artifact
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Although the usual formalism of quantum mechanics allows constructing quantum computers that could solve some problems exponentially faster than ordinary Turing machines, this will likely not reflect ultimate physical reality but only idealizations in current models.

claims.title: Inverse problems are exponentially harder than forward evolution
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: In almost any system whose behavior seems complex there is, in a fundamental sense, an almost exponential gap between the effort needed to compute behavior from given initial conditions and the effort needed to determine which initial conditions, if any, produce given behavior.

claims.title: Computational irreducibility makes short theorems with only long proofs inevitable
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Because the proof processes of almost every area of mathematics are computationally irreducible, adding axioms cannot remove the problem: there will essentially always be theorems that are short to state but whose shortest proofs are very long.

claims.title: An irreducible multiway system cannot be both complete and consistent
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: If questions about the long-run evolution of a multiway system (an idealized axiom system) are undecidable, then the system cannot be both complete and consistent, because completeness plus consistency would give a procedure that always terminates to decide whether a string is reached.

claims.title: Every axiom system used in current mathematical research is universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Basic logic and pure predicate logic are not universal, but adding a function or relation with more than one argument gives universality; arithmetic, set theory, group theory and ring theory are universal, and every axiom system actually used in current mathematical research is known to be universal, while heavily cons

claims.title: Beyond a low threshold almost every axiom system should be universal
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: The Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that, beyond a low threshold of complexity, almost any axiom system (including very simple ones) should be universal, and so should exhibit undecidability and have no general upper limit on proof length.

claims.title: Gödel's Theorem follows from the universality of arithmetic, shown via rule 110
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: An integer (exponential Diophantine) equation can be built whose solutions emulate the rule 110 cellular automaton; since rule 110 is universal, the axioms of arithmetic support universality, which implies Gödel's Theorem that arithmetic contains statements that cannot be proved true or false. Wolfram presents Gödel's

claims.title: Simple integer equations should exist whose lack of solutions is unprovable
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Although known universal integer equations are very complicated (the simplest having 9 variables and an immense number of terms), there should be much simpler integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the standard axioms of arithmetic.

claims.title: Many open number-theory problems may be unprovable from arithmetic's axioms
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: A fair fraction of the unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory will turn out to be questions that cannot be answered using the standard axioms of arithmetic.

claims.title: Undecidability appears in almost any area of mathematics beyond easy questions
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Undecidability and unprovability will begin to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond questions that are always easy to answer, as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.

claims.title: Mathematics avoids undecidability by choosing questions its methods can answer
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Undecidability and unprovability have seemed rare in mathematics because mathematics, shaped by its history, has defined itself around the questions and systems that proof-based methods can address, concentrating on limited patches of computational reducibility; so present-day mathematics is a small and uncharacteristi

claims.title: Complete and consistent means exactly half of all strings are generated
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: For a multiway system serving as an axiom system, with negation any length-preserving involution on strings, the system is complete and consistent exactly when half of all possible strings of each length are eventually generated from the string representing true; more than half implies inconsistency and less than half

claims.title: Axiom systems used in mathematics are usually close to complete
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: The axiom systems widely used in mathematics, though usually incomplete, are typically close to complete, because they were built to describe definite kinds of objects; as a result, the alternative objects (nonstandard models) that also satisfy them, such as those for standard arithmetic, differ only in obscure ways.

claims.title: Most simple axiom systems admit many different operator forms
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Enumerating simple axiom systems for a binary operator shows that the vast majority allow operators of many different forms (many models), so they are not about any one particular operator and are far from complete; only a few, such as those for logic, force essentially a single form.

claims.title: Very short single-axiom systems for logic exist among the simplest axiom systems
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Propositional logic can be axiomatized in terms of Nand by a single axiom with only six Nands (found by searching small axiom systems), far shorter than textbook systems, so an axiom system for logic is likely to be found among the simplest few thousand axiom systems.

claims.title: Traditional axiom systems are not fundamentally special; others could found new fields
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Apart from history, nothing fundamentally distinguishes the axiom systems traditionally used in mathematics (logic included), and many other axiom systems, often simple ones, could serve as foundations for new fields of mathematics as rich as the traditional ones.

claims.title: Named textbook theorems of logic are those not derivable from simpler ones
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: If the theorems of basic logic are listed in order of increasing complexity, the ones that cannot be derived from simpler theorems earlier in the list are almost exactly the ones traditional textbooks single out and name as interesting.

claims.title: Judgments like deep or powerful reflect the structure of the theorem network
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Mathematicians' intuitive descriptions of theorems (difficult, powerful, surprising, deep) reflect features of the network of statements connected by theorems, and fields regarded as more successful should have more compact networks while fields full of isolated facts, such as elementary number theory, should have spar

claims.title: No general definition of intelligence independent of human details
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: General features proposed as marks of intelligence (learning and memory, adaptation, abstraction) occur in systems such as simple cellular automata and fluids, so there is no workable general definition of intelligence; any usable one must be tied to specific details of human intelligence.

claims.title: Proposed general features of life occur in many simple-rule systems
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Almost any general feature proposed to characterize life, including self-organization, self-reproduction and complexity, occurs even in many systems with very simple rules, so life can only be recognized by specific shared details with life on Earth.

claims.title: Human artifacts look simple because engineering requires predictability
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Human-made artifacts tend to look simpler than natural objects because engineers need to foresee what their systems will do, which requires computational reducibility, whereas nature has no such constraint and many natural systems are computationally irreducible.

claims.title: A minimal rule for a feature hints that a system was made for a purpose
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Since purposes can always be reinterpreted as mechanisms, purpose cannot be identified for certain from behavior; the best criterion is that a system is the minimal or optimal one producing a given feature, which suggests it was built for that purpose, as advanced technology should increasingly use minimal systems.

claims.title: Efficient extraterrestrial communications would show no detectable regularities
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.title: Sophisticated computation, or primes, are not signs of intelligence
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Producing a signal by sophisticated computation is no evidence of intelligence, because such computation is common in ordinary physical processes; for instance, turbulence in the gas around a star quickly does more computation than all of human intellectual history, and sequences such as the primes can be generated by

claims.title: Recognizing extraterrestrial intelligence depends on similarity to humans
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: The difficulty in finding extraterrestrial intelligence is not finding systems that compute in sophisticated ways, which are common, but finding ones whose details are similar enough to humans that we would recognize them as intelligent; somewhat generalized intelligence is likely to exist but to behave in bizarrely un

claims.title: Engineering has explored only a tiny unrepresentative fraction of possible systems
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Traditional engineering has used only a tiny and unrepresentative fraction of possible systems and processes, those simple enough to predict, and using simple-rule systems with complex behavior will make a vast amount of new technology possible.

claims.title: Simple universal rules like rule 110 could be built into computers from atoms
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Since very simple rules such as the rule 110 cellular automaton are universal, computers could be built from many kinds of components, and a simple chemical process could plausibly assemble a rule 110-like computer at the atomic scale, with one or a few atoms per cell.

claims.title: Exhaustive search is the only reliable way to find programs with given behavior
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: Because simple programs can do so many unexpected things, and computational irreducibility can make finding a behavior take irreducible work, the only reliable way to find a simple program with a desired behavior is essentially exhaustive search, so building a library of basic knowledge about simple programs is a bette

claims.title: Humans are not computationally more sophisticated than other systems in nature
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: By the Principle of Computational Equivalence, human brains, turbulent fluids, simple cellular automata and the universe as a whole all achieve the same level of computational sophistication, so humans are not fundamentally special in intelligence or complexity.

claims.title: Computational irreducibility puts permanent limits on scientific prediction
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence
claims.statement: The Principle of Computational Equivalence and computational irreducibility show that science will never predict everything: even if the universe follows simple rules, there is in general no way to know all their consequences except by watching them unfold.

claims.title: Self-assembly emerges from cells sharing a common model of organismal form

claims.statement: In simulations based on variational free-energy minimization (active inference), cells that share a common genetically and epigenetically specified model of the organism's form self-assemble into that form, offering a proof of principle that self-assembly can be an emergent property of such cells.

claims.statement: Under the free-energy account of morphogenesis, genetic codes can be interpreted as parametrizing a generative model that predicts the signals each cell would sense in the target morphology, and epigenetic processes (signalling-dependent transcription) as the inversion of that model.

claims.title: Free energy is minimized only when every cell occupies a unique inferred place
claims.chapter: Friston K 2015, Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation › Introduction
claims.statement: In the active-inference model of morphogenesis, where identical pluripotent cells share one generative model, the minimum of variational free energy is reached only when every cell is at a unique location and has correctly inferred its place, so free-energy minimization guarantees convergence to the target form.
